title: Pope Leo begins South American visit in Uruguay less than a month after lung surgery
summary: Pope Leo XIV has arrived in Uruguay to start a three-nation tour of South America
story: Pope Leo XIV has arrived in Uruguay to start a three-nation tour of South America

MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay -- MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay (AP) — Pope Leo XIV arrived in Uruguay on Friday to begin a three-nation South American tour, less than a month after lung surgery and eight years after a pope last visited the continent.

The pontiff landed in Montevideo after a nearly 14-hour flight from Rome. It is the first papal visit in nearly four decades to Uruguay, Latin America’s most secular country; Pope John Paul II last visited in 1988.

Uruguay separated church and state more than a century ago, and the government still officially calls Christmas “Family Day” and Holy Week “Tourism Week.” Over the church’s objections, it was among the first countries in the region to legalize abortion and same-sex marriage.

After Uruguay, Leo will travel to Argentina, the homeland of the late Pope Francis, who never visited during his 12-year papacy. His last stop is Peru, where Leo holds citizenship and spent two decades as a missionary and bishop.
THIS IS A BREAKING NEWS UPDATE. Check back for updates. AP’s earlier story follows below.

MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay (AP) — Pope Leo XIV is kicking off a three-nation tour of Latin America on Friday with a visit to Uruguay, the region’s least Catholic and most secular country, three weeks after undergoing lung cancer surgery that had put the entire trip into question.

Leo is due to arrive in Montevideo after a 13½-hour flight from Rome. He has a packed three-day itinerary in Uruguay including a visit to a neighborhood plagued by gang violence, a Mass in Paysandú, around 375 kilometers (230 miles) from the capital, and another Mass in the city of Florida, about 100 kilometers (60 miles) from Montevideo.

The atmosphere at the airport before Leo’s arrival was calm and unhurried, much like the rest of Uruguay’s capital. Gradually, however, people began gathering at Plaza Independencia, one of the country’s most prominent public spaces and the site of Leo's first public event.

“It’s definitely a major event, which is great, even though I’m not a believer myself. It’s wonderful to see so many people coming together,” said musician Diego Vázquez, 28. “I think it’s a lovely initiative that has also put Uruguay, to some extent, in the eyes of the world.”

The Uruguay leg is the first stop on what will be the longest and farthest trip of his pontificate, all being undertaken as the 71-year-old pope continues his recovery. The trip will also bring him to neighboring Argentina and finally back home to Peru, where Leo served as a missionary priest and bishop for two decades.

“His stamina is fantastic. The way that he's singing is incredible. And you can only sing if your lungs are really strong,” said María Montserrat Alvarado, the Vatican's new communications chief. She noted that Leo has passed the 14-day convalescence period required by doctors after his Oct. 13 surgery and is eager to get on the road.
“His doctors are very confident and he'll have plenty of medical care on board should something happen, but we don't see that in his prognosis or even in the way that he's acting,” she said.

In Uruguay, which hasn’t had a papal visit since 1988, Leo is expected to try to remind the 3.5 million people of their strong Catholic heritage stemming from the times of Spanish colonial rule. He's likely to propose the faith anew as an answer to today’s challenges and problems.

Upon arrival, Leo will meet with President Yamandú Orsi, leader of the center-left alliance that assumed power in March 2025, and then deliver his welcome address to government officials and diplomats. He finishes the long day with a vespers service at the city's cathedral.

Leo will find in Uruguay a country unlike any other in Latin America, which is home to around 40% of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics. Uruguay is considered the most secular country in the region, where only a fraction of people who identify as Catholic actually go to Mass regularly.

Uruguay’s secularism has roots in the weakness of its colonial church. With no gold or silver to mine, Spain valued the land of cattle ranches mainly as a buffer against Portuguese Brazil and left it largely unsettled. Montevideo was founded only in the 1720s, roughly two centuries after Mexico City and Lima.

With few priests and no local bishop, the church never became the powerful institution it was elsewhere in the empire. “Uruguay was colonized late, and that made Catholicism weaker,” said Gerardo Caetano, a Uruguayan historian.

Montevideo awoke to its usual calm. Along the waterfront, joggers were out for their morning runs and residents walked their dogs along the very same promenade that the pope is set to visit just a few hours later.

“We still don’t understand why he chose Uruguay, given that it’s a secular country, but we hope he leaves something positive behind," said Mary Fernández while drinking mate, Uruguay's beloved beverage.

The origins of the separation between church and state can be traced back to the 19th century, particularly to the spread of liberal ideas promoted by European intellectuals, who viewed religion as a symptom of backwardness or a lack of rationality, said Luis Bahamondes, a professor at the Center for Judaic Studies at the University of Chile.

“While Latin America also experienced a separation of church and state, the Catholic Church has nonetheless maintained strong ties with the various states in the region,” he said. “In this context, Uruguay stands out as a paradigmatic example of how secularism can be implemented.”

This process went so far as to include the renaming of certain holidays to reflect their secular character — such as “Family Day” and “Tourism Week” — signaling that the “inherent weight of Catholicism had no place within the State’s official framework,” Bahamondes added.

Since then, Uruguay has become the first country in the world to legalize marijuana for recreational use, the second country in Latin America to decriminalize abortion, and the third country in the Americas to legalize same-sex marriage.
More recently, it became the first country in the region to approve assisted dying legislation despite the strong opposition of the Catholic Church.

Uruguayan church officials have marveled at the apparent enthusiasm that the visit has provoked, with reports that tickets to Leo’s prayer vigil at Montevideo’s Centenario Stadium were snapped up after two days.

“It seems that the pope’s presence is shifting something here and is gradually breaking down this veil that has always sought to obscure and diminish the presence of the Catholic tradition that lies at the country’s foundation,” said Guzmán Carriquiry, the Uruguayan former head of the Vatican’s pontifical commission for Latin America.
Carriquiry said that he expects Leo will seek to revive the Catholic roots of Uruguay, especially when he travels to the city of Florida on Sunday to mark an important Catholic feast day.

The Nov. 8 feast commemorates the Virgin of the Thirty-three, a small wooden icon of the Virgin Mary that is intricately connected to Uruguay’s independence movement. According to tradition, 33 independence patriots acquired the Guaraní statue and had it with them when independence was declared from the Brazilian empire in Florida on Aug. 25, 1825.

“So the number 33 is an ecclesiastical symbol, a national symbol,” said Carriquiry. “And so the pope will speak there about the Catholic tradition that lies at the origin of Uruguay — that stems from Uruguay and gave rise to Uruguay — in order to revive and renew the Catholic tradition in the hearts of Uruguayans.”

Andrew Chesnut, chair of Catholic studies and an expert in the Latin American church at Virginia Commonwealth University, said that he wasn’t surprised that Leo’s visit had generated enthusiasm and that he will be welcomed warmly.

“But that’s not necessarily going to translate into folks in the pews,” he said. “If the overarching goal is trying to revitalize Catholicism in the most Catholic region on Earth, Uruguay is kind of a lost cause, and it has been for decades.”
Nayara Batschke contributed from Montevideo, Uruguay.

title: Shorter days and dark afternoons can trigger depression. Here's how to fight back
summary: People prone to seasonal depression are bracing themselves as winter approaches
story: People prone to seasonal depression are bracing themselves as winter approaches
As winter approaches and daylight hours grow shorter, people prone to seasonal depression can feel it in their bodies and brains.

The millions of people estimated to have seasonal affective disorder, or SAD, typically have episodes of depression that begin in the fall and ease in the spring or summer. One trigger for SAD is when clocks revert to standard time, which happened Sunday across much of the U.S., bringing darker afternoons. A milder form, subsyndromal SAD, is recognized by medical experts, and there’s also a summer variety of seasonal depression, though less is known about it.

In 1984, a team led by Dr. Norman Rosenthal, then a researcher at the National Institutes of Health, first described SAD and coined the term. “I believe that because it is easy to remember, the acronym has stuck,” he said.

No single cause for seasonal affective disorder has been identified. The disorder affects many more women than men, according to the NIH. Symptoms can be similar to depression, and can include persistent feelings of hopelessness or pessimism and difficulty concentrating, remembering, or making decisions.

In one effort to better understand what's going on, scientists are learning how specialized cells in our eyes turn the blue wavelength part of the light spectrum into neural signals affecting mood and alertness.
Sunlight is loaded with the blue light, so when the cells absorb it, our brains’ alertness centers are activated and we feel more wakeful and possibly even happier.

Researcher Kathryn Roecklein at the University of Pittsburgh tested people with and without SAD to see how their eyes reacted to blue light. As a group, people with SAD were less sensitive to blue light than others, especially during winter months. That suggests one possible cause for wintertime depression.

Many people with SAD respond to light therapy, said Dr. Paul Desan of Yale University’s Winter Depression Research Clinic. The therapy can involve exposure to bright light for about a half hour in the morning, powered by devices that emit light about 20 times brighter than regular indoor light.

Research supports using a light that’s about 10,000 lux, a measure of brightness. You need to use it for 30 minutes every morning, according to the research. Desan said this can help not only people with SAD but also those with less-severe winter blahs.
Special lights run from $50 to more than $400. Some products marketed for SAD are too dim to do much good, Desan said.
Yale has tested products and offers a list of recommendations, and the nonprofit Center for Environmental Therapeutics has a consumer guide to selecting a light.
If your doctor diagnosed you with SAD, check with your insurance company to see if the cost of a light might be covered.
Antidepressant medications are a first-line treatment for SAD, along with light therapy. Doctors also recommend keeping a regular sleep schedule and walking outside, even on cloudy days.

Light therapy’s benefits can fade when people stop using it. One type of talk therapy — cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT — has been shown in studies to have more durable effects, University of Vermont researcher Kelly Rohan said.
CBT involves working with a therapist to identify and modify unhelpful thoughts.

Working with a therapist can help people take small steps toward having fun again, Rohan said. Try planning undemanding but enjoyable activities to break out of hibernation mode, including getting out and seeing a friend for coffee.
Carla K. Johnson, the principal writer of this story, retired from The Associated Press in 2025.

title: Cyberattack hits French blood bank site but no blood products were compromised
summary: French authorities have reported a cyberattack on several blood banks that attempted to raise temperatures to dangerous levels
story: French authorities have reported a cyberattack on several blood banks that attempted to raise temperatures to dangerous levels

PARIS -- A cyberattack on several blood banks sought to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but was thwarted before it could do any damage to blood products or samples, French authorities said.

The incident comes after supermarkets in a number of European countries reported this week that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars (euros).

The French Blood Establishment, or EFS, said “temperature and defrosting thresholds were raised to extremely high levels” on Monday at three of its cold-storage sites for plasma, in a statement released late Tuesday.
“No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost,” it said. The cyberattack hit a supplier of refrigeration equipment at three EFS sites.
The products stored were bags of plasma intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines, and were either transferred or secured, the statement said.
“Monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the anomalies, allowing staff to take action to ensure that no blood products or samples were compromised,” it said.
The EFS said blood collection and distribution operations remain uninterrupted, ensuring continued services for patients at hospitals and other healthcare.
France’s national cybersecurity agency and the Health Ministry are investigating the incident.

title: Indonesia's vice president offers resignation as questions mount over his eligibility
summary: Indonesia’s Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has offered to resign amid mounting pressure over his academic credentials, officials say
story: Indonesia’s Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has offered to resign amid mounting pressure over his academic credentials, officials say

JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Indonesia's vice president offered to resign during a meeting with President Prabowo Subianto on Tuesday, according to officials, adding to the turmoil at the highest levels of the country's leadership.
Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, held over two hours of talks with Prabowo, according to State Secretariat Minister Prasetyo Hadi.

It was not immediately clear whether Prabowo accepted the resignation, Hadi told reporters at a news conference at the presidential palace. The president advised Raka to “continue pursuing legal avenues to defend the validity of his academic documents,” Hadi said.
As he left his office later in the day, Raka made a brief statement to reporters without addressing the resignation offer.
“I respect all criticism and feedback from the public regarding the developments that are taking place,” Raka said. “I do not want the current situation to become a prolonged political controversy.”

The resignation offer comes amid growing pressure on Raka over a court dispute involving his academic credentials. It was apparently not related to an ongoing probe into allegations that top police officials, including the president's chief of staff Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo, had been involved in a wiretap targeting the president. Three other police generals have also been implicated in the case.
Listyo previously served as national police chief under Widodo, who has not been implicated in the wiretapping investigation.
The developments come amid a widening political rift between Prabowo and Widodo. The popular former president backed Prabowo's presidential bid after he chose Raka as a running mate.

The controversy over Raka's academic qualifications escalated last month after the Supreme Court ruled that the documents he submitted regarding his overseas education did not meet election requirements.
The ruling intensified political pressure on Raka and fueled calls from some lawmakers for his impeachment.
Widodo faces unrelated allegations that he used a fake university diploma, which he denies.

title: Rwandan man in the US sent back home to face genocide charges
summary: A Rwandan man suspected of participating in the country’s 1994 genocide was deported from the United States and is due to stand trial for his alleged crimes, according to local authorities
story: A Rwandan man suspected of participating in the country’s 1994 genocide was deported from the United States and is due to stand trial for his alleged crimes, according to local authorities

KIGALI, Rwanda -- A Rwandan man suspected of participating in the country’s 1994 genocide has been deported from the United States and will stand trial for his alleged crimes, according to local authorities.
Jean ​Léonard Teganya, who arrived in the East African nation on Monday, faces charges related to genocide, said Justin Nkusi, a spokesperson for the prosecution.
Teganya is currently being interrogated by police before prosecutors receive his file, Nkusi said.

Teganya, 55, was indicted in 2014 over his alleged involvement in genocidal crimes in several areas in the district of Huye, in Rwanda's south. Rwandan authorities say he allegedly committed some of his crimes at a university campus and a medical school in Huye.

The 2014 indictment triggered an investigation into Teganya's presence in the U.S., with Rwanda seeking his deportation. At the time, Teganya denied playing a part in the genocide, in which an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed by extremist Hutus.

Teganya fled Rwanda in July 1994 and later sought asylum in Canada. According to the U.S. Justice Department, he evaded a Canadian deportation order and crossed into the U.S. in 2014. In 2019 a federal jury in Boston found that Teganya had committed immigration fraud and perjury after seeking asylum in the U.S.
One survivor of the genocide told The Associated Press in Kigali, the Rwandan capital, that she welcomed the decision to send Teganya home to face justice.
“Genocide crime and crimes against humanity are never time-barred and perpetrators will be hunted, arrested, deported and prosecuted," said Yolande Mukakasana.
“As survivors, we remain hopeful that justice will be done no matter how much time has passed.”

title: 5 Cambodian schoolgirls killed as a bus skids off a road into a pond
summary: Five girls died Tuesday morning in Cambodia when a school bus veered off the road and plunged into a pond
story: Five girls died Tuesday morning in Cambodia when a school bus veered off the road and plunged into a pond
KHSACH KANDAL, Cambodia -- Five girls died on Tuesday morning in Cambodia when a bus taking them to school veered off the road and plunged into a deep pond, police said.

The crash took place in Kandal province, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) north of the capital, Phnom Penh, said a statement posted on Facebook by the provincial police. It said witnesses reported that a motorcycle suddenly crossed in front of the fast-moving bus, causing its driver to slam on the brakes and making the vehicle skid into the roadside water.

Video posted on social media showed the bus sank just a few feet from shore, but deep enough to make escape very difficult, even with assistance from villagers who rushed to try to pull the children out. The rescuers performed CPR on some of the children they extricated, said Sun Kunthy, one of those who rushed to help.
It said 26 students, aged 12 to 14, were on the bus. In addition to the five who died, three others were in critical condition and 18 were lightly injured.
Police detained the 31-year-old driver for questioning.

Nov Sokhon, chief traffic police of Khsach Kandal district, said all five girls died by drowning. He added that the death toll could have been even higher if the local residents had not rescued them in time.
According to a report by the National Police released in early November, traffic accidents across Cambodia killed more than 1,300 people in the first 10 months of this year.
A separate report from the Transport Ministry said that 1,467 people were killed in traffic accidents in 2025, making it by far the leading cause of accidental deaths in the Southeast Asian nation.

In May this year, two accidents in a single day killed at least 14 garment factory workers and injured 79 others, mostly women. They were on flatbed trucks, the usual method of transportation available for workers. The vehicles often lack seats or benches, forcing passengers to stand and significantly increasing the risk of injury or death in a crash.

title: Malaysian high court clears final hurdle for former Prime Minister Najib's transfer to house arrest
summary: A high court in Malaysia has cleared all legal hurdles for former Prime Minister Najib Razak to serve the rest of his graft sentence under house arrest
story: A high court in Malaysia has cleared all legal hurdles for former Prime Minister Najib Razak to serve the rest of his graft sentence under house arrest

KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia -- A high court in Malaysia on Tuesday cleared all legal hurdles for the transfer of imprisoned former Prime Minister Najib Razak to his home to serve the remainder of his graft sentence under house arrest, his lawyer said.

Najib has been behind bars since August 2022, when the Kuala Lumpur High Court upheld his graft conviction linked to a multibillion-dollar looting of the state investment fund 1MDB. In September, Najib was granted royal clemency, allowing him to serve the rest of his sentence under house arrest once he pays a court-imposed fine.

Last Friday, he left prison after his political party paid the 50 million ringgit ($12.3 million) fine but he was brought back hours later after the attorney general blocked the transfer, seeking legal clarifications.

The attorney general's request sparked a public rebuke from the palace, which said that King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar’s prerogative of pardon for Najib that allowed the house arrest was clear and must be respected. It said any attempts to challenge it would amount to defying the royal order.
Najib's lawyer Muhammad Shafee Abdullah said Tuesday all was settled for the former prime minister's transfer to house arrest at his Kuala Lumpur home, where he is to remain until Aug. 23, 2028.
Najib appeared in court on Tuesday; the transfer was expected to take place later in the day. Police later sealed off the road leading to his home.
“It’s a final relief, you know, great sigh to him because he has been waiting for this,” the lawyer said.

The house arrest covers only Najib's reduced, six-year sentence in his first trial for graft and not a separate, 15-year sentence handed down last December for corruption and money laundering. That sentence followed a second major trial tied to the 1MDB scandal.
Najib is also appealing that sentence, which he is to serve after the end of his first sentence. If his appeal fails, he could return to prison after his house arrest ends.

Najib, who served as prime minister from 2009 to 2018, has denied any wrongdoing. He is Malaysia’s first former leader to be imprisoned under a sentence related to the 1MDB scandal. It marked one of the world’s largest financial scandals, rippling across global markets and triggering investigations in the United States and other countries.

title: At least 12 people killed in crashes on a foggy Bulgarian motorway, minister says
summary: A thick fog on a motorway in eastern Bulgaria caused a string of vehicle crashes that killed at least 12 people and injured dozens
story: A thick fog on a motorway in eastern Bulgaria caused a string of vehicle crashes that killed at least 12 people and injured dozens
SOFIA, Bulgaria -- A thick fog on a motorway in eastern Bulgaria caused a string of vehicle crashes that killed at least 12 people and injured dozens on Tuesday, a government minister said.

Dense fog on the motorway linking the capital Sofia with the Black Sea port of Burgas led to two pileups. The accidents forced the closure of the road in both directions, Health Minister Katya Ivkova said.
Ivkova said 10 people “died on the spot” and two others died while being transported to a hospital.
She said 46 people were transported to medical facilities for treatment.

title: Myanmar army seizes key resistance HQ and bases held by opposition, state media says
summary: Myanmar’s military has seized a key resistance command headquarters and 10 other bases in the country’s southern region
story: Myanmar’s military has seized a key resistance command headquarters and 10 other bases in the country’s southern region

BANGKOK -- Myanmar’s military has seized a key resistance military command headquarters and 10 other bases in the south of the country, state media reported Tuesday, marking a new gain by the army in the civil war as it seeks control of regions long held by resistance forces.
The capture of the bases in the jungle along the border between Mon state and the Bago region marks the latest setback suffered by pro-democracy armed groups and ethnic militias fighting the army.
The reported capture could not be independently confirmed because the military does not allow journalists free access to the area, but the claim has not been challenged.

The military-backed government, which took office in April following controversial elections earlier this year, has stepped up activity in recent months on the ground and with airstrikes to retake areas controlled by the People’s Defense Force, the armed wing of the major opposition National Unity Government, and ethnic militias that have been fighting the central government for greater autonomy for decades.
The PDF emerged after the army seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in February 2021 and has since formed loose alliances with ethnic militias fighting the military.

A report in the state-run Myanma Alinn newspaper on Tuesday said the army captured 11 bases operating in the jungle area straddling the border between Mon and Bago during a six-day operation that began a week ago.

The captured positions included the special region command headquarters of the NUG and a battalion headquarters of the Karen National Liberation Army, the armed wing of the Karen National Union, a major Karen ethnic rebel group.
The paper published photos showing soldiers who captured the bases alongside ammunition seized during the operation.
Small arms, ammunition supplies, vehicles, drones and computers were captured after four armed engagements, the report said, adding that the military would continue security operations in the region.
The NUG and KNU did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The captured regions, about 120 kilometers (75 miles) northeast of Yangon, the country’s largest city, have seen intense conflict since the 2021 military takeover that prompted widespread public protests. The violent suppression of the demonstrations by government security forces triggered an armed resistance that has led to civil war.

The NUG’s special region command headquarters said in a previous social media statement that it had 12 PDF battalions, seven drones with specialized support units, as well as six combat and defense units under its command. It also said it was conducting military operations across the southern Kayin and Mon states, as well as the Bago region. Kayin state is also known as Karen state.

In another statement at the end of September, the NUG headquarters said its communications outpost had been hit by airstrikes involving two fighter jets, killing five members of its force, including a former soldier who had defected.

title: Past talks involving Russia and Ukraine have yielded little progress toward peace
summary: Negotiators from Moscow, Kyiv and Washington are scheduled to meet in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, on Tuesday and Wednesday for talks aimed at trying to end Russia's 4 1/2-year-old full-scale invasion of Ukraine
story: Negotiators from Moscow, Kyiv and Washington are scheduled to meet in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, on Tuesday and Wednesday for talks aimed at trying to end Russia's 4 1/2-year-old full-scale invasion of Ukraine
Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, in the latest bid to end the war.
Key developments from past sessions since Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor on Feb. 24, 2022:

Feb. 28, 2022: Ukrainian and Russian delegations meet in neighboring Belarus for the first time after the invasion. Talks continue for two weeks, deciding only on humanitarian corridors for evacuating civilians.
March 10, 2022: Russian and Ukrainian Foreign Ministers Sergey Lavrov and Dmytro Kuleba meet in Antalya, Turkey.
March 21, 2022: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy calls for direct talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, an idea rebuffed by Lavrov.

March 28-30, 2022: Delegations meet in Istanbul to work on a draft peace agreement. Moscow says it's willing to “fundamentally cut back” military activity near Kyiv and the northern city of Chernihiv; Ukraine says it's open to discussing neutral status for Ukraine if its security is backed by other nations.

April 7, 2022: Lavrov rejects a Ukrainian proposal as “unacceptable," saying Kyiv has walked back on an agreement to exempt the Crimean Peninsula from wider Ukrainian security guarantees. Russia illegally annexed Crimea in 2014.
April 26, 2022: U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres visits Russia to discuss ending the war.
May 13, 2022: U.S. Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin calls his Russian counterpart, their first contact since war began.
July 22, 2022: Russia and Ukraine, with mediation by Turkey and the U.N., agree to unblock grain supplies stuck in Ukraine’s Black Sea ports. Russia withdraws from the deal a year later.

Sept. 30, 2022: Russia illegally annexes the Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, even though it doesn’t fully control any of them. Ukraine responds by applying to join NATO and by enacting a decree that declares negotiations with Putin “impossible.”
Nov. 15, 2022: Zelenskyy unveils a 10-point peace plan at the G20 summit in Indonesia.
June 16-17, 2023: African leaders travel to Kyiv and St. Petersburg on a peace mission, without success.

June 25, 2023: Officials from 15 countries, including the U.S., India, Brazil, South Africa, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and several representatives from the European Union, meet in Copenhagen, Denmark, to discuss Zelenskyy’s peace plan.

Aug. 5-6, 2023: Two days of discussions on the war begin in Saudi Arabia with delegates from 40 countries, including China, India, South Africa and Brazil, but not Russia. No joint statements are issued.

Oct. 28-29, 2023: Delegates from 65 countries meet in Malta to continue talks on Zelenskyy’s peace plan. Russia, which dismissed the talks, was not invited. China, though invited, did not participate.

June 15-16, 2024: Representatives of 92 nations meet in Nidwalden, Switzerland, to discuss Ukraine’s peace plan, but a consensus remains elusive. The summit’s final statement is backed by most — but not all — participants.
Dec. 7, 2024: U.S. President-elect Donald Trump travels to Paris and meets Zelenskyy and other European leaders.
Feb. 12, 2025: Trump and Putin speak directly via telephone and agree to begin negotiations on ending the war. The conversation ends a three-year U.S.-led effort to isolate Putin.

Feb. 18, 2025: Russian and U.S. officials, including Lavrov and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meet in Saudi Arabia and agree to work toward ending the war, as well as restoring bilateral ties. Ukrainian officials are not invited.
Feb. 28, 2025: Zelenskyy holds a contentious meeting with Trump, Rubio and Vice President JD Vance in the White House. A proposed minerals deal between the countries is left unsigned.
March 11, 2025: U.S. and Ukrainian officials meet in Saudi Arabia, with Americans proposing a plan for a 30-day ceasefire. Kyiv agrees to the proposed truce.

March 13, 2025: Putin effectively rejects the ceasefire plan, stating certain issues still must be resolved. He also meets with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in Moscow. Witkoff travels to Russia twice more in April to meet Putin.
March 23-24, 2025: The U.S. holds separate talks with each side in Saudi Arabia. The White House says they agreed to a Black Sea truce.

May 16, 2025: Russia and Ukraine meet directly in Istanbul, under Turkish mediation, for the first time in three years and agree to swap 1,000 prisoners from each side. Ukraine's delegation was led by Defense Minister Rustem Umerov, while Russia's was headed by Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky.
June 2 and July 23, 2025: Two more rounds of talks between Russia and Ukraine in Istanbul produce an exchange of draft memorandums.

Aug. 15, 2025: Trump and Putin meet in Anchorage, Alaska. The summit produces no concrete peace agreement, ceasefire deal, or specific resolution on the war in Ukraine. International observers widely view it as a symbolic boost for Moscow.
Aug. 18, 2025: Trump hosts Zelenskyy and European leaders at the White House. Discussions center on establishing robust security guarantees for Ukraine.

November 2025: A 28-point U.S.-Russian peace plan emerges, and critics say it favors Moscow. On Nov. 23, it's cut to 19 points during discussions involving Washington, Kyiv and Ukraine’s European allies in Geneva.

Dec. 2, 2025: Putin, his adviser Yuri Ushakov and Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev meet Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner in Moscow. Ushakov describes the meeting as constructive but says much work remains.
Dec. 4-6, 2025: Witkoff and Kushner meet a Ukrainian delegation headed by Umerov and Chief of General Staff Gen. Andriy Hnatov in Miami.

Dec. 14-15, 2025: Ukrainian officials, including Zelenskyy, travel to Berlin for talks with Witkoff and Kushner. U.S. officials say Washington agrees to provide Kyiv with unspecified security guarantees.
Dec. 20-21, 2025: Dmitriev holds talks with Witkoff and Kushner in Miami. The Americans meet separately with a Ukrainian delegation.
Dec. 28, 2025: Zelenskyy meets in Florida with Trump, who calls Putin beforehand.

Jan. 6-7, 2026: Zelenskyy and other Ukrainians attend a summit of the “Coalition of the Willing” in Paris and hold talks with Witkoff and Kushner. Kyiv’s allies tout major progress for defending Ukraine if a peace deal is struck, saying they were ready to provide international guarantees to deter Russia from attacking again.
Jan. 17, 2026: A Ukrainian delegation arrives in the U.S. for talks.

Jan. 20-22, 2026: Witkoff and Kushner meet separately in Davos, Switzerland, with Ukrainian and Russian delegations. Zelenskyy then meets Trump for what the U.S. leader calls “very good” talks. Zelenskyy calls them “productive and meaningful.”
Jan. 23-24, 2026: Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. delegates meet in Abu Dhabi in the first known instance of Trump administration officials sitting down with both countries to try to halt the war.
Feb. 4-5, 2026: A second round of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi leads to swapping 157 prisoners from each side.
Feb. 17-18, 2026: The third round of trilateral negotiations in Geneva, Switzerland, ends without a breakthrough.
Feb. 28, 2026: The U.S. and Israel begin a war with Iran, leading the Trump administration to wind down talks with Russian and Ukrainian officials.
May 7, 2026: Umerov meets in Miami with U.S. officials, as negotiations remain stalled.
Sept. 5-6, 2026: Witkoff and Kushner meet Putin in Moscow on Sept. 5, and in Kyiv with Zelenskyy the next day.
Oct. 21, 2026: Ushakov says Putin agrees “in principle” with Witkoff to resume talks after Nov. 10.

Oct. 27-Nov. 1, 2026: After intervention by U.S. first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, a localized ceasefire is reached for the region around the Russia-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine to allow the evacuation of some of its residents and the delivery of food and other supplies.

title: G7 attention turns to Ukraine while US-mediated talks get underway in Abu Dhabi
summary: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his counterparts from the Group of 7 developed democracies are turning their attention toward Ukraine and how to support it in its struggle to defend itself from Russia
story: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his counterparts from the Group of 7 developed democracies are turning their attention toward Ukraine and how to support it in its struggle to defend itself from Russia

PARIS -- U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his counterparts from the Group of 7 developed democracies are turning their attention toward Ukraine and how to support it in its struggle to defend itself from Russia. As three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States get underway in the United Arab Emirates, top G7 diplomats are meeting Tuesday with Ukraine’s foreign minister in France.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha will start his day in Paris in talks with Rubio before heading to the French foreign ministry for a larger group meeting with the entire G7. They will discuss defense and security assistance to Ukraine, which President Donald Trump's administration has reduced, causing consternation not only in Kyiv but in capitals across Europe, the largest of which — Paris, Berlin, Rome and London — are G7 members.
It was not immediately clear if the U.S. or any of its G7 partners would announce any new assistance for Ukraine.

Meanwhile in Abu Dhabi, Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will be meeting Russian and Ukrainian officials in part to persuade Moscow to agree to broader negotiations that would include key European officials on how to end nearly five years of war.

In Paris, Europeans have been clamoring for a seat at the table in Abu Dhabi, but two U.S. officials said Monday that representatives from Britain, Germany, France, NATO and the European Union would not join the main talks but rather discuss potential security guarantees and the long-term security architecture between Russia and Europe beforehand.

Russia has resisted European participation in negotiations and insisted the talks should proceed strictly as a trilateral format involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States. The three last held talks in February.
But on Monday in Paris, German Foreign Minister Johan Wadephul, who met separately with Rubio on the sidelines of the G7, was emphatic that Europe must be included.

“I am still very grateful to the United States of America for making every effort to get the parties to the conflict to the table,” he said. “But I made clear again here that Europe belongs at this table. There can be no solution without Europe, only with Europe.”
Rubio said the U.S. has no objection to eventual European involvement in the direct talks, but that it wasn’t yet time.

“Ultimately, it would be a positive, but we’ve got a ways to go,” he told reporters after a full day of group and bilateral meetings with G7 counterparts. “But, no, it’s good that they’re talking, it’s good that the trilateral talks are on again. It’s better than not having talks.”
On the eve of the talks, Russia battered Ukraine’s power grid again on Monday and Ukrainian forces hit another of Russia’s biggest oil refineries.

The two countries remain locked in battle with no sign that either side is ready to budge from their demands. The war has already killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians, analysts and humanitarian organizations say.

title: How North Korean defectors view Kim Jong Un's daughter as his possible successor
summary: Kim Jong Un’s teenage daughter is at the center of global media speculation that she is being groomed to be her father’s heir
story: Kim Jong Un’s teenage daughter is at the center of global media speculation that she is being groomed to be her father’s heir

SEOUL, South Korea -- The teenage daughter of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has drawn intense international media attention as their frequent public appearances together fuel speculation that he is grooming her to succeed him one day.
There are debates about her status, but most experts expect Kim to eventually hand over power to one of his children and extend his family's rule into a fourth generation.
Here's a look at how North Korean defectors and others think about the girl, who is reportedly about 13 and named Kim Ju Ae, and the family's dynastic rule.

Tae, a former minister at North Korea’s Embassy in London, defected to South Korea in 2016 and later served as a member of South Korea’s parliament. Tae said it's deeply lamentable to observe what he believes are Kim's moves to prolong his family's rule.

“It's a wretched reality that unchecked power in an absolute monarchy is being passed down to a fourth generation in the 21st century," Tae said. “North Korea will likely fall further behind the outside world if it has a fourth-generation power succession.”

Kim fled North Korea in May 2023. She said many North Koreans are unhappy to see Kim’s daughter wearing her hair long down past her shoulders, walking around in high heels and dressing like a grown-up, because such styles aren’t allowed for ordinary teenagers in North Korea. But she said they have no choice but to keep their frustration to themselves out of fears of harsh punishment.
“People would now think Ju Ae would become their monarch,” she said.

Lee came to South Korea in 2013 and heads the Seoul-based Free North Korea Radio station. She said North Koreans wouldn't have complaints about the girl's hairdo and outfit because they've been so thoroughly brainwashed.
“They wouldn't know whether her clothes are designer brands but they think she can wear them because she's the daughter" of their supreme leader, she said.
Choi, who fled North Korea in 2015, said that Kim’s daughter kissing her father on the cheek is “an extremely uncommon” display of affection between a father and his daughter in the North.

Living under a cult of personality centering on the Kim family, Choi said some North Koreans likely feel proud of such a scene, venerating Kim as “the father of all people," and "not a tyrant who killed even his uncle" in a series of brutal executions of his potential rivals.

Lee is a defector and lawyer who runs a website meant to provide North Koreans with outside information. He said that given the North's deep-rooted male-centered hierarchy, North Koreans wouldn't readily accept a woman leader. Lee noted even South Korea has had only one female leader, President Park Geun-hye, who governed from 2013-2017.

“Even South Korea is a very patriarchal society where women find it difficult to hold leadership roles. I can't buy the idea of a woman becoming leader in North Korea, which is virtually a dynasty,” he said.

Oh, an analyst at Seoul’s Korea Institute for National Unification, cautioned against concluding that the girl is Kim's heir. But he said that if she's formally anointed as her father's heir, she could quickly cement her authority because members of the ruling elite with shared interests would rally around her and eliminate potential opponents.
“Whether the successor is a male or female doesn't really matter,” Oh said.

Ahn, a researcher who has interviewed hundreds of defectors, said Kim would need to deliver economic improvements and raise living standards to make his people accept his succession plan in a more positive way. Ahn said that despite living under their country's repressive rule, younger North Koreans have changed how they think due to the spread of South Korean TV and other cultural content, posing a burden on Kim.
“North Korean people won't rise up against Kim. But what matters is whether he can have his people accept his plan happily or begrudgingly,” Ahn said.

Jo, who runs an online news site, said contacts in North Korea told him they weren’t yet sure if the girl is Kim’s heir. Jo himself believes she is, and that Kim’s concerns about his health have likely prompted him to rush the process of preparing her as his successor.

In late September, South Korea’s main spy agency told lawmakers that Kim showed no other significant signs of poor health, though he remained severely obese and at high risk of cardiovascular disease. Both his father and grandfather, who ruled North Korea before he inherited power in 2011, died of heart problems.

title: ‘Like gods reigning over humans’: Many defectors see daughter of North Korea's Kim as heir apparent
summary: It's been about four years since the teenage daughter of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un first publicly accompanied her father on major state events
story: It's been about four years since the teenage daughter of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un first publicly accompanied her father on major state events

SEOUL, South Korea -- Until she fled North Korea three years ago, Kim Yumi felt deeply frustrated whenever state TV showed leader Kim Jong Un with his young daughter. The message, she felt, was clear and worrying: North Korea was laying the groundwork for an eventual hereditary transfer of power, this time to Kim's daughter.

Publicly questioning the Kim dynasty's hold on power would mean severe persecution. Already angered by draconian pandemic regulations that ruined her family’s fishing business, she defected to South Korea by boat with her family.

“My husband and I didn’t want our children to live under a fourth-generation dictatorship. As parents, we thought the best thing we could do for our children was to give them freedom,” said Kim Yumi, 32, who now lives in Seoul.

North Korea allows no dissent and harshly punishes attempts to flee the country. Established in 1948, the nation is nominally a socialist republic, but in reality it is an authoritarian dynasty, with three generations of the Kim family ruling in succession. There was no known public resistance during its previous two successions — from state founder Kim Il Sung to his son Kim Jong Il in 1994 and then from Kim Jong Il to his son Kim Jong Un in 2011.
This time, North Korea is apparently trying something radical.
Kim Jong Un's repeated public appearances with his daughter over the past four years have led to speculation that she’s being groomed as her father’s heir.

The question of who will become North Korea's next leader is crucial because that person will face a huge challenge — governing an impoverished, nuclear-armed nation whose 26 million people have little political freedom and live under strict state surveillance while being cut off from much of the outside world.
North Koreans have no say in the selection of their future leader, and analysts and defectors say they will passively accept a third dynastic succession — at least publicly.

To gauge North Koreans' private views, The Associated Press spoke with nearly a dozen defectors who still have contacts in North Korea or witnessed the country’s previous power successions, as well as several experts.
Not much is known about Kim’s daughter except that she’s reportedly about 13 and named Kim Ju Ae.

Since late 2022, she has made dozens of public appearances, all of them with her father at big events like weapons tests and military parades. State media has called her Kim’s “most beloved” and “respected” child. Her status has been emphasized by images showing an elderly general kneeling before her and her standing in front of her father.
South Korea’s spy agency says she is Kim’s likely heir. Eight of the 11 defectors interviewed by the AP shared that view; the others disagreed, citing the North's deeply patriarchal culture.

“During her visits to missile launch sites and factories, the way senior North Korean officials treat Kim Ju Ae involves protocols reserved for a successor, not the ones simply for a daughter of Kim Jong Un,” said Tae Yongho, a former minister at North Korea’s Embassy in London who defected to South Korea in 2016. “They are repeating the same protocol and treatment they provided for Kim Jong Un,” when he accompanied his father as his heir.

Kang Mi-Jin, a defector who runs a company analyzing North Korea’s economy, said her contacts inside the North told her over smuggled phones that they think Kim Ju Ae is in line to succeed her father.
Jung Gwang-il, a defector who specializes in smuggling outside information to North Korea, said the North Koreans he meets as they visit Chinese border towns also hold the same belief.
Former NBA star Dennis Rodman was the first to reveal her identity, holding her as a baby during a 2013 trip to Pyongyang.
Much of the skepticism about Kim Ju Ae as a potential leader stems from her being female. South Korean officials believe she has a younger sibling whose gender hasn't been confirmed.

Women in North Korea remain deeply underrepresented in senior posts. Only one of 17 department directors for the ruling Workers' Party is a woman. That woman is Kim Jong Un’s influential younger sister, Kim Yo Jong, according to South Korea's Unification Ministry.

“My contacts in North Korea say it would be nonsensical to revere that little girl as their supreme leader,” said Kim Jeong-Ah, a former North Korean army officer who resettled in South Korea in 2009.

Lee Si-young, a defector who heads the Seoul-based Free North Korea Radio station, said that some of her older contacts in North Korea aren't happy with a woman taking power. But she said members of the Kim family “are like gods reigning over humans so gender really doesn't matter.”

Whether or not the girl succeeds her father, observers agree that Kim Jong Un, 42, is likely to designate one of his children to prolong his family's rule, a move they expect would face little resistance at home. South Korea’s spy agency recently assessed that Kim is extremely obese and at high risk of cardiovascular disease but shows no other signs of poor health.

North Koreans will passively “accept a hereditary succession as something that they should go along with,” said Ahn Chan-il, a defector and scholar who heads the World Institute for North Korean Studies in Seoul.

During North Korea’s first leadership transition, in 1994, the new leader, Kim Jong Il, then 52, had already spent two decades as the official successor working alongside his father to run the country.

The second succession, in 2011, was more uncertain. Kim Jong Un, who was then 27, was seen by outsiders as too young and inexperienced. He quickly consolidated his grip on power, however, by orchestrating high-profile executions and purges, including the 2013 killing of his powerful uncle Jang Song Thaek.

“A hereditary power succession system has been institutionalized in North Korea, just like presidential elections in our system,” said Oh Gyeong-seob, an analyst at Seoul’s Korea Institute for National Unification. “North Korea’s ruling elite accepts it as a matter of course. So do its general citizens.”
Choi Song-juk, who fled North Korea in 2015, said she had been so brainwashed that she had no complaints about the North's two earlier power successions. She now calls them “nonsense.”
Defector Jeon Jae-hyun said North Korea's pervasive surveillance apparatus keeps people from voicing their discontent with the government and helps enforce political loyalty.
Defector Kim Yumi said she had never heard about the girl until Kim Jong Un publicly introduced his daughter at a long-range missile launch site in November 2022.

“Ordinary people know absolutely nothing about private lives of the Kim family,” said Kim Yumi, who now runs a YouTube channel on North Korea. “They don't really try to know about it and don't pay attention to it because doing so could put them in danger.”

title: Peru's move to reconsider protections for Mashco Piro raises fears of Amazon logging
summary: Indigenous leaders in Peru are warning that a government decision to reconsider protections for the Mashco Piro could expose their Amazon rainforest territory to logging
story: Indigenous leaders in Peru are warning that a government decision to reconsider protections for the Mashco Piro could expose their Amazon rainforest territory to logging

MEXICO CITY -- Indigenous leaders in Peru are warning that a government decision to reconsider protections for one of the world’s largest uncontacted Indigenous groups could expose more of their Amazon rainforest territory to logging, raising fears of violent encounters and the spread of life-threatening diseases.

The Mashco Piro, who live deep in the forests of southeastern Peru and avoid contact with outsiders to preserve their traditional way of life, have increasingly been spotted near encroaching logging concessions in recent years, highlighting growing pressure on their ancestral lands.

Eusebio Rios Iviche, vice president of the Indigenous organization FENAMAD, told The Associated Press on Monday the decision threatens to reverse years of efforts to protect the Mashco Piro, exposing them to greater risks of encounters with outsiders and diseases to which they have little immunity.

The controversy centers on a 2016 government study that recommended expanding the Madre de Dios Territorial Reserve, a protected area established in 2002 for the Mashco Piro and other Indigenous peoples living in isolation.

A government commission responsible for protecting isolated Indigenous peoples decided last week to revisit that study rather than proceed with the proposed expansion, according to Indigenous organizations and the advocacy group Survival International.

The move has raised concerns that logging concessions overlapping with the proposed expansion could continue operating in areas Indigenous organizations say are essential to the Mashco Piro’s survival.
Peru’s Ministry of Culture, which oversees protections for Indigenous peoples living in isolation, did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.

Ramon Rivero, who headed the Peruvian government office responsible for protecting isolated Indigenous peoples in 2014, questioned the decision, saying authorities should complete the reserve’s expansion rather than revisit studies already approved. He said the government should also consider compensation for logging companies whose concessions could be affected.
Images released by Survival International in 2024 showed dozens of Mashco Piro people near logging concessions in Madre de Dios, a region bordering Brazil and Bolivia.
That same year, violent encounters involving the Mashco Piro and loggers left at least two loggers dead. It remains unclear whether any Mashco Piro were killed or injured.

Following the confrontations, the Forest Stewardship Council, an international organization that certifies responsibly managed forests, suspended certification for Maderera Canales Tahuamanu, a logging company operating in the area. The certification was withdrawn permanently in 2025.
Survival International says logging has continued in the region despite the loss of certification.

Caroline Pearce, the organization’s executive director, condemned the government’s decision, saying it effectively put the Mashco Piro’s territory up for sale and prioritized commercial interests over Indigenous lives.
The dispute comes as Peru faces increasing scrutiny over its protection of Indigenous peoples in isolation.

In September, FENAMAD and the environmental legal organization EarthRights International brought a case before the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, accusing Peru of failing to protect the Mashco Piro’s ancestral territory and their right to remain isolated.
Rios Iviche urged the government to honor the 2016 agreement, expand the reserve and remove overlapping logging concessions.
“The lives and survival of the Mashco Piro people must not come second to economic interests,” he said.

title: Trinidad and Tobago Coast Guard searches for at least 5 missing after boat crash
summary: Authorities in Trinidad and Tobago are conducting search and rescue operations for several people missing after a boating accident
story: Authorities in Trinidad and Tobago are conducting search and rescue operations for several people missing after a boating accident
PORT-OF-SPAIN, Trinidad -- Authorities in Trinidad and Tobago said search and rescue operations were being conducted on Monday for several people who went missing after a boating accident.

Crews spent most of Monday searching for at least five people who were reported missing after the collision, according to the Hunters Search and Rescue Team, a local nongovernmental organization that assisted authorities with the search.

The Trinidad and Tobago Coast Guard said two boats collided on Sunday evening in waters off the northwestern peninsula of Trinidad, the larger of the two main islands that make up the twin-island Caribbean nation.
“Preliminary reports indicate that several persons remain unaccounted for as search efforts continue,” the coast guard said in a statement on Monday.
As the two vessels collided, one vessel pitched into the air, throwing its occupants into the water, according to eyewitness Jonathan Salandy, a boat captain with local tour company Pontoon Tours TT.
“I saw people just in the water all over,” Salandy said in a video statement.

Salandy said he and his crew raced toward the scene and began rescuing survivors under the cover of darkness. He said they threw life jackets out to the crash victims and pulled some of the victims on to the tour boat.
“One guy had a serious laceration to his head and a lot of blood,” Salandy said.

The coast guard confirmed that some of the people who were rescued were taken to local hospitals to be treated for injuries. However, officials did not immediately say how many people suffered injuries.

Relatives and friends of those missing gathered along the coastline at a nearby beach in the town of Chaguaramas, on Trinidad’s northwestern tip, on Monday. They spent hours praying as they awaited updates from authorities.

A chain of smaller islands is located just off Trinidad’s northwestern peninsula. Those smaller islands, which are part of Trinidad and Tobago’s territory, are popular for weekend getaways and events. Small boats are used to transport people between the mainland and the smaller islands.

title: Pope meets with survivors of clergy abuse in Argentina as it reckons with legacy and ongoing cases
summary: Pope Leo XIV have met with survivors of clergy abuse during his visit to Argentina
story: Pope Leo XIV have met with survivors of clergy abuse during his visit to Argentina

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina -- BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AP) — Pope Leo XIV met with survivors of clergy abuse on Monday during his visit to Argentina, a country that has been reckoning with the Catholic Church’s legacy of sex abuse and cover-up, including in cases in which the Argentine Pope Francis intervened.

The Vatican said Leo spent about an hour meeting individually, and then as a group, with five victims of abuse by clergy and “church institutions” who were chosen by the local church. The meeting took place at the Catholic University of Argentina.
Leo listened to their “painful stories and proposals to consolidate paths of healing in the church,” said a statement from Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni.

Acknowledging that there were other groups of victims who had wanted to meet with Leo, “the pope expressed his closeness and desire to reinforce paths of protection, of welcome and accompaniment in the church,” it said.

Victims groups had said they wanted to meet with Leo and were denied, including a group of 43 women who allege they were subjected to human trafficking and forced labor at centers of the conservative group Opus Dei in Argentina.

Their allegations implicate senior members of Opus, some of whom have been formally accused in a criminal investigation into the women's claims. Prosecutors have requested that the members be summoned for questioning, but the judge has not ordered it. Opus has denied wrongdoing.

Given the ongoing criminal investigation, it is perhaps unlikely that Leo would have intervened by meeting with them in this case. However, in general, the American pope has followed in the footsteps of Francis and to a lesser extent Pope Benedict XVI by meeting with abuse survivors on his foreign trips, and another meeting is expected when he arrives later this week in Peru.

Ahead of the Argentine visit, survivors had also demanded stronger action from the Vatican against those accused or convicted in criminal courts but whose fates within the church’s internal legal processes haven’t been made public.

Survivors’ groups have cited several high-profile priests convicted of serious crimes, including Julio Grassi and former Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta. Francis intervened in both cases in favor of the priests who were subsequently convicted by criminal courts.

Grassi, once a prominent figure who ran homes for orphaned children, is serving a 15-year sentence for sexually abusing a minor. Francis, who at the time was still Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio and the archbishop of Buenos Aires, in 2010 commissioned a four-volume, 2,000-plus-page forensic study of Grassi’s case that concluded he was innocent, that his victims were lying and that the case never should have gone to trial.

Zanchetta, a former bishop close to Francis, was sentenced in 2022 to 4 1/2 years in prison for sexually abusing two seminarians. He was granted parole in 2025, prompting renewed demands that he be defrocked. Francis had initially rejected the accusations against Zanchetta and created a job for him at the Vatican that got him out of Argentina. The late pope eventually authorized a canonical criminal proceeding against Zanchetta in 2019, but the Vatican has not publicly announced a ruling.

The Vatican tends to not initiate canonical trials until all criminal appeals are exhausted, to not prejudge the outcomes, though it does recommend that bishops take precautionary measures during investigations such as removing priests from active ministry.

title: Honduran court delays verdict in disappearance case that exposed sex trafficking ring
summary: A Honduran court has postponed a verdict in a sex-trafficking case linked to the 2022 disappearance of Angie Peña
story: A Honduran court has postponed a verdict in a sex-trafficking case linked to the 2022 disappearance of Angie Peña

MEXICO CITY -- A Honduran court postponed a verdict Monday in a sex-trafficking case linked to the 2022 disappearance of Angie Peña, delaying a decision until Nov. 20 as relatives, lawyers and women's rights groups demanded justice.
The case has drawn attention to allegations of impunity and corruption that advocates say have allowed widespread gender violence in the Central American country.

Four men are on trial for crimes related to Peña’s disappearance. Two U.S. citizens, Harold Green and William James Murdock, face human trafficking charges, while another U.S. citizen, Gary Lee Johnston, and Honduran Gustavo Trejo are accused of criminal association.

The case has implicated public officials and exposed a criminal ring known as “Delta Teams” that has drawn comparison to the Jeffrey Epstein network in a country with high rates of gender violence and low conviction rates for related crimes.

Lawyers representing the family have questioned the lack of transparency of the investigation and trial, which was not open to the press or general public. Peña's family said it has received death threats, and the August killing of Dereck McNeil, a key protected witness, further exposed the dangers of seeking justice in Honduras.

“There are many more women and girls who have been victims of trafficking networks, and those cases are silenced, they go unpunished,” said Kenia Paz, a lawyer for the Legal Team for Human Rights who represents Peña's family.
She said the case has exposed a criminal network “beyond what we can even imagine” and called for the state to provide answers on what happened to Peña.

Peña, 22, disappeared on Jan. 1, 2022, after taking a Jet Ski ride while on vacation with her family in Roatan, an island off the coast of Honduras. Initially, authorities investigated her disappearance as a possible accident, but the case expanded into a trafficking investigation after the Jet Ski she used was found in Belize, some 90 nautical miles (170 kilometers) away.

In August 2022, authorities searching Johnston’s house in Roatan in connection with Peña's disappearance found a minor there. Johnston was accused of commercial sex trafficking and child pornography and sentenced to 32 years in a case separate from the proceeding involving Peña.

In April 2024, authorities ordered arrest warrants for four more people, including Green, Murdock and Trejo. Honduran authorities have sought an Interpol notice for the fourth, U.S. citizen Antony Frank Grayson.

The Honduran public prosecutor’s office has said the suspects are all part of a sex trafficking network that included minors and that the group also carried out other crimes, including drug trafficking. It alleges police and at least one judge helped facilitate the criminal network, without naming the officials.

Defense lawyers for the accused have denied involvement and requested an acquittal. McNeil, the protected witness who was killed, alleged further corruption within a special unit of the public prosecutor’s office known as the ATIC. In videos made public after his death, he accused the unit of leaking information about the case and being linked to drug trafficking networks. The ATIC director has denied any corruption and said that the unit has not been involved in investigating Peña’s disappearance.

Julissa Villanueva, a former vice minister of security who was involved in the investigation, said that prosecutors have mishandled the case from the start. They have tried to push a “tunnel vision” explanation of what happened, she said, that hides the larger criminal structure around it, which she compared to Epstein’s sex trafficking network.
An analysis by Honduran media found that the country was mentioned more than 100 times in the Epstein files, including multiple references to Roatan.
Villanueva called for justice in the case.

“There are connections with other larger networks, and only by making them public will this family be able to get justice,” she said. “It’s not just Angie. It’s all those women around Angie. There are many.”
Follow AP’s Latin America coverage at https://apnews.com/hub/latin-america

title: Teachers strike in Paraguay to demand pension fund protections following bank's collapse
summary: Thousands of public schoolteachers went on strike in Paraguay and took to the streets of several cities following the collapse of a major bank that resulted in the removal of the nation’s president last week
story: Thousands of public schoolteachers went on strike in Paraguay and took to the streets of several cities following the collapse of a major bank that resulted in the removal of the nation’s president last week

Public schoolteachers went on strike in Paraguay Monday and took to the streets of several cities following the collapse of a major bank that resulted in the removal of the nation’s president last week.

Silvio Piris, the president of the Federation of Paraguayan Educators, said that teachers in Paraguay are concerned over the fate of around 60 million dollars in pensions funds that had been deposited in Ueno, the bank that was intervened by Paraguay’s government last week.
“We want the return of that money to be a priority,” Piris told Paraguay’s Channel 9.

More than 3 million people were frozen out of their bank accounts last Tuesday after Paraguay’s government intervened in Ueno Bank. Its closure has also affected pension funds and government-owned accounts.

The bank’s collapse led to the removal of Paraguayan President Santiago Peña, who was accused by legislators of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno while regulators overlooked risky insider lending.

Peña was charged on Saturday with two crimes related to the bank's collapse, as an anti-corruption probe that also involves the former head of Paraguay’s central bank expands. The former president is being held at a military base while investigations continue. He has been replaced by his vice president, Pedro Alliana.

In a press conference Saturday, prosecutors said Peña would be investigated for the crimes of breach of trust and administration for personal gain, and could face up to 20 years in prison if found guilty.

The impeachment charges against Peña allege that the former president held a stake in Ueno’s holding company, which he divested under pressure last year, and appointed a former Ueno executive to run the central bank that regulated it. Lawmakers also accuse Peña of letting the state pension fund deposit $355 million at the bank, beyond legal limits. Peña has denied wrongdoing.

The Central Bank last week began to return deposits to account holders, and said that by Saturday it had partially or fully refunded more than 1.2 million Ueno customers. Bank deposits in Paraguay are insured up to an amount of around $37,000.

The crisis has sparked multiple protests from account holders that have resulted in clashes with police. It has also generated doubts over the stability of Paraguay’s financial system. The nation’s currency, the guarani, has lost about 8% of its value against the U.S. dollar since Ueno was intervened.

title: France blames Iran for the last month's cyberattack on supermarket fridges
summary: France has blamed Iran for a cyberattack on supermarket fridges last month
story: France has blamed Iran for a cyberattack on supermarket fridges last month
PARIS -- France on Monday blamed Iran for last month's cyberattack on supermarket fridges and summoned the Iranian ambassador, the French Foreign Ministry said.

In a statement, the ministry said: “France condemns in the strongest possible terms the unacceptable cyberattacks carried out on its territory by the Islamic Republic of Iran against French interests.”
The Oct. 12 attack sent refrigerator temperatures soaring, affecting about 700 of the country’s 10,000 supermarkets.
Paris prosecutors said investigators found that Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard was behind the large-scale cyberattack.

title: How Mandela's ANC lost its way in South Africa and voters deserted it
summary: The African National Congress party in South Africa faces growing dissatisfaction and an exodus of supporters
story: The African National Congress party in South Africa faces growing dissatisfaction and an exodus of supporters

CAPE TOWN, South Africa -- CAPE TOWN, South Africa (AP) — The African National Congress once rose above politics in South Africa as a movement dedicated to freeing the country from the oppression of apartheid with the lofty principles of democracy, equality and a better life for all.

It was widely revered as a force for good when it became South Africa's ruling party in 1994 under Nelson Mandela, who was imprisoned for 27 years by the apartheid regime for his opposition to the system of racial segregation.

But three decades after the ANC transformed from a liberation movement to a political party in government, it faces growing dissatisfaction from South Africans who feel it has failed to live up to its promises.

Results released Sunday from last week’s local elections showed the party's share of the vote dropped 15 percentage points to just 31%, as South Africans rebuked it for failing to deliver basic services such as water and electricity.

The ANC, which once commanded 70% of the vote and had no challengers, conceded to being humbled in the local elections — its worst performance at the ballot box ever. The party's secretary-general called it a “catastrophic outcome” for the ANC and said it would enter a period of soul-searching to see how it could win back the trust of South Africa's people.

Two years ago, the ANC lost its parliamentary majority in a national election with 40% of the vote. It considered that a disaster, and a chance for self-reflection, but its supporters have continued to desert it.

While the end of apartheid gave every South African the right to vote and other basic freedoms, the challenge for the ANC was to convert that into a better standard of living for people, especially for the poor Black majority.

That was difficult for the ANC government to sustain after some early success. South Africa has one of the highest unemployment rates in the world and is still ranked as one of the most unequal countries.

Its widespread poverty — which still disproportionately affects Black people — spurs most of the criticism of the ANC, which became the leading party in a national coalition government after losing its dominance in 2024.

The ANC has often pointed to the difficulties in reversing nearly a half-century of racist laws under apartheid and hundreds of years of European colonialism before that. It maintains that South Africa is a far better country without apartheid and that is undoubtedly true.

But the most pressing problems for many South Africans in 2026 boil down to a failure of basic government services, with communities across the nation faced with a lack of electricity in their neighborhoods, broken or nonexistent water and sewage systems, garbage piling up on streets and a shortage of housing that leaves millions living in shacks.
Those issues were seen as the driving force behind the ANC's latest slump in support.

While nearly 40% of South Africa’s population of 62 million live under the lower poverty line, according to the World Bank, ANC officials and allies have been implicated in enriching themselves in a succession of corruption scandals.
Corruption is alleged to have been especially bad under former President Jacob Zuma, who was accused of allowing a decade of rampant graft to play out before he was pressured to step down in 2018.

Current President Cyril Ramaphosa promised to clean up the ANC when he succeeded Zuma, but he has been involved in his own scandal over the source of more than half a million dollars in cash that was hidden in a couch at his ranch and stolen.

A judicial commission investigating corruption in the Zuma era exposed shocking graft. A new commission is looking into more recent allegations of collusion between senior police officers, political officials and corrupt businessmen that include more than $120 million allegedly being misappropriated from a hospital meant to serve a poor community.
The new scandals are also seen as the ANC's failure.
The ANC has been hampered by infighting since Mandela stepped down as president in 1999 after one term.
His successor, Thabo Mbeki, was forced out as Zuma undermined his position as the head of the ANC. The party turned on Zuma when the corruption allegations became overwhelming.
Zuma split from the ANC in a feud with Ramaphosa and started the new MK Party, which has further bled the ANC vote.
In its early days, the ANC celebrated that it was a “broad church” of people dedicated to freedom and democracy. It now has factions and divisions much like any other political party.
Zuma once said that the ANC would govern South Africa “until Jesus comes back.”
Yet from a dominant position, the ANC has lost swathes of support, especially among young urban South Africans who don’t remember apartheid.

It has clung on as the biggest party nationally and locally as South African politics becomes fragmented with many new parties winning small shares. But the ANC's longtime opposition, the white-led Democratic Alliance party, won 25% of votes in last week's municipal elections to come closer than ever to overtaking it.
The Democratic Alliance said that showed its potential to be South Africa's biggest party, which would have been seen as a preposterous claim a few years ago.
