title: Susie Wiles' old lobbying firm in crosshairs of MAGA feud
summary: Former top HHS aide Calley Means alleged in an interview with "Face the Nation" that Ballard Partners "controlled" White House policy. The firm and Wiles said the claims are false.
story: For the last two years, Brian Ballard's ties to President Trump made his lobbying firm one of the most sought-after in Washington. Now those same ties have made it a target in the Republican Party's post-midterm infighting.

Calley Means, a former top aide to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., alleged in an interview Sunday with CBS News' "Face the Nation" that Ballard Partners "controlled" White House policy. Mr. Trump's former chief of staff, Susie Wiles, worked at the firm for nearly a decade as a managing partner, leaving in 2019.

Means claimed Ballard Partners' rise to become the top-earning lobbying firm "did not happen by accident." He accused Wiles and other top advisers to Mr. Trump of catering to industries that funded Republicans ahead of the midterms. Ballard and Wiles both called the claims false.
The firm's interactions with Wiles as chief of staff "have been limited and have been the exception, not the rule," Brian Ballard, a longtime Trump fundraiser, said in a rare statement Sunday.

Ballard Partners' more than $88 million in lobbying revenue last year was, at the time, the most any firm had reported since the Lobbying Disclosure Act took effect in 1996, even after adjusting for inflation, a CBS News analysis of Senate lobbying disclosures found. Through the first three quarters of 2026, the firm has already surpassed that, reporting more than $98 million.

The fortunes of Washington lobbying firms tend to rise and fall with changes in administrations, as companies hire them to try to influence policy. But after an election that saw government corruption polling as a top issue for voters, questions about who has profited from political connections are intensifying. Ballard Partners is now among those ensnared in the MAGA feud.

That tension could deepen ahead of 2028, as Republicans who cheered Mr. Trump's promise to "drain the swamp" speak out about the realities of an entrenched lobbying industry that has continued to thrive in Washington.

"The Democrats are going to start investigations as soon as they're sworn in, and White House fighting about who was making money will just elevate the topic," said Marc Short, a former chief of staff to Vice President Mike Pence.
The White House said in a statement that the Trump administration "has never allowed and will never allow outside groups to influence policy decisions."
A fight over vapes

Brian Ballard has been one of Mr. Trump's top fundraisers for years, having reeled in $50 million for his campaign in 2024, according to a source familiar with the number who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Since 2008, he has chaired Florida finance committees for previous Republican presidential nominees. His firm opened a Washington office in 2017 and once employed both Wiles and Pam Bondi, who went on to serve as Mr. Trump's attorney general.

When Mr. Trump won a second term, the firm signed up hundreds of clients, though its relationship with the administration has seen ups and downs. For a brief period in 2025, Brian Ballard was banned from the West Wing after his firm's lobbying approach for a cryptocurrency client frustrated White House officials, two Trump advisers told CBS News. (Ballard apologized in May 2025 and returned to the White House's good graces, Axios reported.)
Among the firm's longest-standing clients is RAI Services Company, a subsidiary of tobacco giant Reynolds American. It has paid Ballard Partners millions of dollars since 2017, lobbying records show.

That relationship placed Ballard at the center of Means' allegations about favorable treatment for vaping interests. Means resigned in late October, claiming the Make America Healthy Again agenda had stalled in the White House. He placed the blame at Wiles' feet, saying she and "her deputies were still relentlessly pushing HHS to find a pathway for fruit-flavored vapes."

In May, the Food and Drug Administration handed the tobacco industry a win with new guidance that could let major tobacco companies sell flavored vapes. The announcement came a week after Brian Ballard and tobacco executives had lunch with Mr. Trump at his golf club in Jupiter, Florida, where the president called Kennedy and other health officials to complain about the FDA, The New York Times reported. The FDA decision also came after RAI Services Company had given $5 million to MAGA Inc., the pro-Trump super PAC, on April 30, Federal Election Commission records show. (FDA Commissioner Marty Makary resigned days after the guidance came out, in protest.) The White House has suggested the donation had nothing to do with the FDA decision.

In his statement Sunday, Ballard said no one at his firm advocated to Wiles or anyone at the White House on authorization for fruit-flavored vapes. He said his advocacy related to "illegal, unregulated vapes from China," some of which, he said, have been found to be laced with fentanyl.
Wiles told CBS News she had nothing to do with the tobacco industry meeting with Mr. Trump at his golf club.

Means also singled out James Blair, the former deputy chief of staff, claiming he was "relentless on helping the fruit-flavored vape industry." Blair, who left the White House in April to oversee the GOP's midterm strategy, has traded barbs with Means on social media, calling the claim that he pushed vapes as a core midterm issue "a complete and total lie."

"I didn't promote flavored vaping specifically at all," Blair told CBS News, adding that he was tasked with making sure the FDA ruled on nicotine product applications swiftly – within six months. "Calley is intentionally misrepresenting my role and my responsibility because he opposes the issue entirely," Blair added.

Blair spoke with Reynolds and other vape companies about the FDA's application process, but not about any specific applications or products, according to two sources familiar with the conversations who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Blair has said he is reviewing his legal options and whether to sue Means for defamation.

A MAGA Inc. spokesperson said the group "is pleased to accept legal contributions from those who agree with President Trump's America First agenda." A spokesperson for Wiles told Axios that Means' accusations of corruption were "outrageous, defamatory, and provably false."
"What Ballard helps you do"

Means' accusations centered on what he called a "very close-knit crew" around Wiles that "explicitly catered to special interests." He alleged that the goal was to serve big business interests in exchange for money for the midterms. Steering those donations, he alleged, "is what Ballard helps you do."

Lobbying firms in Washington routinely advise clients on political giving, and many lobbyists raise money for candidates themselves. The practice is legal, though federal law requires lobbyists to disclose their own contributions twice a year.

Means also pointed to a long-running dispute about glyphosate, the active ingredient in the weedkiller Roundup, which has been linked to cancer. He accused administration officials of siding with Bayer, which makes Roundup, by formally supporting the company's argument at the Supreme Court to block state lawsuits over the herbicide. A White House official told CBS News that Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote a brief at the court's request.

Bayer has paid Ballard Partners since January 2024 to lobby Congress and the administration on a number of issues, according to lobbying disclosures. Ballard said no one at the firm lobbied Wiles or the White House on glyphosate.

Means' claim that Wiles was hostile to the MAHA agenda has drawn pushback from her allies. Two sources, who requested anonymity to describe a private meeting, recounted a White House meeting last year in which an administration official derided MAHA supporters as "nuts." Wiles shot back: "I'm one of those MAHA nuts," the sources said.
A White House official told CBS News that Wiles "has been an essential leader in Making America Healthy Again."

Mr. Trump's longtime pollster Tony Fabrizio, whom Means accused of working to help pharmaceutical interests, said in a statement that Means' allegation that he is "in the pocket of Big Pharma" was "ridiculous" and "demonstrably false." Fabrizio previously urged Republicans to campaign on lowering prescription drug prices, finding in an April 2025 poll that the issue could give GOP candidates in toss-up districts a 20-point boost.

The fight is unlikely to fade soon. California Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said he will look into the claims against Wiles. Attorney General Todd Blanche has dismissed Means as a "disgruntled former administration official," and told CNN the Justice Department would not investigate "something that someone says on a podcast."

title: Nvidia investigates CEO Jensen Huang over Chinese spy concerns
summary: The board of Nvidia said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
story: Nvidia has launched an independent investigation of its co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, over allegations he was the target of an intelligence effort by China.

The allegations center around a Chinese business executive named Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence agencies believe was an asset of China's Ministry of State Security, the country's main intelligence agency.
The CIA, NSA and ODNI did not immediately respond to CBS News requests for comment.

The New York Times reported last month that U.S. authorities were investigating Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen), a former executive of the Singapore-based Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia. The report claims Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security.

Two law enforcement sources confirmed to CBS News on Monday that the Justice Department's National Security Division is investigating Megaspeed. The investigation involves potential violations of U.S. export restrictions on advanced AI chips, the sources said.

In a message to Nvidia employees Sunday, Jensen Huang admitted, "I was unfaithful to my wife," and apologized for hurting her and their children, although he did not name the woman involved. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he wrote.

"The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," Nvidia's board of directors said in a statement Sunday. "A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation."
The board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," the statement said.
John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, told CBS News on Sunday, "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us."
Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters Monday, "The so-called Chinese spy narrative is entirely baseless and constitutes slander and smear."
A company spokesperson said Jensen Huang "fully supports the review" and is committed to continuing to lead the company.
Jensen Huang said he had fallen short of his responsibilities to the company's employees, board and shareholders. He said he is "fully committed to NVIDIA" and will work to earn back their trust.

"Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation," he said in a statement. "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully."
"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American," he added.

Alice Huang was previously a television reporter in China before becoming a top executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which has become one of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia. Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to The Times.
Asked about the report on Sunday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he couldn't comment, saying it was an "internal corporate matter."

On Monday, President Trump called Jensen Huang a "very high-quality person," saying during a White House briefing that "the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape." Mr. Trump also said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday to see how he was doing, and that Huang "said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy."

Nvidia, the world's most valuable company, has regularly surpassed Wall Street's earnings expectations in the past three years since its high-end chips emerged as AI's best building blocks. The Santa Clara, California-based company reported quarterly profits of $59.69 billion in August.

title: FDA warns of rare vision-loss side effect from GLP-1 drugs
summary: The Food and Drug Administration is adding a new warning about possible rare cases of vision loss reported with GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic, Wegovy and other brands.
story: Popular weight loss and diabetes drugs, including Ozempic and Wegovy, will carry a new warning about a possible rare side effect that can sometimes lead to permanent vision loss, U.S. health regulators announced Monday.

The Food and Drug Administration said the risk will be added to the labeling of all GLP-1 drugs, the blockbuster medications used to treat obesity, diabetes and several other medical conditions. The class includes a dozen injectable or pill-based drugs, including widely used brands like Zepbound and Mounjaro.

The eye condition, known as non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, can cause significant vision loss. The problem, which has been reported with all GLP-1 drugs, is caused by decreased blood flow to the optic nerve, although the underlying cause isn't understood, the FDA said.

FDA scientists began looking into the problem after the publication of a 2024 medical paper tying the condition to certain patients taking semaglutide, the active drug in Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy.

Dr. Joseph Rizzo, a neuro-ophthalmologist who co-authored that paper, told CBS News on Monday that he and his team had been working with the FDA to gather and review data on the issue for some time and that, while he didn't know the agency was ready to make a decision, he wasn't surprised it chose to add the warning.

He stressed that while he believes the evidence shows GLP-1 usage increases the risk of developing NAION, he doesn't discourage patients from taking them, saying, "The medicines have really been profoundly beneficial to a large number of people."
People who aren't on GLP-1s can also develop NAION, which affects somewhere between 2 to 10 of every 100,000 adults over age 50, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology.

Novo Nordisk, the maker of Wegovy and Ozempic, said it "continues to believe the data do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship and we remain confident in the benefit-risk profile of our GLP-1 medicines."

"We recognize that NAION can have a profound impact on patients and their families," it said. "Patient safety is a top priority for Novo, and we continue to monitor the safety of our medicines, review new research and work with health authorities around the world."
Eli Lilly, which makes Zepbound and Mounjaro, said in a statement Monday it was "carefully evaluating the update and will respond to FDA promptly."

"Patient safety is Lilly's top priority," the company said. "FDA's drug safety communication applies to all medicines with GLP-1 RA activity and does not reference any findings specific to Lilly medicines."

An FDA analysis of more than 125 clinical trials found that the problem occurred in roughly 6 of every 100,000 patients who took a GLP-1 for at least one year. The comparable rate for people taking a placebo or other types of glucose-lowering medications was less than 4 per 100,000, the FDA said.
The agency also found reports of the problem in its electronic reporting system for drug injuries and side effects.

Symptoms of the problem include blurred vision, blind spots, distorted colors and other visual disturbances, according to the FDA. Patients experiencing such problems should contact a healthcare professional immediately, the agency said.
Rizzo noted that the vision loss from the condition tends to be irreversible and can become progressively worse, even if a patient stops taking the medication.

"Usually when you lose vision, although there may be some mild degree of improvement, it's usually not a large degree of improvement," he said. "And unfortunately, a great frustration for so many of our patients and doctors who take care of patients with NAION  is the fact that we do not really know how to mitigate the risk."
Rizzo also said the condition does not necessarily affect each eye the same.

"The degree of visual loss in the first eye does not inform the degree of visual loss that would occur in the second eye," he told CBS News. "So you could have mild visual loss in one eye, and then the next eye could be severe."

title: Massie introduces Hegseth impeachment articles, teeing up vote
summary: Rep. Thomas Massie on Monday introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war against Iran without congressional authorization.
story: Washington — Rep. Thomas Massie on Monday introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war against Iran without congressional authorization and abusing the powers of his office.

The impeachment effort could attract more bipartisan support, since members of both parties are frustrated with Hegseth's handling of the war with Iran and Republicans are reeling from their defeats in the midterm elections. Lawmakers returned to Capitol Hill on Monday to reconvene for the final weeks of the GOP-controlled Congress, and Massie's move will force leaders to bring the impeachment resolution up for a vote within two legislative days.

Even before the midterm elections highlighted voters' concerns about the war in Iran and its impact on the cost of living, the push to impeach Hegseth was underway in Congress. Massie, a Kentucky Republican who has broken with the administration on a number of fronts over the past year, originally introduced impeachment articles against the defense secretary in September. House GOP leaders recessed the chamber early, pushing off a vote on the issue until November.
Massie introduced updated impeachment articles on the House floor on Monday, restarting a two-day clock for GOP leaders to schedule a vote.

The Kentucky Republican accused Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanours in a 34-page impeachment resolution with eight articles. Three charges accuse him of abusing the powers of the Department of Defense by waging war against Iran without congressional authorization.

Massie also alleged that in the conflict, Hegseth ignored laws that minimize civilian casualties, citing the strike on an Iranian school earlier this year. Another impeachment article points to the Pentagon's boat strikes in the Caribbean, while one cites the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. Another centers on free speech and the Pentagon's scrutiny of Sen. Mark Kelly after he was among a group of lawmakers who released a video calling on service members to "refuse illegal orders."

Massie argued that Hegseth "has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law."
"Peter Brian Hegseth thus warrants impeachment and trial, removal from office, and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust, or profit under the United States," Massie wrote.

Massie urged the GOP-controlled Senate to take up the resolution if it passes the House, noting that the articles will survive into the next Congress, when the upper chamber has a Democratic majority.

"If the Senate doesn't deal with this before the end of this Senate, they're turning it over to a Democrat Senate who can then have the trials and deal with it," Massie said at a news conference Monday afternoon.
Massie argued he was being "polite" with the impeachment effort and that "when the Democrats get in charge, they are going to be very vicious."

"What is an impeachment? An impeachment is just firing somebody, really. You don't go to prison. You don't go to jail. You don't pay a fine," he said. "But the Democrats are going to have hearings. They won't have just eight articles of impeachment. … The Democrats are going to bring people in here who have served under him and with him, give them protection."
Hegseth has criticized the effort by Massie, who's leaving Congress after losing his primary earlier this year.

"A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice," Hegseth said in a video posted on X last week. "You see, their policies don't work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents. It's all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me."
Hegseth told reporters Monday, "we're not worried about that." He said he planned to hold a news conference on the impeachment effort Tuesday morning.

Whether other Republicans support the effort remains to be seen. But some GOP members appeared more open to the prospect, and more eager to criticize the defense secretary, after the brutal losses for their party in the midterms.
Rep. James Comer, a Kentucky Republican who leads the House Oversight Committee, said on News Nation that "there's a lot of questions about Hegseth."

"We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one's happy about Iran," Comer said. "I think the Republican voters are more upset about what's going on in Iran than the Democrat voters."

GOP Rep. French Hill of Arkansas indicated that he's still considering whether to support the effort, saying on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday that he wants to hear the debate on the issue "to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president if he's not getting the job done in leading the Department of War."
"If you don't think he's done a good job conducting his job, that doesn't mean per se that he's committed an impeachable offense," Hill said.
Retiring GOP Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, who has been critical of the administration on some issues, said he's "wrestling" with whether to support the impeachment resolution.
He said Hegseth's handling of a number of topics "bothers me" and "I feel like he deserves a little bit of his own treatment, but that's not the right way to handle impeachment."
"I don't think he's been a good secretary, but do you impeach a guy for that? It has to be a high crime or misdemeanor," Bacon told reporters Monday at the Capitol.
House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, said Monday that impeaching Hegseth amid hostilities abroad "would be a terrible, terrible look."

Democrats are widely expected to support the impeachment effort. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said on ABC's "This Week" on Sunday that he's a "hard yes" on the impeachment effort. But with a narrow GOP majority, Republican votes will be needed.

Massie said in a post on X on Monday that he's seen some of his colleagues say "Hegseth has been effective and they agree with the war, so they'll vote not to impeach." But he said "that's not the question."
"The question is whether he committed impeachable acts," Massie said. "And the answer is yes, eight times."

Hegseth would be the third Cabinet secretary in history to be impeached. Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached in 1876 over corruption allegations. Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas was impeached by the GOP-controlled House in 2024 over the Biden administration's handling of the southern border. Belknap was acquitted by the Senate. Mayorkas had his charges dismissed.

title: Mississippi Senate race still a toss-up; Democrat holds slim lead
summary: The Senate race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved, as Democrat Scott Colom has mounted a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
story: Washington — The Senate midterm race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved, with Democrat Scott Colom mounting a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
At one point Wednesday morning, just a few dozen votes separated the candidates, a stunningly close result in the Magnolia State. As of Monday night, Colom was leading Hyde-Smith by over 2,500 votes.
State officials say several thousand ballots still need to be counted, and both campaigns have expressed confidence.

Hyde-Smith, 67, has been in the Senate since 2018 and is seeking reelection. But Colom, a district attorney, launched a formidable challenge in a state President Trump won by 20 points in 2024. Mississippi hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982.

Democrats saw a slew of wins in Senate races Tuesday night, including in states that President Trump won by double digits in the 2024 elections. Democrats have secured enough seats to take control of the chamber in the new year. If Colom manages to pull off a victory, he would add to their majority.

Colom, 43, is a seventh-generation Mississippian who campaigned on cost-of-living and healthcare issues. Democrats began investing in the race in recent weeks, seeing an opportunity for a pickup. But the possible outcome still appeared exceedingly unlikely heading into Election Day.
Speaking to supporters in the wee hours of the morning on Wednesday, Colom said, "The results are all trending in our direction."
"We are trending in counties that people thought we had no chance to compete in," Colom said. "And we're winning them."

Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said Friday there are approximately 3,300 outstanding mail ballots. The state is also processing an unknown number of affidavit ballots, or provisional ballots, from voters whose eligibility needs to be confirmed. Mail ballots must be received within five business days, while affidavit ballots must be processed within the 10-day window that counties have to certify results, which ends Nov. 13.
Mississippi does not allow recounts, so a winner will be decided based on a plurality of votes.
Both parties are keeping a close eye on the process. CBS News has confirmed the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has deployed lawyers and resources to the state to monitor the count.
"I'm confident that ultimately Mississippi has decided to go in a new direction," Colom told reporters after greeting campaign volunteers Thursday morning in Jackson.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee and Hyde-Smith campaign filed a request for all counties to separate and preserve all affidavit ballots. The Colom campaign called the move a "desperate stunt." His counsel also sent a new letter to Mississippi's 82 counties asking them to respect election procedures.

Hyde-Smith predicted that she will win reelection, posting on X: "We believe thousands of votes remain to be counted from dozens of Republican counties, and we are confident those votes will reinforce her path to victory."

At a news conference Thursday, Mississippi Republican Party Chair Mike Hurst insisted the election "is far from being over" and noted the state party has attorneys and observers throughout the state to ensure all legally cast ballots are counted.
Colom and Hyde-Smith have faced off before.

Then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom for a federal judgeship in the Northern District of Mississippi, but Hyde-Smith declined to back his nomination in April 2023, citing questions about Colom's stance on transgender issues and other concerns. Colom won the support of Mississippi's other Republican senator, Roger Wicker.

Under the Senate's "blue slip" tradition, the Senate Judiciary Committee generally does not move forward with federal district court nominees unless the senators who represent the judicial district sign off — preventing Colom from being confirmed to a lifetime judicial appointment. About two and a half years later, Colom launched his campaign for Senate.
Colom told CNN that "not having a federal judgeship is not a motivating factor for me at all" in his Senate campaign, saying he forgives Hyde-Smith.

The Mississippi contest is one of just two still-unresolved Senate races. Alaska's Senate race between GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is also outstanding, leaving the size of Democrats' majority up in the air.

title: Judge dismisses Dolly Parton's estate's lawsuit against her nephew
summary: The details of the resolution between Dolly Parton's estate and her nephew, Bryan Seaver, were not immediately known.
story: Update: A Tennessee judge on Monday dismissed the lawsuit filed by Dolly Parton's estate against her nephew and former head of security, Bryan Seaver. The judge dismissed it without prejudice, meaning it can be filed again.

The estate of the late country music icon Dolly Parton has filed to dismiss its lawsuit against her nephew and former head of security, Bryan Seaver, following accusations he threatened to commit acts of violence and destroy Parton's brand.
The details of the resolution were not immediately known.

"Mr. Seaver is grateful to put this misunderstanding behind him so that the entire family can continue to grieve peacefully and ensure that the bright light of Dolly's legacy remains completely untouched," attorneys for Seaver told CBS News in a statement.
Attorneys for Parton's estate did not respond to a request for comment.

Seaver, who heads the private security firm Squadron Augmented Protection Services, had been tasked with announcing Parton's death in August. But in September, Seaver and SAPS were fired by She's Alive, which manages Parton's estate and business interests. Parton's longtime manager, Danny Nozell, who runs She's Alive, then filed for a restraining order against Seaver and SAPS.

Parton died of cancer at the age of 80. Seaver rose to national prominence when he announced Parton's death in a prerecorded video, in which he said it was "something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality."

She's Alive, or SAL, had alleged in its request for a restraining order that Seaver "made repeated, written threats to Ms. Parton's staff, partners, legal and business advisors, and others" and that he "sought to extract money from SAL and trusts through an obscene, deliberate, and escalating campaign of threats."

In one instance prior to Parton's death, SAL alleged that Seaver threatened to "destroy the entire brand" over a disagreement involving Dollywood, the theme park and resort opened by Parton in 1986. The lawsuit also alleged that Seaver repeatedly referenced his security business, which it described as a "heavily armed, paramilitary-style force capable of projecting threat and coercion against SAL's personnel and business partners."
Seaver made many of these alleged threats via text, according to the lawsuit.

Seaver, in a response to SAL's request to extend its restraining order last month, denied "each and every allegation." He said he and Nozell had been close friends for many years and that, until his firing, the two had never had an argument "apart from a minor disagreement years ago over a company logo."

While he admitted to using coarse and blunt language, he denied threatening anybody, including Parton or her estate's business partners, saying the text messages were "private messages" between himself and Nozell.

"They were sent in the course of private conversations between two friends who were both frustrated, grieving, and discussing strategy following Ms. Parton's illness and death," the court filing states.

He insisted the messages about the Dollywood disagreement were not threats of violence but that he was "privately warning" Nozell that he thought certain associates were "harming [Parton's] brand and imploring him to help."

Seaver also said in his response that Nozell didn't respond to the various texts cited in the lawsuit with any sort of pushback or alarm. In fact, Seaver claimed Nozell urged him to publicly play up his military and security history before trying to use those ties as evidence that Seaver was dangerous and threatening.

"I have declined to speak with the media about this case and have asked my attorneys to handle all media communications," Seaver wrote at the end of his affidavit. "I care about Ms. Parton, her music, her legacy, and her family. I do not want this dispute to harm her legacy."
This story published first on CBS News at 6:19 p.m. on Nov. 5, 2026.

title: U.S. Marshals official sidelined over alleged racist incident, sources say
summary: One of the top officials at the U.S. Marshals Service has been placed on administrative leave pending an internal investigation over his alleged involvement in a racist incident targeting a Black colleague, sources told CBS News.
story: One of the top officials at the U.S. Marshals Service has been placed on administrative leave pending an internal investigation over his alleged involvement in a racist incident targeting a Black colleague, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

Peter Marketos, the assistant director of the Investigative Operations Division, was relieved of his duties after he was allegedly involved in an incident in which a watermelon was left on the desk of a deputy assistant director, who is Black.  That employee worked directly under Marketos in the same division, the sources said.

It was not immediately clear what prompted the incident — which some deputies are calling "watermelon-gate." It was also not immediately clear whether Marketos placed the fruit himself, or if it was placed by someone else under his supervision.
"The U.S. Marshals Service takes seriously any allegation of misconduct by USMS personnel," a spokesperson said.

"The alleged actions do not reflect the core values of the USMS: Justice, Integrity and Service.  While we recognize the public interest in transparency and accountability, federal privacy laws prohibit discussion of personnel matters."
CBS News has reached out to Marketos and the target of the alleged incident for comment.

The allegations have raised new questions about accountability and workplace dynamics within the leadership ranks of the federal law enforcement agency, housed under the Department of Justice. Watermelon imagery has a long history of use in derogatory racial stereotypes against Black Americans.

Internally, the incident has sparked concern among deputy marshals, who believe it is beneath the Marshals Service and reflects disturbing racist behavior that should not be tolerated, the sources added.
Marketos' bio on the website has since been removed, and he is expected to be terminated, one of the sources said.

Staff at the U.S. Marshals Service were informed in a brief email last week that Don Snider would assume leadership of the Investigative Operations Division on Monday, Nov. 9, according to a source familiar with the personnel change.

Marketos is a veteran of the Marshals Service and previously held a number of prominent leadership positions during his more than two decades with the agency. He began his career as a deputy U.S. marshal in 2002 and he subsequently oversaw sex offender investigations, fugitive apprehensions and tactical operations.

In March 2023, Marketos was assigned to be acting U.S. marshal for the District of Columbia, before being named assistant director of the Investigative Operations Division later the same year. Nearly three years later, he was also designated acting U.S. marshal for the Eastern District of Virginia. Marketos has previously served as acting associate director for investigations and testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee in September 2025 about the federal law enforcement task force operating in Washington, D.C.

The Investigative Operations Division oversees some of the Marshals Service's core law enforcement functions, including fugitive investigations and the agency's efforts to track and arrest wanted criminals.

Marketos' sister, Rose Marketos, is an agent at the FBI who was assigned to investigate the so-called "grand conspiracy" case that is probing whether Obama- and Biden-era intelligence officials conspired to keep President Trump out of office. The top federal prosecutor overseeing that investigation in South Florida announced his resignation last week.

Peter Marketos' replacement, Snider, has long served in the Marshals Service. He previously held the title of chief inspector and commander of the Capital Area Regional Fugitive Task Force, which coordinates efforts among federal, state and local law enforcement agencies to apprehend violent fugitives in the Washington metropolitan area.
This story published first on CBS News at 6:12 p.m. on Nov. 9, 2026.

title: Trump admin. proposes stricter unemployment work search rules
summary: Under a proposed federal rule, Americans seeking unemployment aid would have to conduct more job searches each week.
story: The Trump administration on Monday proposed stiffer rules for Americans seeking unemployment benefits that, if adopted, would require them to conduct more weekly job searches.

The proposed Department of Labor regulations, set to be published in the Federal Register on Tuesday, would require people applying for or collecting jobless aid to complete at least five unique work searches per week. Currently, many U.S. states require two to three qualifying work searches per week, while only four states require five. Some states require only one work search activity to qualify for unemployment benefits.

The Trump administration said the change is necessary to create consistent eligibility requirements for unemployment benefits nationwide. A national minimum weekly work search standard would "improve program integrity and strengthen labor market attachment," the Labor Department said in its proposal.

"This action is necessary to reduce inconsistencies beyond those created by local labor markets in State-level requirements for individuals to actively seek work," according to the agency. "The intended effect is to hold States accountable for administering [an unemployment compensation] program that provides temporary wage replacement to eligible individuals while they are actively seeking work through a meaningful engagement with the labor market."
The public has 60 days following publication of the proposed rule to offer comment.
Costly for states and workers
Labor advocates criticized the proposed change in work search rules, saying the new threshold would be hard for unemployed people to meet and costly for states to administer.

"Not only is the proposed change devastating to claimants who may not have five search options for every week they are unemployed, but it will likely cost states hundreds of thousands of dollars," Michele Evermore, senior director of economic security and worker transitions at the National Employment Law Project, a worker advocacy group, said in a statement to CBS News. "Nearly all states will have to change their claimant intake forms, and with it, their technology — a costly fix. Many states will have to rewrite their laws to meet this rule."

Evermore also said the proposed rule would disadvantage applicants who already struggle to navigate the unemployment benefits systems. Employers "want candidates enthusiastic about their job opportunities, not ticking boxes for the work search form," she added.
More level playing field?

The Labor Department acknowledged that the policy could temporarily raise costs as states and jobless aid applicants adapt to the new work requirement, but said the change is necessary to ensure that the eligibility rules are applied consistently across the U.S.

"These inconsistencies can create confusion for individuals, lead to uneven enforcement when allowable activities are not clearly defined, and increase the likelihood that otherwise eligible individuals may fail to meet requirements simply because expectations are unclear," the Labor Department said. "Additionally, variability in how States notify individuals of work search requirements can result in individuals engaging in activities that may not support reemployment or may not satisfy the State's rules."

Various activities would satisfy the proposed requirement that people seeking jobless aid conduct at least five work searches per week, according to the Labor Department. For example, beyond contacting a prospective employer, registering with or contacting a job placement agency or union would also count as a qualified work search.

Under the proposal, states could also designate other activities as satisfying the requirement. Additionally, states could adapt the weekly job search threshold to account for local labor market conditions through a points-based system that would allow someone applying for jobless aid to accrue multiple points for a single activity.
"Under such a system, States may assign point values to qualifying work search activities and require individuals to accumulate a minimum of five points per benefit week," the Labor Department said.

title: Judge sets trial date for Charlie Kirk's accused killer
summary: Tyler Robinson, 23, is set to stand trial on a charge of aggravated murder, which could see him face the death penalty
story: Tyler Robinson, the man accused of assassinating conservative activist Charlie Kirk, is set to stand trial beginning June 21, 2028, a Utah judge announced on Monday.

Attorneys for Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, last month asked the court for a speedy trial no later than Oct. 4, 2027, while Robinson's representatives requested that the trial take place in the third quarter of 2029, citing massive amounts of discovery. Prosecutors proposed the trial begin in January 2028, rather than hold the proceedings during the Thanksgiving and Christmas holidays.
Judge Tony Graf on Monday set a date between the three parties' requests.
Kirk's family called the decision "deeply disappointing."

"While nothing will restore the time we have lost with Charlie, every additional day without justice prolongs our family's pain and forces us to wait even longer for accountability," the family said in a statement.
The court has allotted 105 court days for the trial, with monthly pretrial status conferences going forward to "protect the constitutional rights at stake."

A hearing is also scheduled for April 11, 2028, during which the court will decide whether attorneys for both sides can complete the essential work before jury selection. Jury questionnaires are due May 3, 2028.

In September, Graf decided in favor of prosecutors who say they have enough evidence against Robinson to put the 23-year-old on trial on a charge of aggravated murder, which could see him face the death penalty, life in prison without parole, or 25 years to life in prison with parole.
Trial proceedings are set to begin at 9:30 a.m. in courtroom 4B in the Fourth District courthouse in Provo, Utah.

Robinson has pleaded not guilty to the aggravated murder charge. He is accused of gunning down Charlie Kirk, 31, as the activist spoke to several thousand people at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025. Court proceedings so far have already lasted more than a year.
The defendant turned himself in a day after the shooting. His lawyers have not offered alternative theories for Charlie Kirk's death.

Charlie Kirk helped galvanize young voters around President Trump during the 2024 election. Mr. Trump weighed in on the trial in a social media post last month, saying Robinson should be tried "within a month." The Republican criticized Graf — a former prosecutor appointed as a judge last year — for "taking forever to ask questions that people already know the answer to."

Utah County prosecutors allege Robinson targeted Charlie Kirk for his political beliefs. They say a bullet found in the rifle used to kill Charlie Kirk was engraved with the words "Hey Facist! CATCH!" and that Robinson wrote in a text message about Charlie Kirk: "I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can't be negotiated out."

Robinson's attorneys said in court filings this week that they must sift through tens of thousands of files turned over by prosecutors. They plan to conduct extensive investigations into Robinson's life in a search for mitigating factors that could influence his sentence if convicted, and to devote "substantial time" to issues such as jury selection.
Elli Fitzgerald contributed to this report.

title: Key moments from ex-cop's trial in the death of Sandra Birchmore
summary: A jury in Massachusetts is deliberating the fate of former police officer Matthew Farwell, who is charged in the 2021 death of 23-year-old Sandra Birchmore.
story: A jury in Massachusetts continues deliberating the fate of Matthew Farwell in his trial over the death of Sandra Birchmore, who federal prosecutors say was killed by the former police officer after years of sexual abuse that started when she was a teenager.
Farwell has pleaded not guilty to killing the 23-year-old and her unborn son in 2021. Prosecutors accused Farwell of staging Birchmore's death to look like a suicide.

Prosecutors said Farwell started sexually abusing Birchmore when she was 15 and he was 27. The two met through a police youth program that's designed to teach children about law enforcement careers. Farwell, who worked for the police department in Stoughton, Massachusetts, was an instructor for the program.

Birchmore's manner of death was initially determined by local authorities to be a suicide, but was later changed to undetermined. After a federal investigation into her death, Farwell was charged in 2024 with killing a witness or a victim, with prosecutors alleging that Farwell killed Birchmore to silence her about the abuse. In 2025, he was charged with causing the death of an unborn child.
Farwell didn't take the witness stand during the trial. Attorneys gave their closing arguments on Friday before the case went to the jury.

During the trial in U.S. District Court in Boston, Farwell's attorneys didn't deny that he had an affair with Birchmore. His lawyers instead tried to cast doubt on prosecutors' theory of the case and how she died.
Here are some key takeaways from the trial:
Birchmore wanted a baby from Farwell

When Birchmore learned Farwell was expecting a third child with his wife, Birchmore said she wanted him to impregnate her or else she would tell his wife about the affair, according to text messages revealed during the trial.
"I gave him an ultimatum and I'm getting his baby. He was not at all happy about it," Birchmore said in a text message to a friend in October 2020.
By late December, she was pregnant. On Dec. 28, 2020, she sent Farwell a picture of a poster that said, "Congrats we are goin' to be parents!"
When Birchmore told Farwell he needed to be with her while she's in labor, he responded, "You are truly the worst person on the face of the earth."
The next day, Farwell texted Birchmore, "You extorted me to get what you wanted."
Prosecutors said they met up, and things didn't appear to go well.
"I'm not going to be around anymore and neither is your kid. Congrats. Hope you're happy," Birchmore texted Farwell.
She also told Farwell she felt scared when he was next to her during that meetup. "I thought you were going to hit me," she said.
Prosecution and defense experts disagree on Birchmore's death

Birchmore's body was discovered Feb. 4, 2021, when police conducted a welfare check at her apartment after she didn't show up to work . She was found hanging in a seated position from a door handle by a duffle bag strap.

Prosecutors argued that Farwell used the strap to strangle her and then staged the scene to look like a suicide. Farwell's attorneys, however, noted that Birchmore had written an apparent suicide note in a journal in 2017 and searched on the internet, "What color is the suicide ribbon," days before she was found dead.

A strangulation expert for the prosecution, Dr. William Smock, told jurors that Birchmore's death was a homicide. He said a clasp on the strap caused an injury on her chest and was hanging from the knob, suggesting that the scene was staged. He also said the fracture of Birchmore's hyoid bone, located in the neck, rarely happens in suicides.

Defense expert Heather Garvin, an anthropologist who has a doctorate in anatomy, said the fracture doesn't definitively prove that Birchmore's death was a homicide. Another defense witness, forensic scientist Alicia McCarthy, testified that she couldn't conclude with certainty that the injury on Birchmore's chest was caused by the clasp.

Dr. Thomas Andrew, a former chief medical examiner for the state of New Hampshire who testified for the defense, said that all of the factors of Birchmore's death made him think it was a suicide. "This is not manual strangulation," he said.
Farwell wasn't the father of Birchmore's child

DNA testing found that Farwell didn't father Birchmore's child, FBI Special Agent Heidi Kelsch testified. Instead, the father was Jason Pickard, a defense contractor for the Air Force who met Birchmore when he was a recruiter for the Army Reserve.
Birchmore, who was 22 at the time, was considering enlisting when she and Pickard, who was married at the time, started texting in December 2019. The relationship eventually became sexual.
When Pickard found out about Birchmore's relationship with Farwell, he said he urged her to report him, but she didn't. He also didn't alert authorities about the relationship.

"I was afraid. I was a married man. I was a recruiter and she was a recruit. I knew what it would do to my marriage, I knew what it would do to my children, I knew what it would do to my career," he said. "I also respected her request not to tell."
When Birchmore became pregnant, she told Pickard the child wasn't his.
Witness says Farwell got upset by call about relationship

On Jan. 20, 2021, about two weeks before Birchmore was found dead, Stoughton police dispatcher James Fitton received a call from a female who "alluded to a relationship between Matthew Farwell and her friend," Fitton said during his testimony.
When Fitton told Farwell about the call, he got angry. "He got visibly and audibly upset with me," Fitton said.
He threw out the note he took about the call after he said his supervisor told him to forget about it.
When Farwell texted Birchmore about the call, she told him the friend owed her money.
Farwell went to Birchmore's apartment before she died

Matthew Dunne, a Massachusetts State Police trooper who initially investigated Birchmore's death, testified that after he learned of the relationship between Birchmore and Farwell, he interviewed Farwell on Feb. 6, 2021.
According to Dunne, Farwell went to Birchmore's apartment on Feb. 1, 2021, which was the last day she was at work.
"The account he provided was that he went over there to break up with her," Dunne said.
Farwell also told Dunne he went to see Birchmore to tell her that the baby wasn't his.
Farwell left Birchmore's apartment building after her phone stopped moving
Dunne confirmed that before Farwell left her apartment, data from Birchmore's phone showed it had stopped moving.
An FBI digital forensic examiner, Christopher Beckstrom, told jurors Birchmore's phone locked for the last time at 9:13 p.m. on Feb. 1, 2021.

Farwell was seen on surveillance video footage entering Birchmore's apartment building that night wearing a hooded sweatshirt and face mask at 9:14 p.m. Birchmore texted Farwell to let him know her door was open, Beckstrom said.
Birchmore's phone recorded eight steps were taken at 9:40 p.m., and no other steps were recorded after that time.
At 9:43 p.m., Farwell was seen on the security camera leaving Birchmore's building. Kelsch testified that Birchmore usually sent Farwell a text after he visited her, but she didn't that night.
Birchmore was excited to be pregnant

Birchmore worked for the school district in the nearby town of Sharon, Massachusetts. She was excited when she learned she was pregnant, according to testimony from Cheryl Carlson, an assistant principal who worked with Birchmore.
Birchmore told Carlson she wanted the baby "to have someone to love."
Birchmore also opened up to Carlson about the baby's father.
"She said that the father was in a committed relationship and that there were children involved, and that the plan was that he was going to leave his situation when her child was born," Carlson said.
She also testified that Birchmore had told third graders that the father was her police officer boyfriend.
Carlson was caught off guard when she learned Birchmore's death was initially called a suicide.
"Suicide didn't make sense to me," she said. "Because she was so excited to have that baby, she was so determined to have the baby, it didn't fit with her character."
Farwell told state police his relationship with Birchmore started much later

Farwell provided Dunne with a different account of his relationship with Birchmore than what prosecutors said. According to Dunne, Farwell said the relationship had been going on for about two to three years, which would have made Birchmore 20 or 21 at the time they began seeing each other.
"I believe he said he was intoxicated at some point and they encountered each other," Dunne said.

But that account conflicts with text messages between Birchmore and Farwell that were read during the trial about how their sexual relationship started when she was 15. When prosecutors asked Dunne if Farwell's contradictory statements were factors in the investigation, Dunne said they were given weight.
"All of this has to be taken into context with the full investigation, but they were definitely given weight," Dunne said.
State police didn't take notes during initial Farwell interviews

Dunne's first interview with Farwell in the school parking lot wasn't recorded and he didn't take any notes. During the trial, he testified that was a tactical decision so Farwell would talk to investigators.
When Dunne and his supervisor, Sgt. John Fanning, who knew Farwell, interviewed him a few days later, neither of them took notes, Dunne testified.

title: Nvidia stock slumps amid board investigation into CEO Jensen Huang
summary: Investors are questioning whether Huang's future as Nvidia's CEO may be at risk amid allegations that he was targeted in a Chinese intelligence operation.
story: Nvidia's stock price slid on Monday amid questions about CEO Jensen Huang's future at the chipmaker, following the board of directors' investigation into allegations that China targeted him in an intelligence operation.

The investigation is raising concerns about Huang's role at the company, which he co-founded and helped build into the world's second-most valuable company, with a $4.5 trillion valuation. Nvidia is barred from selling its high-end chips, specifically designed to power artificial intelligence models, to China due to competitive concerns.
Nvidia shares sank 4.3%, or $7.97, to $178.67, shrinking the chipmaker's market valuation by about $193 billion.

The allegations center around reports that Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, the country's main intelligence agency. On Sunday, Nvidia's board said it is starting an "independent investigation" into the allegations, sparking questions about the CEO's future with the company.

"This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons," Dan Ives, a tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, said in a research note. "The key question investors will be asking is: Will Jensen remain CEO of Nvidia?"

Ives added, "There is clearly risk that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the board investigation, and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally."

In a statement to CBS News, an Nvidia spokesperson said that "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption." The company didn't respond to a question about whether Huang had violated any of its corporate policies.

The company's board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised. John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, told CBS News on Sunday, "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us."

The Chinese government dismissed allegations that it targeted Nvidia's chief executive, who co-founded the company in 1993, as part of an espionage operation. "The so-called Chinese spy narrative is entirely baseless and constitutes slander and smear," Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said in a statement.
Who is Alice Huang?
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a former executive at a Singapore-based data center company, Megaspeed International, whose website touts its partnership with Nvidia.
Many offices in Singapore were closed on Monday for a holiday. Megaspeed and the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
Succession challenges

Replacing Jensen Huang, 63, would prove challenging because he is viewed as integral to the company's success, tech analysts said on Monday. Huang also serves as the public face of Nvidia, appearing at industry events and media interviews in his trademark black leather jacket.
Huang is the company's fifth-largest shareholder, with about 3.4% of its shares, according to financial data provider FactSet.

"There is no known succession plan, and there is no leader in the company who would be the clear next step if he had to step down. In many ways, Jensen is Nvidia's Steve Jobs," said Daniel Newman, CEO of tech consulting firm Futurum, in an email.
He added, "That does not mean they cannot find a Tim Cook in the future, but it would be a massive changing of the guard, and the company has not been set up for that."
Another blow for the AI trade

The scandal puts more pressure on Nvidia shares, which have already been bruised by mounting investor concerns about the valuations of companies driving AI growth. Prior to Monday's early decline, Nvidia's shares had tumbled almost 20% over the last month amid a broader sell-off in AI stocks.

The board investigation into Huang could loom over Nvidia and raise the risk that U.S. regulators could impose additional restrictions on the company's chip exports, according to Adam Crisafulli, an analyst at Vital Knowledge.

"The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised," said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a Washington-based consultancy.

In recent years, Jensen Huang has lobbied federal authorities to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China, winning approval from President Trump to sell its H200 chips this year. Those chips are not Nvidia's most advanced models, but they are still considered important products for Nvidia.
Previously, Huang also lobbied Mr. Trump to be allowed to sell Nvidia's less-advanced H20 chips, which were designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China.

"The real potential fallout from the Jensen Huang scandal will be the U.S. government imposing dramatically more draconian restrictions on sales of sophisticated chips to China (the issue isn't the H200 but instead the fact that a large amount of higher-end Nvidia products are still making it into the hands of Chinese buyers)," Crisafulli said in a research note.

title: Supreme Court allows border wall construction in Big Bend region
summary: The Supreme Court agreed to lift a district court order that temporarily stopped construction of the border wall and other infrastructure in the Big Bend sector.
story: Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for the Trump administration to resume building a border wall and other infrastructure through a remote area of West Texas while litigation over the project moves forward.

In an unsigned decision, the high court agreed to lift a district court's injunction that temporarily stopped construction of the wall and related infrastructure in the Big Bend sector, which covers more than 500 miles of the southern border and includes Big Bend National Park.
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson said she would have denied the Justice Department's request for emergency relief.

In its five-page decision, the Supreme Court said in part that the lower court's order delays construction of the border barrier and roads in the Big Bend region and "impedes the Government from advancing its 'compelling interests' in border security and integrity."

The challengers to the wall project "claim that construction in the Big Bend Sector will diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area," the court said. "But Congress's enactment of [immigration law] — which permits the Secretary to waive the requirements of environmental-protection and other conservation laws — reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert."
The Center for Biological Diversity, one of the plaintiffs that sued to stop wall construction, lambasted the Supreme Court's decision.

"The Trump administration and its contractors are hellbent on destroying one of America's greatest national parks, and the Supreme Court just gave them the green light," Laiken Jordahl, the group's national public lands advocate, said in a statement. "This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal. They're signing off on the permanent destruction of the wildest place in Texas, and the theft of a great American river from all of us."

The Trump administration had asked the Supreme Court last month to step into the legal fight over the border wall in the Big Bend region and argued that the halt ordered by U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone frustrated its ability to combat illegal border crossings in the area.

Stopping construction of the wall and roads along that portion of the U.S.-Mexico border would have serious consequences, Solicitor General D. John Sauer warned, including "disruption of the government's ability to secure a quarter of the southern border against cartel incursions, drug trafficking, and illegal entry; creation of a massive vulnerability in border protection that risks funneling illegal entry and trafficking into the unsecured Big Bend Sector; and irreversible delays, costs, and operational harms from halting already-begun construction."

But an environmental nonprofit, a professional riverboat guide and a religious organization, which filed a lawsuit challenging the project, argued that allowing the Trump administration to resume construction of roads and the wall would permanently alter an "irreplaceable landscape" that includes Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, and nearly 200 miles of the Rio Grande Wild and Scenic River corridor.

"Once habitat is destroyed, vegetation cleared, historic resources damaged, livelihoods and private property destroyed, and wilderness landscapes fragmented by roads, barriers, and associated infrastructure, no final judgment can restore the status quo," lawyers for the plaintiffs wrote in a Supreme Court filing.
President Trump has promised to build a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border for more than a decade and has made the 30-foot barrier a cornerstone of his plan to tackle illegal immigration.

To speed up construction of the wall and other barriers along the southern border in Texas, the secretary of Homeland Security — first Kristi Noem and then Markwayne Mullin — issued a total of three waivers for project areas in the Big Bend region beginning in February.

The federal government would typically have to ensure compliance with federal environmental protection and historical preservation laws before moving forward with construction. But the Department of Homeland Security invoked a 1996 federal immigration law that gives the secretary the authority to waive all legal requirements deemed necessary to ensure "expeditious" construction of barriers and roads near the southern border.

In response to the move, the plaintiffs filed their lawsuit to stop the Trump administration from building new 30-foot bollard walls and other infrastructure in the Big Bend region. The waivers issued by DHS, they said, would "authorize massive projects that would cleave through the Chihuahuan Desert, sever public and wildlife access to iconic sections of the Rio Grande, and mark one of the final—and most consequential — steps towards completing 'the Wall.'"

Separate from the litigation, the president's planned wall garnered pushback from Republican and Democratic lawmakers, cattle ranchers and local law enforcement in Texas when photos and videos shared to social media in August showed bulldozers arriving at Big Bend National Park.

In response to the backlash, Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott announced that construction inside the park would be paused until the end of September. Scott has said that the proposed 30-foot border wall will not cut through Big Bend National Park, but other infrastructure would, including more than 200 miles of patrol roads and roughly 17 miles of a vehicle-barrier system, according to CBP.
Construction of a 47-mile-long stretch of wall in Hudspeth County, which is part of the Big Bend region, began in September, according to immigration agencies.

But last month, Cardone, the district judge, granted a preliminary injunction that barred the Trump administration from building border barriers or related infrastructure, or engaging in "any construction or ground disturbing activities" in the Big Bend sector.
Cardone found that the secretary of Homeland Security exceeded his authority when issuing the waivers that allowed construction of the wall to proceed.
The Trump administration and the challengers to the project were at odds over whether the Big Bend sector is an area of "high illegal entry" requiring additional border barriers.
The government has argued that immigration officers apprehended more than 89,000 people trying to cross into the U.S. illegally in that area between 2021 and 2025.

But the plaintiffs said that Big Bend ranks last for apprehensions compared to the other six sectors along the southern border. While the area covers more than 25% of the U.S.-Mexico border, annual apprehensions in the Big Bend Sector ranged between 0.3% and 2.2% of total border-wide apprehensions, according to court filings.

title: Reported Iran threat sees U.S. moves planes from second U.K. base
summary: The reported movement comes just over a month after a security incident at a separate air base hosting U.S. aircraft used in the war with Iran.
story: The U.S. military moved nine Stratotanker refueling planes from a base in England to facilities in Germany and Spain on Monday, and The Wall Street Journal quoted sources as saying they had been repositioned due to a threat from Iran.
It is unclear whether the threat was imminent or general, the sources told the newspaper.

CBS News Confirmed found public aircraft tracking data showing 10 KC-135 Stratotankers were moved from Royal Air Force Base Mildenhall, in southeast England to other locations. One landed at Glasgow Prestwick Airport in Scotland, while four went to Spangdahlem Air Base in Germany and one landed at Ramstein Air Base, the headquarters of the U.S. Forces Europe, also in Germany.
Four more Stratotankers left Mildenhall and arrived Monday at Morón Air Base in southern Spain.

"We take proactive measures to ensure our aircraft, our people, and our installations remain safe and secure," a U.S. official told CBS News on Tuesday, without commenting on specific aircraft movements.

Three U.S. Osprey tiltrotor transport planes also departed RAF Mildenhall and arrived Tuesday at RAF Lakenheath, another base used by the U.S. in England. It is unclear whether all of the movements were linked to the reported threat from Iran.
A U.S. Air Force spokesperson told CBS News that aircraft routinely "rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons including training and real world requirements."

The spokesman added that "U.S. military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our Allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets."

The U.S. Air Force 100th Air Refueling Wing, which has been based at RAF Mildenhall for years, did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment on the aircraft movements. The 100th air wing is the only permanent U.S. refueling wing in Europe.

The relocation of the aircraft comes just over a month after the U.S. Air Force decided to remove all of its long-range bombers from RAF Fairford, another air base in England that had been used to launch strikes on Iran, following a security incident there.

On Sept. 27, five British men were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses close to the Fairford base. The suspects were later released on bail. A month later, two men were charged with security-related offenses in connection with the incident.

Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, was charged with "assisting a foreign intelligence service" and "engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out U.K.-related activities."

Nouman Essghir, also 24, was charged with a national security offense after he "approached or was in the vicinity of a prohibited place and his conduct was for a purpose that he knew, or having regards to other matters known to him ought reasonably to have known, was prejudicial to the safety or interests of the United Kingdom."
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said at the time that Iran was believed to have "played a part" in the September incident, though he did not provide any details.

"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America," Burnham told the BBC in October.

U.K. counterterrorism police said no explosives were found in extensive searches of the three vehicles operated by the men arrested near RAF Fairford, only some fuel and a number of large, mostly empty plastic drums.

title: U.S. becoming first nation to refuse U.N. Human Rights Council review
summary: "This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own 'values' as it pushes anti-American rhetoric," a State Department spokesperson said.
story: Geneva — The United States is set on Tuesday to become the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the U.N.'s top rights body since it was created two decades ago.
The Trump administration last year pulled the U.S. out of the Human Rights Council, accusing it of an anti-U.S. and anti-Israel bias, and alleging that it didn't uphold the very values it promotes.

Supporters back the council's mandate to keep tabs on human rights in all U.N. member states including the U.S., which has drawn criticism for its policies including strong-arm deportations and targeted killings of alleged drug-runners in the Caribbean and Pacific — which the administration has said are designed to protect U.S. workers and help keep the country safe.
The Geneva-based council regularly examines the rights records of all 193 U.N. member states — generally about every four to five years — as part of a process known as the universal periodic review.

The United States, under President Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago. The scheduled November 2025 review was pushed back until Tuesday in hopes that the U.S. government might change its mind.
It did not.
"(W)e give no credibility to the agency," a State Department spokesperson said in an email to The Associated Press.

"This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own 'values' as it pushes anti-American rhetoric," the spokesperson said, alleging the council has a "persistent failure to condemn the most egregious human rights violators."
The council says the process requires participation of the country in question, and in the case of an absence of any national representatives, the review cannot go forward.

As part of such reviews, national delegations - which at times can include a dozen officials or more - make a presentation, face questions and hear recommendations from other national envoys. It's supposed to be a sweeping and constructive process, akin to holding up a mirror to governments to improve their human rights policies.
Critics of the U.S. move warn that the walkout could encourage other countries - many of which bristle about intense scrutiny from human rights monitors - to follow suit.

Jamil Dakwar, director of the American Civil Liberties Union's human rights program, said: "The administration is saying to the world, 'we don't care about whether you would review us or not, we're going to continue to violate human rights unabashed.'

"And we are saying: 'No, enough is enough. This council should hold the United States accountable,'" he told reporters Monday in Geneva, as part of a push by some groups to raise awareness about the U.S. rights record.
He said the ACLU and its allies have called on the U.N. human rights chief to respond by presenting an update on rights in the United States early next year.
Eric Tistounet, a visiting professor at the Geneva Graduate Institute, who was the council's first secretary, said the U.S. walkout could affect the credibility of the council's review system.
"If the predominant global power — which has always claimed to adhere to the human rights norms — doesn't show up and doesn't even justify why, then you are in big trouble," he said.
