title: Struggling with depression? Psychiatrist says 6 habits may be making it worse
summary: Dr. Daniel Amen reveals the everyday habits that worsen depression, from alcohol use and isolation to processed foods and unchecked negative thoughts.
story: Dr. Daniel Amen, founder of Amen Clinics, identifies six behaviors people should avoid when experiencing depression, including drinking alcohol, withdrawing from others and consuming highly processed foods.

Depression rates among Americans ages 12 and older rose nearly 60% over a decade, increasing from 8.2% in 2013–2014 to 13.1% in 2021–2023, according to a recent report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Finding the right treatment for depression can take time, and antidepressants usually take four to eight weeks to work, per the National Institute of Mental Health.

For those struggling with the condition, clinical psychiatrist Dr. Daniel Amen – founder of Amen Clinics in California – says avoiding the following habits may help to manage symptoms and support mental health.
IS DRINKING EVERY DAY ALCOHOLISM? EXPERTS EXPLAIN WHERE CULTURE AND ADDICTION COLLIDE
No. 1: Drinking alcohol
Alcohol may offer temporary relief from depression symptoms, but as its effects wear off, mood can worsen.
Dr. Daniel Amen (right) is the founder of brain scan company Amen Clinics in California. (Katie Levine; iStock)
As the brain adjusts to alcohol’s relaxing effects, it can leave people feeling more anxious and restless after the buzz fades, making them feel "worse than before," Amen warned.
Drinking can also disrupt sleep, adding to next-day fatigue, according to the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism.
No. 2: Staying in bed
It might be tempting to linger in bed when you wake up, but Amen encouraged people with depression to get up and start their day.

"When people are depressed, they tend to have pretty low activity, especially in the front part of their brain, but burying yourself under the covers just makes things worse," he said. "Get up, get out."
SCIENTISTS REVEAL SURPRISINGLY EASY EXERCISE THAT MAY BOOST YOUR MOOD IN JUST 10 MINUTES
Amen's advice aligns with a broader approach called behavioral activation, a type of therapy that helps people gradually return to meaningful activities rather than withdraw from them.
Behavioral activation has been shown to be beneficial for treating depression, according to a 2020 Cochrane review of 53 studies involving 5,495 adults.
"Burying yourself under the covers just makes things worse," Amen said in reference to depression. (iStock)
No. 3: Believing your negative thoughts
A negative mindset can make it easier to believe things that aren’t true — or, as Amen puts it, every "stupid" thought. He refers to these as "ANTs," or automatic negative thoughts.
"The thoughts that come into your mind automatically and ruin your day – they drive depression," he said.
"Burying yourself under the covers just makes things worse … get up, get out."
When feeling strong emotions – such as sadness, anger, anxiety or just lack of control – Amen recommends writing down what you’re thinking and then asking yourself if it’s true.
"My favorite part – and there's a whole method to this – is flipping the thought and actually meditating on the opposite of the thought you have," he said. "So, taking each thought captive."
No. 4: Isolating yourself
Depression can lead people to withdraw from others, but social isolation may worsen symptoms, Amen said.
"The more isolated you get, the louder the ANT chorus gets, and it makes [depression] worse," he cautioned.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

A 2025 study published in General Hospital Psychiatry tracked more than 339,000 U.K. adults for roughly 12 years. Loneliness was associated with a 77% higher risk of developing depression, while social isolation was linked to a 14% higher risk.
No. 5: Eating highly processed foods
Eating more ultraprocessed foods, including many fast-food items, has been linked to a higher risk of depression, Amen said, although research has not established cause and effect.
"There's actually a lot of consensus now among psychiatrists that inflammation drives certain types of depression," the doctor told Fox News Digital.
A negative mindset can make it easier to believe things that aren’t true — which Amen refers to these as "ANTs," or automatic negative thoughts. (iStock)
A 2025 review in the American Journal of Psychiatry supports inflammation’s role in some cases, but notes that elevated inflammatory markers occurred in only a subset of people with depression.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Amen recommends adhering to an anti-inflammatory diet emphasizing "vegetables, healthy protein and healthy fats."

A 2024 review of five randomized trials involving 1,507 adults found that Mediterranean-style diets reduced depressive symptoms compared with control groups, although results varied considerably among studies.
No. 6: Taking medication without a proper assessment
Depression treatment is individualized, so not every medication is right for everyone — and not every patient requires medication.
Amen emphasized the importance of receiving a thorough assessment prior to receiving antidepressants, which he said can be "lifesaving."
Some supplements, like omega-3 and saffron, have been found to be more effective than antidepressants in recent research. (iStock)

For milder depression, psychotherapy is often the first approach. People with moderate or severe depression are usually prescribed medication as part of their initial treatment plan, according to the National Institute of Mental Health.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

For those who have done "all the right things" but still struggle, Amen encouraged seeking further medical evaluation. Depending on symptoms and medical history, a clinician may order blood tests to check for conditions such as anemia or thyroid disease that could contribute to symptoms.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The doctor also recommended considering approaches beyond medication, such as exercise — or, as Amen suggested, "walking like you're late" — which has been proven in studies to perform better than some depression medications.
Some supplements, like omega-3 and saffron, have been found to be more effective than antidepressants in recent research.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Simple bedtime change may help some individuals lose weight, study finds
summary: An NYU clinical trial found that moving bedtime just one hour earlier led to weight loss in prediabetes patients, even without longer sleep.
story: Metabolic health expert Jim LaValle explains how chronic stress, inadequate sleep and everyday dietary choices can affect blood sugar regulation and contribute to insulin resistance.
Falling asleep earlier was linked to greater weight loss in adults with prediabetes, according to new research.

An analysis of data from a randomized trial led by the NYU Rory Meyers College of Nursing found that each hour earlier participants fell asleep was associated with roughly 1. 3 pounds of weight loss over eight weeks, although the finding does not prove that moving bedtime earlier causes weight loss.

"When we fall asleep — not just how much we sleep — seems to be an important and overlooked factor for weight loss and metabolic health," Susan Kohl Malone, an assistant professor at the nursing college and the study's lead author, said in a press release.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY PREVENT PREDIABETES FROM TURNING INTO DIABETES

The investigation, published in the journal Nursing Research, evaluated 196 adults diagnosed with prediabetes who routinely logged fewer than 6.5 hours of sleep nightly. Half the group took part in an eight-week lifestyle education course on diet, exercise and stress.
Going to bed earlier was linked to weight loss in adults with prediabetes, independent of the total number of hours they spent asleep. (iStock)
The other half received the same training alongside behavioral coaching meant to get them to go to bed earlier in gradual phases.
DIETITIAN REVEALS SIMPLE EATING STRATEGY FOR BETTER SLEEP — AND ONE HABIT TO AVOID
Researchers tracked participants’ blood sugar, sleep and activity using sensors, sleep logs and wrist-worn monitors.

Neither group showed significant improvements in blood sugar. Both groups lost weight, but those receiving sleep coaching did not lose significantly more than those receiving lifestyle education alone.
Participants who received sleep coaching did report better sleep quality and less daytime drowsiness, and they gradually began going to bed earlier. (iStock)
"While we expected that extending sleep would improve glucose levels and weight loss in adults with prediabetes who sleep for shorter periods, this wasn't the case in our study," Malone said.
Participants who received sleep coaching did report better sleep quality and less daytime drowsiness, and they gradually began going to bed earlier.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
In a separate analysis across both groups, participants who shifted their sleep earlier tended to lose more weight.

The researchers suggested the body’s internal clock may help explain the findings. Staying up late can increase exposure to artificial light, which may activate the body’s stress response and affect hormones that regulate hunger.
A statistical projection from the study found that every 60 minutes earlier a participant fell asleep was associated with roughly 1.3 pounds of weight loss across eight weeks. (iStock)
Remaining awake late also coincides with the hours when human insulin sensitivity is at its lowest.
"In contrast, falling asleep earlier may limit late-night eating and better align food intake with the body's optimal metabolic window," Malone noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The trial ran for only eight weeks, which means it's unclear whether participants could maintain earlier bedtimes or sustain weight loss over the long term.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
While participants wore wrist monitors, key sleep metrics like rest quality and daytime drowsiness relied heavily on self-reported logs.
Researchers noted that staying awake late elevates hunger hormones like ghrelin and increases the likelihood of late-night eating when the body's insulin sensitivity is at its lowest. (iStock)
The findings also show an association across the study group rather than proven cause and effect.
Participants receiving sleep coaching fell asleep about 12 minutes earlier on average, according to Malone, which produced no measurable improvement in blood sugar levels.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The study received funding from the National Institute of Nursing Research, a division of the National Institutes of Health, and was conducted in collaboration with researchers from the University of Delaware.

title: Certain sleep habits could offer clues to hidden type of depression, scientists say
summary: A study of over 11,000 Australian adults links specific sleep habits and circadian rhythm disruptions to a newly proposed subtype of depression.
story: Metabolic health expert Jim LaValle explains how chronic stress, inadequate sleep and everyday dietary choices can affect blood sugar regulation and contribute to insulin resistance.
A person's sleep habits may help identify a newly proposed subtype of depression linked to the body's internal clock.
In a study of 11,380 Australian adults with a history of depression, about 23% met researchers' criteria for what they called "circadian depression."

The profile included at least three of six features: being an evening person, waking up feeling very tired, sleeping longer during the worst periods of depression, experiencing seasonal changes, having a later midpoint between falling asleep and waking up, and experiencing "social jetlag," a large shift in sleep timing between workdays and days off.
The seasonal changes could involve sleep, mood, activity, appetite, weight or energy.
THE DAYTIME HABIT THAT COULD TRANSFORM YOUR SLEEP, ACCORDING TO NEW STUDY
The study, published on Oct. 20 in The British Journal of Psychiatry, could eventually help guide more personalized care for patients with depression, according to the researchers.

"Depression is not a uniform illness, and understanding the characteristics of different subtypes means we can give people earlier access to treatments that will be most effective for them," first author Emiliana Tonini, Ph.D., from the University of Sydney's Brain and Mind Centre, said in a statement.
Researchers are studying whether disrupted sleep-wake rhythms may help identify a proposed subtype of depression. (iStock)
The label, however, is not a formal diagnosis and needs independent replication and further study, the researchers noted.
Treatment questions

People in the circadian group reported an earlier onset of depression and more severe symptoms than those who did not meet the criteria. They were also more likely to report weight gain during depressive episodes.

They also reported poorer responses and more side effects with two common classes of antidepressants, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs).
POPULAR SLEEP AIDS BEFORE SURGERY COULD PREVENT PAINKILLER DEPENDENCE LATER
Participants reported how well their medications worked, but the study did not explain why some were less effective and did not test treatments aimed at adjusting the body’s internal clock.
Researchers said light exposure, regular sleep schedules and melatonin-related approaches warrant further study.
The proposed circadian profile includes features such as waking very tired, oversleeping during depression and being an evening person. (iStock)

Dr. Ian Hickie, a study co-author and professor of psychiatry at the University of Sydney, said the proposed profile "cuts across existing historic subtypes" of depression, most commonly atypical and bipolar depression, because they share features such as low energy and oversleeping.
COMMON GYM SUPPLEMENT COULD HELP FIGHT DEPRESSION, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS

Atypical depression can also involve weight gain, while bipolar depression refers to depressive episodes in people with bipolar disorder, which also involves periods of unusually elevated or irritable mood and increased energy.
"We define circadian only by sleep-wake and circadian features," Hickie told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

For some people with this profile, Hickie said sleep-wake disruption may be more than a symptom of depression. "This type of circadian disturbance is not simply a consequence, but the underlying cause," he wrote.
The study itself, however, could not establish whether body-clock disruption caused depression or resulted from it.
Staying up late or struggling to wake up does not, by itself, mean someone has depression, the researchers noted. (iStock)
Staying up late or having trouble waking does not necessarily indicate depression. Participants had already reported depression, which in some cases was severe, recurring or long-lasting.

Participants in the circadian group also reported more manic-like experiences. John Puls, a psychotherapist and adjunct professor at Florida Atlantic University, said those symptoms could help explain their reported response to antidepressants.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"SSRIs are not meant to treat these more significant mental health symptoms that go far beyond depressive symptoms," Puls, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital. "In fact, some SSRIs can actually worsen manic symptoms, which lead to poor sleep."
Study limitations
There were several limitations to the study, the researchers acknowledged.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Participants reported their own sleep patterns and treatment experiences, and the cross-sectional analysis didn't show whether sleep disruption preceded or followed depressive symptoms.
All participants were of European ancestry, so the findings may not apply to other populations.
Researchers used six sleep-related features to identify the proposed circadian depression profile, including having social jetlag and being an evening person. (iStock)
Jillian Amodio, a Maryland-based psychotherapist and founder of Moms For Mental Health, cautioned against using the findings as "a benchmark for treating each person in the same way."
"Biological, environmental, social and psychological factors all need to be accounted for," Amodio, who was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Researchers should examine more populations, including people who work night shifts, and account for differences in time zones and seasons, according to Amodio.
The study was led by researchers at the University of Sydney and QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute, with co-authors from institutions in Australia, the U.K. and the U.S.
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: Popular drinks linked to heart attacks, cardiac arrest in young adults, study finds
summary: Energy drinks with caffeine and stimulants were linked to cardiac arrest reports 11 times more often than non-stimulant products, per AHA research.
story: Colin Kane, M.D., a pediatric cardiologist and professor at UT Southwestern Medical Center, discusses new research that found a connection between energy drinks, stimulant-containing supplements and reports of serious heart problems.
Energy drinks and stimulant-containing supplements have been linked to the risk of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attacks, particularly among young adults.
That’s according to new research released by the American Heart Association, which will be presented at the AHA Scientific Sessions in Chicago, Nov. 6-9, 2026.

A retrospective observational analysis looked at more than 28,000 reports submitted to the Food and Drug Administration of cardiovascular events, including cardiac arrest, myocardial infarction (heart attack), ventricular arrhythmias (abnormal rhythms), palpitations, tachycardia (rapid heart rate), chest pain and syncope (fainting).
EVEN OCCASIONAL MARIJUANA USE LINKED TO HIGHER STROKE RISK, STUDY FINDS
Cardiac arrest appeared in reports involving caffeine- and stimulant-containing products about 11 times as often as in reports involving products without those ingredients.
Heart attacks were reported about 4½ times as often, while ventricular arrhythmias (abnormal heart rhythms) or palpitations were reported about four times as often, according to the AHA.
Energy drinks and stimulant-containing supplements have been linked to the risk of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attacks, particularly among young adults. (iStock)
Elevated heart rate, chest pain and fainting also increased among the group consuming those substances.
Approximately 45% of reported cardiovascular events associated with stimulant products involved adults ages 18 to 34.
"We don't know how many people consumed these drinks and didn't report symptoms or those who maybe had symptoms and didn’t report them."

The stimulants included in the study were caffeine, methylxanthines, guarana, Yerba maté, synephrine, yohimbine and other compounds. They were consumed in products such as soft drinks, meal replacement shakes, protein bars, smoothies and vitamins.
Caffeine and heart risks

Colin Kane, M.D., a pediatric cardiologist and service chief at Children's Health and professor at UT Southwestern Medical Center, said the findings build on earlier case reports about potential heart risks from high caffeine intake.

"We've known through case reports and anecdotal evidence that caffeine in high amounts can be potentially dangerous to people with underlying heart conditions and even those who have normal hearts," Kane, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
WHY STACKING SUPPLEMENTS WITHOUT A BLOOD TEST FIRST CAN DO MORE HARM THAN GOOD

It is generally safe for adults to consume up to 400 milligrams of caffeine per day, which equates to up to five 8-ounce cups of regular black caffeinated coffee, according to a 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease.

"Some energy drinks have up to three times more caffeine per fluid ounce than brewed coffee, and some pre-workout supplements have more than 12 times as much," senior study author Dr. Pamela Benavidez, a cardiothoracic anesthesiologist at Fairfield Medical Center in Lancaster, Ohio, told Fox News Digital.
Approximately 45% of reported cardiovascular events associated with stimulant products involved adults ages 18 to 34. (iStock)
"This means one small serving can easily surpass the advised daily limit or more."
Benavidez also warned that these products often include other stimulants like synephrine, yohimbine and methylhexanamine.
"These can interact with caffeine in ways that are not fully understood, especially in young, healthy people," she said.
YOUR DAILY COFFEE HABIT MAY AFFECT YOUR BRAIN AND MOOD IN UNEXPECTED WAYS, STUDY FINDS

The researchers recommend that young people carefully monitor their consumption of caffeine and watch for heart-related symptoms, such as palpitations, chest pain or tightness, lightheadedness, fainting or a racing or irregular heartbeat during or after use of these products.

"If you notice any of these symptoms, seek medical help right away," Benavidez advised. "If you have a known heart condition, a family history of sudden cardiac events or take medications that are classified as stimulants or can affect your heart rate/rhythm, you should talk to your doctor before using these products at all."
"Some energy drinks have up to three times more caffeine per fluid ounce than brewed coffee, and some pre-workout supplements have more than 12 times as much," the lead researcher said. (iStock)

Kane identified people with underlying heart conditions, particularly those with potentially dangerous heart rhythms and older adults with coronary artery disease, as groups needing particular awareness.
"And there's a whole group of people who may have an underlying heart condition that they're not diagnosed with yet," he added.
Study limitations
The findings are preliminary and have not yet been published as a full peer-reviewed manuscript.
Because the study was observational, it could only show an association and could not prove that the products caused the cardiac events.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"We don't know how many people consumed these drinks and didn't report symptoms or those who maybe had symptoms and didn’t report them," Kane said.
Also, because the FDA reports were voluntary, they may contain incomplete, inconsistent or selectively submitted data.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
It is possible that other factors, such as alcohol or drug use, strenuous exercise and undiagnosed heart conditions, may have contributed to the cardiovascular events.
"Anytime you're mixing stimulants and other substances or medications, it can certainly bring up a potential for harm," Kane said.
Industry response
The American Beverage Association, based in Washington, D.C., sent the statement below to Fox News Digital in response to the study:
"Energy drinks have been enjoyed by billions of people around the world for more than 30 years and are recognized as safe by government food safety agencies worldwide.

"The U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Health Canada, the European Food Safety Authority all relied on the highest quality science when they determined that a moderate daily intake of 400 milligrams of caffeine from all sources is safe for adults.
The researchers recommend that young people carefully monitor their consumption of caffeine and to watch for heart-related symptoms (iStock)
"Energy drinks have less caffeine than coffeehouse coffee, and no regulatory agency has found that their other ingredients interact harmfully with caffeine."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Andrea Wong, chief science officer of the Council for Responsible Nutrition in Washington, D.C., also reacted to the study’s findings.

"Because the analysis does not account for how many consumers actually used these products, whether they were overused or misused or even the amount of caffeine (or other ingredients) per serving, it cannot determine the incidence of cardiovascular events or quantify the associated risk," she told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Importantly, the reported 11-fold difference in cardiac arrest reporting does not mean consumers are 11 times more likely to experience cardiac arrest."
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Fitness influencer's vacation getaway takes scary turn after headache leads to ICU
summary: Khiana Smith was rushed by ambulance to a Bali hospital after a severe headache and light sensitivity led to a meningitis diagnosis in the ICU.
story: Emergency physician Dr. Alfred Joshua discusses a fitness influencer's reported hospitalization overseas.
A 23-year-old fitness influencer's vacation took a frightening turn after she suddenly became seriously ill in Bali.

Australian fitness coach Khiana Smith said in a TikTok video that she was hospitalized after developing a severe headache and sensitivity to light. She later revealed in another video that she had been diagnosed with meningitis.
Smith said she knew something was wrong when she woke up with what she described as the "worst headache."
DEADLY LEGIONNAIRES' DISEASE OUTBREAK SPARKS CONCERN IN MAJOR US CITY: KNOW THE SYMPTOMS
"I couldn't even get out of bed," Smith said in the TikTok video. "It was so intense I couldn't even open my eyes properly. I was really sensitive to light. I couldn't stand up without falling over."

She initially waited to see whether she would feel better, but said she woke up the following morning feeling "10 times worse." She was eventually taken to a hospital by ambulance, where testing revealed the infection.
Australian fitness coach Khiana Smith, pictured, said in a TikTok video that she was hospitalized after being diagnosed with meningitis. (Khiana Smith/Instagram)

Dr. Alfred Joshua, a California-based board-certified emergency room physician and former chief medical officer, told Fox News Digital that Smith's reported symptoms included several warning signs that should be taken seriously.
"She started having symptoms of severe headache, having difficulty with light," Joshua said. "And then she started having difficulty walking, and then eventually slurred speech."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Meningitis occurs when the protective layers surrounding the brain and spinal cord become inflamed, according to Joshua.

Symptoms can include headache, fever, stiff neck and sensitivity to light. Trouble walking or speaking, confusion and extreme tiredness are more serious signs that should prompt immediate medical attention, Joshua said.
Khiana Smith, pictured left, was vacationing in Bali, pictured right, when she became seriously ill and was later diagnosed with meningitis. (Khiana Smith/Instagram; iStock)
The seriousness of the illness can also depend on what is causing it.
Joshua said viral meningitis often resolves on its own, while bacterial meningitis can progress rapidly and requires prompt treatment with antibiotics.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES
"Certain strains over a couple of hours [can cause] the person [to] get really, really sick," he said.
Doctors initially did not know whether her meningitis was bacterial or viral, according to Smith, so she was being treated for the bacterial form as a precaution.
Viral meningitis often resolves on its own, while bacterial meningitis can progress rapidly and requires prompt antibiotic treatment. (iStock)

Smith's condition later appeared to improve enough for her to leave the ICU, but she said she had to return after continuing to experience head pain, light sensitivity and slurred speech. She also reported memory loss, and said swelling in her brain was preventing her from flying home.
When meningitis is suspected, Joshua said doctors can use blood tests, brain imaging and a lumbar puncture to determine whether the infection is bacterial, viral or caused by something else.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Smith's experience has highlighted a concern for travelers who become seriously ill far from home.
Joshua said recommended vaccines can protect against some forms of bacterial meningitis, and advised travelers to consider insurance that includes medical evacuation coverage.
"It was so intense I couldn't even open my eyes properly."
Smith's mother also stressed the importance of travel insurance, saying her daughter's hospital expenses were covered because she had purchased a policy before leaving Australia.
Joshua said worsening symptoms, including changes in speech, walking or other brain functions, should not be ignored.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"When symptoms are progressing in a more complicated manner with neurological dysfunction, do not wait and try to see this out," he said. "Go and seek prompt emergency treatment."
Fox News Digital reached out to Smith for comment.

Kelly McGreal is a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. She and the team cover travel, food and drink, health, relationships and more. She also produces the weekly American Culture Quiz and handles other special projects.

title: Alzheimer's warning signs could emerge years before memory loss, study finds
summary: A Science Advances study reveals how brain scan connectivity patterns predict Alzheimer's disease years before memory loss or cognitive decline.
story: Dr. Jeremy Koppel, co-director of the Litwin-Zucker Center, discusses a new blood test capable of predicting Alzheimer's risk up to 10 years in advance. The test identifies elevated levels of a tau protein biomarker, P-tau217, indicating a higher likelihood of cognitive decline. Koppel highlights its potential for early diagnosis and understanding Alzheimer's progression.

Small changes in how parts of the brain communicate with one another can help predict a person’s likelihood of developing Alzheimer’s disease years before any memory lapses appear, according to a study published in Science Advances.
Stanford Medicine researchers used brain scans and a computer model to look for early clues about why some older adults develop memory and thinking problems while others stay sharp.

Investigators examined resting brain scans from two opposing groups: patients diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and older individuals known as "super agers," whose memory capabilities match people decades younger.
SUBTLE CHANGE IN HOW YOU SPEAK COULD BE EARLY SIGN OF DEMENTIA RISK, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS
Instead of looking for physical hallmarks like amyloid plaque accumulation or brain shrinkage, the researchers studied how different parts of the brain communicate with one another.

By comparing the two groups’ brain activity patterns, the researchers calculated a measurement called the Alzheimer’s resilience-vulnerability connectome score, or ARC score, that distinguishes super agers from people with Alzheimer’s with about 85% accuracy.
Researchers developed a brain activity scoring model, the ARC score, which can predict Alzheimer’s disease risk years before noticeable memory lapses occur. (iStock)

"I'm excited we established a signature that can help us better understand the difference between people who can maintain excellent cognitive performance and people who show cognitive decline," Yu Zhang, the study's senior author and an assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford Medicine, said in a press release.
DEMENTIA RISK MAY BE LINKED TO SEEMINGLY HARMLESS DAILY HABIT, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS
Next, the scientists applied the scoring model to more than 1,300 cognitively unimpaired adults aged 55 to 70.

Although all the adults scored normally on memory tests, their brain scans showed differences: Some had activity patterns similar to super agers, while others had patterns more like those seen in people with Alzheimer’s.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Over follow-up periods of up to 12 years, with most participants tracked for five to six years, those whose brain activity more closely resembled Alzheimer’s patterns showed faster declines in memory and thinking, developed more amyloid plaques and were more likely to be diagnosed with the disease, the researchers found.
The model successfully differentiated between the two extreme cognitive groups with approximately 85% accuracy. (Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images)
The team found that the ARC score matched or outperformed standard risk measures, including amyloid and tau biomarkers as well as genetic testing, in spotting early decline.

"We compared the ARC score with existing biomarkers in predicting people converting to Alzheimer's disease," lead author Kanhao Zhao, a postdoctoral scholar in psychiatry at Stanford Medicine, said in the release.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Our model shows comparable or better prediction ability, and it can do so at an earlier time point. And if we combine our score with the existing biomarkers, the prediction performance improves."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Alzheimer’s disease affects millions of older adults worldwide, according to major health institutions.
A central challenge in treating the disease is that physical damage often begins decades before patients notice memory lapses, at which point treatments offer limited benefit.
Across follow-up periods spanning up to 12 years, individuals with Alzheimer’s-like brain patterns experienced faster cognitive decline and higher diagnosis rates. (iStock)

Researchers stressed that the brain scan method is not yet ready for doctors to use on its own to diagnose Alzheimer’s. More studies are needed to confirm its accuracy and compare it with other new tests.

However, understanding how brain activity differs between healthy aging and neurodegeneration could help researchers test future treatments, including techniques that stimulate the brain without surgery.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"There are two main components: One is to know which part of the brain to target. The other is how we should change it," Zhang said.
"That's why identifying the super ager brain resilience pattern is a critical component — so we know what a good pattern should be."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Even occasional marijuana use linked to higher stroke risk, study finds
summary: A study of nearly 450,000 adults found that both casual and heavy marijuana users faced higher odds of stroke and cardiovascular disease than non-users.
story: American Heart Association expert Robert Page warns that cannabis use may increase cardiovascular risks, even in younger adults who don't smoke tobacco. He urges patients to discuss cannabis use with their doctors.
A new study of nearly 450,000 American adults links cannabis use to an increased risk of stroke and cardiovascular disease.

The findings, scheduled for presentation at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago Nov. 6–9, show that both casual and heavy marijuana users have higher odds of heart conditions compared to non-users.
Researchers analyzed survey responses collected between 2020 and 2024 through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System.
SHARON STONE'S TERRIFYING WEED WITHDRAWAL SPARKS WARNING ABOUT TODAY'S POTENT MARIJUANA

People who reported using cannabis between one and five days per month had 23% higher odds of reporting a history of cardiovascular disease than non-users. Those using it 16 to 30 days per month had 21% higher odds.

"This study raises important concerns about cannabis use and cardiovascular health, particularly stroke," Dr. Kristen "Nicke" Worth, an Ohio-based physician and medical adviser at NuggMD, a telehealth platform for medical marijuana evaluations, told Fox News Digital.
A study of nearly 450,000 U.S. adults found that cannabis use is linked to significantly higher odds of cardiovascular disease, especially stroke. (iStock)

"One finding I found particularly interesting was that people who used cannabis just one to five days per month had somewhat higher reported odds of a previous stroke than people who used it more frequently," added Worth, who was not involved in the study.
Low-frequency users had 40% higher odds of a reported stroke, while heavy users had 25% higher odds. The study found no statistically significant link between cannabis use and heart attacks.
MARIJUANA USERS MAY FACE HIDDEN DRIVING DANGER THAT STANDARD TESTS CAN MISS

"That isn't what we'd necessarily expect from a straightforward dose-response relationship, where greater exposure is associated with greater risk. But we shouldn't interpret this as evidence that heavier use is safer," Worth said.
The method of consumption did not change the outcome. Whether participants smoked, vaped or consumed edibles like gummies, the risk remained consistent, according to the researchers.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"We were surprised to find that the link between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease was not straightforward," said lead author Dr. Aabha Divya, an assistant professor of cardiothoracic surgery at Tulane University School of Medicine, in an AHA press release.

"We expected that the chances of heart disease would gradually rise as people used cannabis more often, but that wasn't the case. Both low-use and heavy-use groups had higher odds of developing heart disease."
While the study showed a strong correlation with strokes, researchers found no statistically significant link between cannabis frequency and heart attacks. (Getty Images)

The study comes amid growing commercial availability and use of the drug across the country. According to the research team, about one in six adults reported past-month cannabis use in 2024, up from one in 10 in 2020 — a 51% increase over four years.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Dr. Robert L. Page II, a professor of clinical pharmacy at the University of Colorado and an American Heart Association volunteer expert who was not involved in the study, said the findings challenge common assumptions about the drug's safety.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"In patients who use both, cannabis has always been considered an innocent bystander; however, this is not the case," Page said in a press release.
"Overall, cannabis is beginning to emerge as a major contributor to premature heart disease in young and older adults, which can lead to serious cardiovascular events."
"People should not discontinue prescribed cardiovascular medications because of this report."
Page added that doctors should question patients about marijuana use just as they do with cigarettes and alcohol.

Researchers noted several key limitations to the findings. Because the study was observational and captured data from only a single point in time, it can only show a statistical link and cannot prove that cannabis causes heart disease or strokes.
Adult cannabis use has surged nationwide, rising 51% between 2020 and 2024 to reach one in six Americans. (iStock)

The data also relied on telephone surveys, leaving room for errors in participants' memory regarding their medical diagnoses and drug use. Additionally, the researchers did not track product strength, THC potency or total amounts consumed.
The findings remain preliminary until vetted through the full, peer-reviewed publication process.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"For patients, I wouldn't recommend making abrupt treatment decisions based on one preliminary study, but I wouldn't dismiss these findings," Worth said. "People should not discontinue prescribed cardiovascular medications because of this report."

"Anyone using cannabis, medically or recreationally, should discuss their cardiovascular history, existing risk factors, medications and treatment alternatives with their healthcare professional," she added.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Wisconsin infant dies of measles as state sees first death from disease since 1990
summary: Wisconsin's health officials announced an infant's measles-associated death, marking the state's first in 36 years, amid 431 cases in 13 counties.
story: An infant in Wisconsin died of measles, marking the state’s first death linked to the disease in 36 years, according to state health officials.
An infant in Wisconsin died of measles, marking the state’s first death linked to the disease in 36 years, the state's Department of Health Services announced on Thursday.

The Department of Health Services said the child died in southwestern Wisconsin but did not provide a more precise location. The department said it would not release any additional details to protect the privacy of the family.
The coroner listed the immediate cause of death as measles.

"It is with a heavy heart we are reporting the first death of an infant connected with a measles outbreak in Wisconsin in many years. My heart is broken for the family," state Department of Health Services Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in a statement.
CHILD'S MEASLES DEATH MARKS NEW YORK STATE'S FIRST IN MORE THAN 30 YEARS AMID OUTBREAK
An infant in Wisconsin died of measles, marking the state’s first death linked to the disease in 36 years. (REUTERS/Shannon Stapleton)

"Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease. Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family," she continued.

Measles can cause life-threatening complications, including pneumonia and swelling of the brain. The department said that while anyone can become seriously ill, children younger than 5, pregnant people and people with weakened immune systems are at increased risk of complications.

Wisconsin has reported 431 measles cases in 13 counties so far this year, reflecting the highest number of cases seen in the state in more than 35 years. Among these cases, nine people required hospitalization for severe symptoms.

State officials urged Wisconsinites to be proactive in preventing illness to protect themselves and their communities, saying the best way to prevent measles is with the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine.
Wisconsin has reported 431 measles cases in 13 counties so far this year. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services previously told FOX News Digital that "Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles."
Earlier this week, a child in New York state's Lewis County died in the first known measles-associated death in the state in more than 30 years.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said she was "heartbroken" to learn of the child's death.
"As a mother and grandmother, I cannot imagine what this family is going through. My heart goes out to everyone who knew and loved this child," Hochul said in a statement.
NEW YORK DECLARES MEASLES DISASTER EMERGENCY AS CASES SURGE IN PENNSYLVANIA

State officials urged Wisconsinites to be proactive in preventing illness to protect themselves and their communities, saying the best way to prevent measles is with the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. (Raquel Natalicchio/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported four measles-associated deaths across the country this year, although state health departments have reported higher figures.

In Pennsylvania, state health officials have confirmed six measles-associated deaths in 2026 and are investigating another reported death that has not yet met the state's criteria to be classified as measles-associated.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Popular weight-loss drugs may prevent prediabetes from turning into diabetes
summary: A large study found GLP-1 medications like semaglutide and tirzepatide are linked to 41% lower all-cause mortality risk versus metformin in prediabetes.
story: Erin Palinski-Wade, a dietitian and diabetes educator, talks about important factors that affect blood sugar and gives an opinion on a recent study suggesting eating with a partner can decrease blood sugar levels.
Adults with prediabetes and obesity who took GLP-1-based medications had a 31% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes and a 41% lower risk of death compared with those taking metformin.

Metformin is an oral medication used primarily to treat type 2 diabetes, widely considered the first-line treatment, combined with lifestyle modifications. It is also sometimes prescribed to people with prediabetes to help prevent or delay progression.

The findings, which come from a large observational study, are set to be presented at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2026 this weekend in Chicago. They have not yet undergone the full peer review process.
DR OZ LINKS OBESITY TO CHRONIC DISEASE SURGE, SAYS GLP-1S CAN 'JUMPSTART' BETTER HEALTH
The study involved health records for 256,492 adults with prediabetes and obesity, averaging 52 years of age.
Approximately half of the group received GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists) medications – including semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide and dulaglutide – and half received metformin.
Adults with prediabetes and obesity who took GLP-1-based medications had a 31% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes and a 41% lower risk of death compared with those taking metformin. (iStock)

Based on a three-year follow-up, in addition to the lower risk of diabetes and all-cause mortality, GLP-1–based medications were associated with 20% fewer strokes, 15% fewer heart attacks and 25% fewer cases of heart failure.

"The 41% lower risk of death from any cause surprised me most," study author Vinicius de Sousa Barzon Serra, M.D., a research fellow in the department of cardiovascular medicine at the Mayo Clinic in Scottsdale, Arizona, told Fox News Digital.
POPULAR DIET SLASHES LIVER FAT BY 67% WHILE REVERSING PREDIABETES IN SOME PEOPLE

"I expected GLP-1 medications to do better than metformin on blood sugar and diabetes risk, because they lead to much more weight loss. I was also struck that the benefit appeared across many outcomes, including heart attack, stroke, heart failure and atrial fibrillation."

Approximately half of the group received GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists) medications – including semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide and dulaglutide – and half received metformin. (iStock)

Nearly 40% of U.S. adults have prediabetes, according to statistics from the AHA. That condition is marked by blood sugar levels that are above normal but not yet elevated enough for a diabetes diagnosis.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
As many as 10% of those with prediabetes will go on to develop type 2 diabetes each year.

"Most earlier research on these medications focused on people who already had diabetes," Serra noted. "Our study suggests the prediabetes stage may be an important time to consider them, rather than waiting until they develop type 2 diabetes."

Nearly 40% of U.S. adults have prediabetes, according to statistics from the AHA. That condition is marked by blood sugar levels that are above normal but not yet elevated enough for a diabetes diagnosis. (iStock)

Dr. Bradley Serwer, an interventional cardiologist and chief medical officer at VitalSolution, an Ingenovis Health company that offers cardiovascular and anesthesiology services to hospitals nationwide, agreed that the study raises the possibility that GLP-1 medications could play a large role in primary cardiovascular prevention.

"We have long known the benefits of controlling blood pressure, cholesterol and urging smoking cessation, but now we should consider aggressively treating obesity and metabolic dysfunction," Serwer, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
Study limitations
While the study found a link between GLP-1 medications and better health outcomes, it does not prove that the drugs were responsible.
The findings are preliminary until published in a peer-reviewed journal, Serra noted.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"We matched patients by age, health conditions and other characteristics to make the groups comparable … even so, other differences between the groups may remain," he said. "We also grouped the GLP-1 medications together, so we could not tell whether individual drugs differ."

The study relied on patients' electronic health records, which may have contained missing or incorrect information. It is also possible that factors not measured in the study, such as medication dosage and compliance, could have influenced the results, the researchers noted.

Metformin is an oral medication used primarily to treat type 2 diabetes, widely considered the first-line treatment, combined with lifestyle modifications. It is also sometimes prescribed to people with prediabetes to help prevent or delay progression. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)
People with prediabetes and obesity should talk with their doctor about all their options and should not stop or change any medication on their own, Serra advised.

"Metformin is a safe, inexpensive option with a long track record, and lifestyle changes such as healthy eating, regular physical activity and weight management remain the foundation of treatment," he emphasized to Fox News Digital.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"For some patients, a GLP-1 medication may be worth discussing, depending on their overall health, other medical conditions, cost and access. The decision should be made together with their doctor."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Serwer emphasized the importance of identifying patients who would benefit most from aggressive treatment to prevent cardiovascular disease.

"Not everyone with prediabetes needs a GLP-1 medication," he said. "We need to identify those with obesity, insulin resistance and multiple cardiovascular risk factors who are most likely to benefit from early intervention."
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: College students discover new muscle attachment that could improve hip surgery
summary: Two Tulane University sophomores found a previously unknown muscle in the hip during a cadaver lab session that even their professor couldn't identify.
story: Tulane University students Dominic Roy and Cooper Bruce join anatomist and professor Dr. Shane Tubbs to discuss their discovery of a previously undocumented pelvic muscle and what it could mean for medical research.
Two undergraduate students at Tulane University in New Orleans discovered an anatomical feature that even their professor couldn’t initially identify.
Dominic Roy and Cooper Bruce were both 19-year-old college sophomores at the time of the finding in 2024.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Roy said it had been an ordinary day volunteering in the cadaver lab with R. Shane Tubbs, Ph.D., professor of neurosurgery and director of surgical anatomy at Tulane School of Medicine.
5 HABITS THAT COULD HELP KEEP YOU OUT OF A NURSING HOME, FROM AN ORTHOPEDIC SURGEON
The students were dissecting several specimens’ hips to compare where the iliacus joins the psoas major, a muscle that runs from the lower back through the pelvis to the upper thigh.
Front view of a woman's thigh and knee muscles with anatomical labels. (iStock)
When looking for a particular muscle, the iliocapsularis, which sits laterally in the hip, Roy found something else instead.
"I spotted a similar looking muscle that was on the other side of the Iliac fascia, close to the inguinal region of the pelvis," he said.
WEEKLY WEIGHTLIFTING SWEET SPOT MAY BE LINKED TO LONGER LIFE, STUDY FINDS
"I called Dr. Tubbs over and asked, ‘What is this?’ We didn't talk about this in our morning meetings ... and I think he was as stumped as me."
After searching through extensive literature and textbooks to see if the muscle had been previously identified, the team came up short, which suggested it was a new discovery.
The new muscle attachment discovered by Tulane undergrad students is illustrated in a diagram. (Tulane University/iStock)
"It was kind of like a reserved excitement," Bruce reflected. "Especially if the great R. Shane Tubbs can't put his finger on exactly what it is."
Physicians from overseas and rising medical school students also assisted with the discovery.
SIMPLE EXERCISE DONE JUST ONCE A WEEK COULD HELP LOWER BLOOD PRESSURE

"Everyone kind of huddled around the same specimen and we started draping and doing the pictures … I was in awe," Roy said. "I was like, ‘Oh, wow, this is happening so quick.’ It was seriously something special."
The findings were recently published in the journal Clinical Anatomy.
Tulane students Dominic Roy, left, and Cooper Bruce made a novel discovery while volunteering in the cadaver lab. (Dominic Roy)
Tubbs, who is also a co-editor-in-chief of the human anatomy reference textbook Gray's Anatomy, said Roy and Bruce’s discovery was "serendipity."
"[They] identified a different part of a muscle that we had not looked at yet," he confirmed to Fox News Digital. "It's deep in the pelvis and runs out to the front of your hip."
KNEE TREATMENT WITHOUT SURGERY OFFERS LASTING PAIN RELIEF FOR 80% OF ARTHRITIS PATIENTS, STUDY FINDS
Potential medical uses
Although the team has not yet determined the muscle’s function, clues suggest it may help stabilize the psoas major, a large muscle involved in bending the hip.
The next step is to determine whether MRI scans can reveal the muscle attachment, allowing researchers to study whether its presence is linked to more or fewer symptoms, according to the doctor.
Dr. Tubbs said his lab uses anatomical donors for education and research to identify clinical problems. (Tulane University)

"More research is needed for us to better elucidate what it does," Tubbs said. "Can you see it on imaging? Does it contribute to patients' problems? But I think this is the first step in identifying something."
As minimally invasive procedures become more common, Tubbs said awareness of this small muscle could improve care, particularly for patients undergoing hip surgery.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"They might use physical therapy to help rehab the muscle, because we did find that the fibers of this attachment directly attach into the front of the hip joint," he added. "So it may be that the muscle’s weak and causes symptoms, so you could rehab it."
Doctors could also use injections to weaken the new muscle if overactivity causes pain or other symptoms.
The muscle discovery could help improve future surgeries and hip pain, the professor said. (iStock)

"Surgeons are replacing hips and doing hip surgery on a daily basis, so if they see the muscle, potentially they could correlate the symptoms of the patient and whether or not maybe cutting the muscle would help the patient," Tubbs said.
Variations in anatomy
This muscle was not found in every cadaver, the researchers noted, as each human body is different.
"When you look beneath the layers of the skin, human beings have lots of variation," Tubbs said. "I tell our students that no two of you are built the same inside or out."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The researchers found the same muscle attachment in gorillas, suggesting a possible evolutionary link.
Bruce said this raises the question of why this muscle would still be present in some humans and not others.
Tulane University School of Medicine is shown in New Orleans on Feb. 12, 2022. (iStock)
"Just by the nature of working with cadavers and not knowing a deep personal history of each individual … maybe this individual played soccer, or this person did a lot of rock climbing," he said.
"They might've had more need for this attachment ... It's difficult to make that connection."
Lessons beyond textbooks
Working with real cadavers has made a big difference in shaping future doctors, Tubbs shared, as the synthetic models that are now circulating in university labs are cookie-cutter.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"Many people have the notion ... that the entire form of the human has been worked out, and we know all the different parts. And they think we've known that for hundreds of years," he said. "But in actuality, people are still discovering things about human anatomy."
Medical students "need to experience that variation" and have the hands-on experience before dealing with real patients, Roy commented.
Dr. Shane Tubbs poses in his office in the Murphy Building on Tulane's Downtown campus on March 27, 2026. (Kenny Lass / Tulane University)
Although the new muscle attachment will have to be studied across geographic regions, Tubbs said he expects the students' discovery will eventually be added to anatomical textbooks.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The discovery inspired the students, now seniors, to further explore a career in medicine. Roy said he plans to enter a master’s program in anatomy.
"The bottom line is that anatomical discovery doesn't end when a textbook is published ... and discovery in the anatomical sciences continues on, even in the year 2026."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: NYC marathoner with 'heart for Jesus' remembered after tragic death for her faith, strength and charity
summary: Athlete Rachel Apa, 24, was running the NYC Marathon to honor her late grandfather and raise funds to fight Parkinson's disease when rhabdomyolysis struck.
story: Dr. Devi Nampiaparampil of the NYU Langone School of Medicine explains rhabdomyolysis warning signs after a runner dies two miles from the NYC marathon finish.
Rachel Apa, 24, died on Sunday, Nov. 1, while running the New York City Marathon after succumbing to complications from rhabdomyolysis, a rare muscle condition.

Apa made it to mile 24 – just 2.2 miles from the finish line – before collapsing. She received immediate medical attention and was taken to Mount Sinai Medical Center, where physicians worked to save her for more than six hours.
The athlete was declared dead at around 9:40 p.m., according to a report from The New York Times.
NYC MARATHON RUNNER, 24, DIES JUST 2 MILES FROM FINISH LINE AFTER SENDING DAD CHILLING TEXTS
Rhabdomyolysis causes the muscles to break down when over-exerted, which leads to muscle death, according to Cleveland Clinic.
When this disintegration occurs, toxic components of the muscle fibers can enter the circulatory system and kidneys, which can cause kidney damage, essentially acting as poison to the body.
Rachel Apa played Division I field hockey for Bucknell University. (Bucknell Athletics)

Apa graduated from Bucknell University, where she played Division I field hockey. Post-grad, she was a product manager for an electrical component company while also working on her MBA at Charleston Southern University (CSU).
In a tribute released Tuesday, the Christian university, where Apa began her graduate school education in August, said the CSU family "mourns the tragic loss."
HEALTHY ATHLETE HAD NO SYMPTOMS BEFORE MANDATORY HEART SCREENING REVEALED HIDDEN DEFECT

"Maxwell Rollins, assistant dean of graduate programs for the Nielsen College of Business, shared a recent class assignment where Apa stated her current mission was to take advantage of the talents and opportunities she had been blessed with to make an impact in any way she could in the lives of those around her," the statement reads.
Rachel Apa, 24, died while running the New York City Marathon on Nov. 1, 2026. (Instagram @rachelapa)

Rollins shared about Apa, "She wrote that her desire was to demonstrate Christ’s love and character in both business and everyday life. Though she had just started her MBA at CSU, her passion for others and heart for Jesus will continue to serve as an inspiration for all our students."

CSU president B. Keith Faulkner added, "The loss of a vibrant young woman in the prime of her life is a sorrow no parent can imagine enduring. The Charleston Southern family is surrounding the Apa family, along with all who knew and loved Rachel, with our prayers and support."
Apa’s former field hockey teams have mourned her loss in tributes posted to social media. (Bucknell Athletics)

"We will never fully understand why this happened to a young woman of such remarkable strength and character. Her final hours are forever marked by Rachel’s selfless dedication to helping others as she ran to raise funds in the fight against Parkinson’s disease."
MYSTERIOUS DISEASE SENDING YOUNG, HEALTHY TEXAS WORKERS INTO KIDNEY FAILURE

Faulkner continued, "We know that true peace comes only from the Lord, and we pray that His presence and comfort will be deeply felt by all who are grieving and by all whose lives were touched by Rachel’s extraordinary life and legacy."
Apa’s former field hockey teams also mourned her loss in tributes posted to social media.
Rachel Apa and teammate Kari Melberger celebrate with a hug during a field hockey match. (Bucknell Athletics)

Kristine Brown, vice president of strategic communications and marketing at Bucknell, shared a statement with Fox News Digital on Wednesday."Bucknell University extends its deepest sympathy for the family and friends of Rachel Apa '24 following her tragic passing while participating in Sunday's New York City Marathon," said Brown in the statement.

"Rachel was a four-year member and key contributor to the Bison field hockey team, scoring 17 goals during her collegiate career and earning Academic All-Patriot League honors. She graduated from Bucknell in 2024 with a bachelor's degree in markets, innovation and design. The Bucknell community mourns her loss and extends its heartfelt condolences to all who knew and loved her."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Central Penn Field Hockey Club, where Apa was a member for nearly a decade before playing for Bucknell, posted that the family is "heartbroken by the loss."

"On the field, she played with intensity and determination," the club wrote. "She was competitive, serious about the game and gave 100% every single time, always with a smile and an unwavering commitment to her teammates."
"We will never fully understand why this happened to a young woman of such remarkable strength and character."
"Watching her play was a beautiful thing. You could see the joy she carried every time she stepped on the pitch."
The statement continued, "Our hearts are with the Apa family, her CPFH and Bucknell teammates and their families, and everyone lucky enough to have shared the field with her."

"Rachel’s spirit will be everlasting; her impact on the people and program will never be forgotten," the post continued. "We hope the Apa family can find some comfort in knowing she helped create something truly special here and will always hold a place in our hearts."
It went on, "We are sending you all our love, strength and support. Our entire Bucknell Field Hockey family is holding you close in our hearts."
Running for Parkinson’s
Apa set out to run the marathon to raise money to fight Parkinson’s disease, in honor of her late grandfather.
On the Parkinson’s Champions fundraising website, Apa wrote what her grandfather meant to her.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"My grandfather was my role model growing up," she said. "He taught me to stay active, push my limits and embrace challenges, shaping my love for sports and movement.

"Later in life, he was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease, and I watched as the disease slowly took away the freedom to move that he once loved so much. He passed away in 2022, but the lessons he taught me continue to drive me forward."
Runners compete during the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon in New York on Nov. 1, 2026. (Xinhua News Agency via Getty Images)
She added, "I'm proud to run with Parkinson's Foundation Champions to raise funds and awareness for research, better care and a cure."
Rachel Apa raised more than $55,000 and counting for the cause.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The Parkinson’s Foundation also released a statement in her memory, expressing that the organization is "saddened by the tragic passing" of Apa, who ran as a member of the Parkinson’s Champions team.

"Rachel’s decision to take on this challenge was deeply personal," the statement reads. "After watching Parkinson’s disease gradually take away the freedom of movement her grandfather once cherished, Rachel was inspired to honor his memory by running and supporting the Parkinson’s community."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"We admire Rachel’s determination and are grateful that she was part of our team. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Rachel’s family, loved ones and fellow members of the Parkinson’s Champions team."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Kushner enters Ukraine peace talks as Trump eyes securing safeguards against another Russian invasion
summary: Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff push a NATO-like security guarantee for Ukraine as first trilateral Abu Dhabi talks tackle territory disputes.
story: Negotiations to end the war could resume after Russian President Vladimir Putin met with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy tells Brian Kilmeade he is open to freezing front lines in exchange for security guarantees. American Military Project director Will Thibeau provides his analysis on the developments during 'Fox & Friends First.'
Russia and Ukraine will finally return to the negotiating table Tuesday for their first trilateral peace talks with the U.S. in nine months.
Ahead of the talks, officials said both Moscow and Kyiv have shown "a little bit of flexibility privately" on territorial disputes that have long stood in the way of reaching an agreement.

U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will sit down with Ukrainian intelligence chief Rustem Umerov and Putin aide and veteran negotiator Vladimir Medinsky in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday.

The Trump administration has asked Russia to accept an "Article Four and an Article Five-like security guarantee" for Ukraine that would be "effectively very similar to NATO," a U.S. official said Monday on a background call previewing the negotiations.

President Donald Trump has not yet decided what security guarantee the U.S. itself would provide, the official said, describing an American guarantee as a "really, really big deal" that would ultimately have to be worked out between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
RUSSIA'S NEIGHBOR REVEALS PERSONAL APPEALS TO TRUMP AS US WEIGHS NATO TROOP PULLBACK IN EUROPE

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, center, and U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys Jared Kushner, right, and Steve Witkoff, left, walk prior to their talks in Kyiv, Ukraine, Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky)

A lot has happened on the geopolitical stage since the latest trilateral talks happened in Geneva, Switzerland, in February. The first being the inception of a new conflict between the U.S. and Iran — and the second being the 2026 midterm elections, which saw a sweeping rebuke of Republicans with a blue wave taking the country by storm.
The latest round of talks will also mark the beginning of structured negotiations over territory.

Russia continues publicly to demand all of Donetsk, while Ukraine has pushed for freezing the conflict along the current line of contact. But behind closed doors, "both sides have shown a little bit of flexibility privately," the official said.
UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY OPEN TO FREEZING FRONT LINES IN CEASEFIRE WITH RUSSIA

Trump also suggested in a "60 Minutes" interview that aired Sunday that Ukraine’s borders could ultimately change under a peace agreement, saying the country could emerge from the war with "a little bit different shape."

U.S. negotiators do not expect to resolve the territorial dispute in Abu Dhabi. Instead, officials say the goal is to clarify where each side stands, identify the remaining gaps and begin exploring potential compromises that can ultimately be taken back to Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelenskyy.
The administration increasingly views the territorial question and postwar security arrangements as inseparable.

Officials believe neither Russia nor Ukraine will make the concessions needed to settle the territorial dispute until each understands what the security landscape will look like after the fighting stops.
INSIDE MELANIA TRUMP'S SECRET DIPLOMATIC ROLE IN THE RUSSIA-UKRAINE CEASEFIRE DEAL

Before sitting down with Russia and Ukraine, U.S. negotiators will meet with national security officials from Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Italy, along with NATO, the European Union and Ukraine, to discuss security guarantees and a broader postwar security architecture.
Washington then hopes to persuade Russia to join a broader multilateral negotiating process involving European governments.

Russia’s President Vladimir Putin meets with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner and Federal Acquisition Service Commissioner Josh Gruenbaum at the Kremlin in Moscow on Jan. 22, 2026. (Alexander Kazakov/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
"We need Europe at the table," a U.S. official said, arguing that direct negotiations between Russia and European countries will ultimately be necessary for a durable settlement.
Among the ideas under consideration is reviving the NATO-Russia Council, which the administration wants to make a more robust forum for communication, de-escalation and resolving future disputes.
Officials are also exploring crisis communications, greater military transparency and reciprocal measures intended to reduce the risk of another conflict.

The administration's goal in Abu Dhabi is not a final agreement. Officials instead hope the talks can establish a framework for more frequent negotiations and eventually move the process from a U.S.-Russia-Ukraine format to broader multilateral talks involving Europe.

The administration also sees sanctions as potential leverage in enforcing an eventual agreement. A U.S. official suggested sanctions on Russia could potentially be eased over time while retaining the ability to "spring back in place" if Moscow violates a peace deal.
Witkoff and Kushner, the son-in-law of the president, are also considering returning to meet Putin and Zelenskyy soon, depending on the outcome of the Abu Dhabi talks.
"This is the first time I feel like we see real desire on the Russian side to finish," the official said.
But officials acknowledged the negotiations remain highly uncertain, with deep distrust between Moscow and Kyiv and major decisions on territory and security still unresolved.
The immediate test in Abu Dhabi will be whether the private flexibility U.S. negotiators say they are seeing can translate into something concrete once Russia and Ukraine are back in the same room.
But the Abu Dhabi talks could also set the stage for higher-level diplomacy.
President Donald Trump, right, and Russian President Vladimir Putin hold a meeting at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on August 15, 2025, in Anchorage, Alaska. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
U.S. officials said Witkoff and Kushner are considering returning to meet Putin and Zelenskyy soon, depending on the outcome of the two-day negotiations.

title: Trump defends Pentagon chief as Massie targets him: 'Hegseth should be praised, not impeached'
summary: President Donald Trump is defending War Secretary Pete Hegseth as GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky targets the Pentagon chief for impeachment.
story: President Donald Trump calls out Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., amid the congressman’s push to impeach War Secretary Pete Hegseth.
President Donald Trump is defending War Secretary Pete Hegseth as outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., targets the Pentagon chief for impeachment.
The president issued a Truth Social post on Monday slamming the congressman as "a total loser" while asserting that the war secretary "should be praised, not impeached."

"Defeated Republican Congressman Thomas Massie, a total loser, is trying to Impeach perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the Country, Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth," Trump declared Monday on Truth Social.
HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT VOTE LOOMS AS HOUSE REPUBLICANS PRIVATELY WARN IT COULD PASS
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., speaks on impeaching U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth outside the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 9, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

"With recruitment at an ALL-TIME HIGH, from an all-time low under Sleepy Joe Biden, and TWO VICTORIES, Venezuela and Iran, Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached. Congress, stand up for Pete!!!" he added.
Massie did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's comment request on Tuesday.
Hegseth shared a screenshot of the president's post and thanked him.

President Donald Trump speaks with Secretary of War Pete Hegseth at the Pennsylvania Defense and Innovation Summit at U.S. Army War College on July 15, 2026, in Carlisle, Pennsylvania. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
"Thank you Mr. President. Like you, we will never back down," Hegseth wrote.

Massie, who has served in the House of Representatives since late 2012, lost the GOP primary earlier this year in Kentucky's 4th Congressional District to Trump-backed challenger Ed Gallrein, a former Navy SEAL who went on to win the seat during the general election.

"My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie said, according to a press release.
