title: Reporter’s Notebook: House leadership up for grabs as GOP reckons with devastating losses
summary: Thomas Massie is reintroducing articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth, and the math suggests House Republicans may not be able to stop it.
story: Capitol Hill freshman orientation begins as incoming progressive Democrats demand major policy updates. Fox News' Chad Pergram details House leadership battles.
Internal House and Senate party leadership elections are some of the most fascinating exercises to unfold on Capitol Hill.
Both House and Senate Democrats and House and Senate Republicans will choose their leaders in the coming days. And the changes are going to be seismic.

But not everyone is on board with heir apparent leaders. That’s what makes this process so intriguing. However, there are only two rules in leadership elections: You can’t beat someone with no one. And — perhaps more importantly — it’s about the math.
Republicans are up first with elections in both chambers starting Tuesday morning.
THE HITCHHIKER’S GUIDE TO WHAT HAPPENS NEXT ON CAPITOL HILL

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, left, and House Speaker Mike Johnson speak during a news conference at the US Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, Nov. 5, 2025. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

For Minority Leader, House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., is running against Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio. Current House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., is not seeking to stay in leadership once his party isn't in charge anymore.

If Democrats have 260 seats, Republicans would have 175. All incoming House Republicans (including nonvoting delegates from U.S. territories) are allowed to vote in conference. The selection of minority leader does NOT go before the entire House like speaker. So, the winning candidate only needs a simple majority. That would be 88.
The same for the race between House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., and Rep. August Pfluger, R-Texas, for Minority Whip.
Senate Republican leader John Thune, R-S.D., is running to keep his leadership position for the party in the new Congress.

Meanwhile, Democrats will begin elections for their House leader on Wednesday, when Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is expected to secure that nomination. No internal Democrat Senate leadership election date has been set.
There are some progressives and Democratic Socialists of America-affiliated Democrats who will be House members next year who want someone other than Minority Leader Jeffries keep his position.
Who do they want instead? Well, no one has said. Again, you can’t beat someone with no one. And frankly, it’s hard to believe that Democrats would not elect the first Black speaker of the House.
But drill down on the math.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and the House's Hakeem Jeffries have spoken out in support of the Supreme Court's Tuesday ruling on birthright citizenship. (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images)

For the sake of argument, let’s say Democrats have 260 House seats in the new Congress. First, Democrats must tap a nominee for speaker in their caucus. That needs a simple majority. So surely Jeffries will score at least 131 votes in a private ballot for speaker.

The speaker of the House is the Constitutional officer for the legislative branch of government – much like the President is for the executive branch and the Chief Justice of the United States for the judicial branch. Thus, the ENTIRE House votes for speaker when it convenes the new Congress at noon on January 3.

There are 435 members. If all members cast ballots, Jeffries simply needs 218. Jeffries could lose 40 votes or so and still prevail. So that is not going to happen. He might not even lose more than a couple votes, frankly.

The Senate Democratic Caucus and Republican Conference work much the same way as the House. A simple majority wins for majority leader in the Democratic Caucus and minority leader in the Republican Conference. However, the selection of Senate majority leader is not a vote which plays out on the floor. The concept of "Senate Majority Leader" has only been around since the early 20th century and is not mentioned in the Constitution. Remember what we said about the House Speaker being the head of this branch of government.
It would be hard to envision a scenario where Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., would not become Majority Leader after Democrats flipped the Senate in a beatdown.

First, who else is running? Well, Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, is very popular among Senate Democrats. But he’s running for Majority Whip to succeed retiring Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin, D-Ill. One could see Democrats defaulting to Schatz if something happens with Schumer.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., said he wants to look at his options and endorsed Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., for majority leader. But Van Hollen isn’t running. Sen.-elect Annie Andrews, D-S.C., told colleague Bret Baier she wants a "generational change" in leadership. Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, D-Maine, and Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, D-Kan., both said they would oppose Schumer.
But again, you can’t beat someone with no one.
REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: HOW MIDTERMS MAY CHANGE THE HOUSE IMPEACHMENT EQUATION FOR HEGSETH

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and the GOP are gearing up for a floor battle with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Senate Democrats over Trump-backed voter ID legislation. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Here’s the math:

Let’s say Democrats do win Mississippi and Alaska, giving them 56 senators who caucus with the Democrats. All Schumer needs is 29 Democrats to support him in caucus, and he’s the next majority leader.

There has not been as much rumbling about the future of Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D. Heretofore, President Trump has not called for new leadership in the Senate. But a group of Senate Republicans are calling on a delay in leadership elections slated for Tuesday. Senate Republicans would choose Thune or anyone else on a secret ballot in the Senate GOP Conference. A simple majority would win. If Republicans are down to 44 seats, the winner would just need 23 votes.

So for the next couple of weeks, there’s a lot of counting. Counting about votes for impeachment. Counting in leadership elections. And next year, counting votes as Democrats try to enact their agenda.
Democrats will say voters are counting on them. And Republicans, well, they may be counting the days.
Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, warned that there was a "problem" with the Senate's bipartisan housing package. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
Everything in the new Congress will come down to the math. And there's the issue of impeaching Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth.
But forget about Democrats pushing the move next year. Try Republicans — THIS year.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., is reintroducing articles of impeachment for Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth this week. The chances are increasingly high that the House could in fact impeach Hegseth.
Why?

Massie tried to impeach Hegseth before the midterms. But the House adjourned a day early in September. That nixed Massie’s effort. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) condemned the effort by the Kentucky Republican. But Johnson insisted that he didn’t send members home early because of fear that the House had the votes to impeach Hegseth.

Massie attempted to execute a parliamentary move which would compel the House to consider the impeachment articles right away. But they expired once the House went out of session. But Massie will resuscitate them.
GOP LAWMAKER SAYS MORE QUALIFIED OFFICIALS SHOULD LEAD PENTAGON, QUESTIONS HEGSETH'S 'MORAL COMPASS
Massie authored a total of eight articles of impeachment, ranging from the "kidnapping" of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro to how the Pentagon is running the war in Iran.

It’s possible the House could move to table the articles, or send them to committee, euthanizing the effort. But a growing number of House Republicans are grumbling about Hegseth. Any effort to dismiss the articles in the House might not work.
It’s about the math.

All Democrats are likely to vote to impeach Hegseth. Some Republicans are exasperated by Hegseth and have said privately they’d like to impeach. There are even more Republicans trying to build distance between themselves and President Trump after the midterms. That’s augmented by the fact that Republicans believe the war in Iran cost them control of Congress. Thus, even more Republicans may be willing to impeach. Finally, the GOP may have attendance problems. Republican members who lost – or were shocked that they lost – might not show up. In other words, there may be more Democrats in the House than Republicans. And don’t forget that some Republicans are now looking for a scapegoat after the election.
A simple majority is necessary to impeach.
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is seen on Oct. 15, 2026, at the Pentagon in Arlington, Va. (AP/Manuel Balce Ceneta)

If adopted, the House would send the articles of impeachment to the Senate. Under Senate rules of impeachment, the Senate must at least receive and consider the articles. But it could move quickly to dismiss. That’s what happened when the Senate considered articles of impeachment for former Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas a few years ago. The bona fide "trial" part of the process never happened where the Senate heard arguments, listened to witnesses and took evidence.

It takes a simple majority to dismiss such articles. Believe it or not, this could happen under a Republican-controlled Senate. But how might outgoing Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and Bill Cassidy, R-La., vote? That’s to say nothing of Sens. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, John Curtis, R-Alaska, Todd Young, R-Ind., and others.
It takes a two-thirds vote to convict and remove in a Senate impeachment trial.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In addition, unlike legislation, articles of impeachment carry over into the new Congress. Would a new Democratically-controlled Senate want to get bogged down in an impeachment trial from the start? Especially when new Democrats want to vote on affordability and healthcare?

Or, would a Democratic Senate embrace the idea of a full-blown impeachment trial for Hegseth – especially since the execution of the war in Iran seems to be one of the main reasons for this week’s electoral shellacking?
Some of this hinges on who both parties in each body select as their leaders.
Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

title: GOP senator withholds support for Thune as leadership showdown looms
summary: Rick Scott says he won't back John Thune for Senate GOP leader without a specific plan for the lame duck session before Democrats take control.
story: Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., isn’t ready to back John Thune for another term as Senate GOP leader. He and other Republicans want specifics on how Thune, or another contender, would get work done as Democrats prepare to take control.
FIRST ON FOX: A Senate Republican isn’t ready to support Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., to stay as the top Republican as the GOP’s leadership elections fast approach.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., in an interview with Fox News Digital, argued that whoever would be the next to lead the Senate GOP and earn his vote in the process needed to lay out a plan on how Republicans would pass key agenda items heading into the lame-duck session of Congress before Senate Democrats take control in January.

Thune plans to run again for another term as the GOP leader, but Scott and a cohort of others want to delay Tuesday morning’s leadership elections to debrief after stunning losses across the board on Election Night. Whether he’ll support Thune for another term depends on his pitch.
SENATE GOP REBELS MOVE TO DELAY LEADERSHIP VOTE, DEMAND RECKONING AFTER MIDTERM DISASTER
Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said he won't support John Thune for Senate GOP leader without a plan to pass key agenda items. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

"I don't want to put the cart before the horse," Scott said. "I mean, I think the first step is what do we want to accomplish? And then anybody, including John Thune, if they want to be that, the first thing I have to say is, ‘Do they want to do that?’"
"If that's not what they want to accomplish, then why would we elect them? But if that's what they want to accomplish, then tell us why they're the best at it," he continued.

Senate Democrats flipped the upper chamber with wins in red states across the country, clinching a 54-seat majority that could grow even more depending on the outcomes of outstanding races in Mississippi and Alaska.
STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE
That gives Republicans little time with a trifecta in government to ram through key remaining agenda items before Democrats officially take over.

Thune still plans on running for leader, too, despite the grumbling among Republicans. He said on Monday after lawmakers returned to Washington that he expected a "very engaged conversation" ahead of the leadership election.
"We'll see where it goes from there, but, yeah, I'm running for leader, and I think it's important that we have that discussion, and we will," Thune said.

Scott said that he wants the candidates to be "specific" on how they can balance the budget and pass a slew of legislation, including a stock trading ban for lawmakers, permitting reform, the National Defense Authorization Act and the SAVE America Act.
SCHUMER TANKS POPULAR INSIDER TRADING BAN IN DEM EFFORT TO DERAIL REPUBLICAN'S AGENDA AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks during a Senate Republicans press conference at the U.S. Capitol on June 2, 2026, flanked by Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., and Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W. Va. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc.)
All of that, he said, would be a show that Republicans are listening to voters after getting pummeled in the midterms.
"Back home, they don't care about anything other than do we make their lives better," Scott said.

Thune is so far running unopposed for the top job — Scott reiterated that he had no interest in running again, trying twice for the gig, once against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022, and in 2024 when Senate Republicans were searching for McConnell’s replacement.
When asked if he would like to see someone else jump into the fray, Scott said, "Oh, I wouldn't do that to anybody."

Scott and Sens. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., Ted Budd, R-N.C., John Kennedy, R-La., and Mike Lee, R-Utah, all signed onto a letter demanding that Republicans meet before holding their leadership elections and delay voting until they have a full debrief on the midterm losses and what comes next.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
They’re joined by Sens. Jim Banks, R-Ind., and Dave McCormick, R-Pa., who called for the elections to be delayed but did not sign onto the letter pushing leadership for a meeting.
When asked how long he’d like to see the leadership elections delayed, Scott said, "I think this first step is how long is it gonna take us to agree on what our path should be?"

"If we can get that done quickly, then we can, you know, have elections after that," he said. "And then people that want to run with that agenda in mind, saying they believe in that agenda and will work hard to get that agenda accomplished, then that's how we would decide how we vote."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Trump's Supreme Court majority faces looming threat after Dem Senate takeover: 'Stuck'
summary: Justice Samuel Alito confirmed he has no plans to retire, but Democrats' Senate takeover raises stakes for the Supreme Court's conservative majority.
story: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito discusses the origins of originalism, his upbringing and the court’s unique position among other branches of government on ‘Life, Liberty & Levin.’

Republicans' loss of the U.S. Senate in the midterm elections could have far-reaching consequences for President Donald Trump's judicial agenda, threatening his ability to reshape the federal courts and raising new questions about the future of the Supreme Court's 6-3 conservative majority.

With Democrats set to take control of the Senate in January, Republicans face a shrinking window to confirm Trump's judicial nominees, while any future Supreme Court vacancy could leave the president dependent on Democratic support to install a replacement.
"Lawless Lawfare" author Alex Swoyer told Fox News Digital the election results could leave the court's oldest conservative justices with a difficult decision over when to retire.

"It's likely the justices — mainly Justices Thomas and Alito — are stuck on the high court for at least six more years with Democrats taking control," Swoyer said. "Both in their late 70s, I could see why they may want to retire now, midterm."
UNDER-THE-RADAR IMPLICATION OF DEM BLUE WAVE MEANS 'ZERO' CHANCE GOP ACCOMPLISHES CRITICAL GOAL, EXPERTS WARN

Supreme Court Justices Samuel Alito, Clarence Thomas and Brett Kavanaugh share a laugh while waiting for their opportunity to leave the stage at the conclusion of the inauguration ceremonies in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 20, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

Justice Clarence Thomas, 78, and Justice Samuel Alito, 76, are the court's two oldest conservatives, making their retirement decisions particularly consequential as Republicans prepare to lose control of the Senate.

Alito, however, confirmed to Fox News on Thursday that he has no plans to retire and is committed to serving through at least the current Supreme Court term, with the justices expected to wrap up their major decisions in late June or early July.
DEMS SEIZE THE SENATE AS BLUE TIDAL WAVE CRASHES DEEP INTO TRUMP COUNTRY, TOPPLES GOP STRONGHOLDS

Members of the Supreme Court pose for a group photo at the Supreme Court on Oct. 7, 2022. Seated from left: Associate Justice Sonia Sotomayor, Associate Justice Clarence Thomas, Chief Justice of the United States John G. Roberts Jr., Associate Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. and Associate Justice Elena Kagan. Standing behind, from left: Associate Justice Amy Coney Barrett, Associate Justice Neil M. Gorsuch, Associate Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh and Associate Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

"While Senate Republicans were able to confirm Justice Barrett in a one-month timeframe in 2020, I don't think this GOP Senate has that same work ethic or ability to push a nominee through ahead of January," Swoyer said.

"I think conservatives would like to see them try; however, a judicial nominations expert told me the Senate work calendar ahead of the holidays would not afford them enough time," she added. "While a five-week window seems workable, it doesn't appear like Senate Majority Leader John Thune would have the support to usher such a move at this time."

The stakes extend beyond the Supreme Court. As of Nov. 8, the federal judiciary had 28 vacancies, with 16 nominees awaiting confirmation for current and future vacancies, leaving Republicans with limited time to advance Trump's picks before Democrats take control of the Senate.

Zack Smith, a senior legal fellow for courts and the Constitution at the Heritage Foundation, said Republicans should focus on confirming Trump's remaining lower-court nominees before their majority expires.
CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER'

Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, celebrating her 20th anniversary on the bench, is photographed in the West conference room at the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, D.C., on Friday, August 30, 2013. (Nikki Kahn/The Washington Post via Getty Images)

"The top priority for Senate Republicans right now should be confirming the lower federal court judges President Trump has already nominated. It will take all senators showing up and doing their part. But it is possible," Smith told Fox News Digital.

"As for the Supreme Court, even if a justice announced his or her retirement today, it could prove difficult to get a replacement confirmed before the end of the current Senate, although Senate Republican leadership has indicated a willingness to try. However, neither Justice Alito nor Justice Thomas has indicated any plan to retire."

The uncertainty surrounding Thomas and Alito echoes the debate over the late liberal Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, who resisted calls to retire before the 2014 midterms despite concerns that Republicans could take control of the Senate and complicate efforts to confirm an Obama-appointed successor.
DEMOCRATIC SENATOR CLAIMS GOP 'STOLE' TWO SCOTUS SEATS IN 2016, 2020, CALLS FOR EXPANSION

Republicans won the Senate in 2014 and, two years later, refused to consider Obama's Supreme Court nominee, Merrick Garland, following Justice Antonin Scalia's death. Trump won the 2016 election and appointed Neil Gorsuch to Scalia's seat in 2017.

Ginsburg remained on the bench until her death in September 2020, just weeks before the presidential election. Trump nominated Amy Coney Barrett to replace her, and the Republican-controlled Senate confirmed Barrett days before Election Day.

Barrett's confirmation gave conservatives a 6-3 majority on the Supreme Court, a balance that has shaped some of the nation's most consequential legal decisions, including the 2022 ruling overturning Roe v. Wade.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Texas governor-elect's plan to freeze electricity prices raises questions over legal authority
summary: Texas Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa plans to freeze electricity rates on Day One, but experts warn the move could trigger energy shortages.
story: Gina Hinajosa plans to use emergency powers in the Lone Star State to lock energy prices in place, raising alarm from Nick Loris, president of a free-market advocacy group.
On her first day in office, Texas Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa plans to freeze residential electricity rates in response to what she described as an affordability crisis.

"On Day One as governor, I’ll freeze residential electricity rates and make corporations finally pay their fair share," Hinojosa said in an interview with a local energy data group. She reiterated the plan in an interview with the Texas Tribune, stating, "Within an hour of taking the oath of office, I will declare a high-cost emergency in the state of Texas and issue an emergency executive order to … freeze electricity rates."

The plan is raising concerns that such a freeze will clash with Texas’ uniquely competitive energy sector, which relies heavily on free-market choice, and that it could inadvertently create energy shortages as suppliers are prevented from adjusting their prices.
DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR

Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat from Texas and former state legislator, speaks to members of the media during a block walk campaign event in San Antonio, Texas, on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. (Christopher Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
That’s the concern of Nick Loris, the president of C3 Solutions, a conservative coalition for climate solutions that focuses on energy, environment and agriculture policy.
He expects the emergency declaration will face legal challenges almost immediately from energy providers. In particular, he cast doubt on the scope of the emergency declaration.

"The Texas Disaster Act lets the governor declare disasters and suspend the regulatory laws and statutes that are in existence. But I think there is a high degree of skepticism, both from courts but also from state policymakers, that this warrants such a claim — and that it is such a disaster," Loris told Fox News Digital.
"I would imagine if there were legal challenges, it would come from those affected parties," he added.
Loris explained that Texas has fostered one of the most competitive energy environments in the country.

In 1999, the state passed Senate Bill 7 — a piece of legislation that opened most of the state to retail choice, allowing customers to pick their preferred retail electric providers (REPs), beginning in 2002.

"The legislature finds that the production and sale of electricity is not a monopoly warranting regulation of rates, operations, and services and that the public interest in competitive electric markets requires that, except for transmission and distribution services and for the recovery of stranded costs, electric services and their prices should be determined by customer choices and the normal forces of competition," the Texas Legislature wrote in the law.
TEXAS GOV. GREG ABBOTT EFFECTIVELY PAUSES NEW DATA CENTER PROJECTS PENDING STATEWIDE GRID AUDIT

State Representative Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat from Texas and then-gubernatorial candidate, speaks during a campaign event with State Representative James Talarico, a Democrat from Texas and U.S. Senate candidate, not pictured, at the Stubbs - Waller Creek Amphitheater in Austin, Texas, on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

As a result of the law, Texas largely operates its own independent energy grid and runs an energy-only wholesale market in which generators are paid primarily for the electricity they produce rather than for standing capacity.
Texas has over 100 REPs that energy consumers can pick from, each competing for consumers' business.
To Loris, the range of choices provides a remarkable amount of flexibility for consumers.

"It's like shopping at a grocery store for cereal for your retail electricity. There's so much choice that you can enter into. Short-term contracts, long-term contracts, use different fuel sources," Loris said.
However, he warned that a utilities freeze undermines that competitive environment, causing providers to shoulder the burden of fluctuating supply.
"If the electricity suppliers are not covering the costs that they incur, that's going to leave them worse off and make it more vulnerable for them to adequately provide that power," Loris said.
AI'S MASSIVE APPETITE FOR POWER, WATER IGNITES FIGHT IN HIGH-STAKES TEXAS SENATE RACE

Texas Democratic gubernatorial nominee state Rep. Gina Hinojosa speaks during an education town hall at a local community center on October 10, 2026, in Cypress, Texas. (Danielle Villasana/Getty Images)
"Price signals really kind of act like a traffic light. They tell people when to speed up, when to slow down, or when to come to a full stop," he added.
Having won her Nov. 3 gubernatorial race, Hinojosa will be sworn in on Jan. 19, 2027.
