title: White House doubles down after Trump angers base by floating illegal alien deal with Dems
summary: Trump signaled willingness to work a deal for illegal immigrants who have lived in the U.S. for over a decade, drawing fierce amnesty backlash.
story: President Donald Trump reflects on the midterm elections with "60 Minutes," revealing where he thinks his administration’s immigration strategy alienated voters.

The White House on Monday morning wouldn't rule out the administration working with Democrats on a "deal" for illegal immigrants who have been living in the U.S. for more than a decade as Republicans prepare to lose control of Congress in January.
President Donald Trump, in his first sit-down interview since sweeping GOP midterm losses, opened the door to the possibility of considering amnesty.
"The President never said the word amnesty," a White House official insisted to Fox News Digital.
"We want Democrats to show their cards," the official revealed.

President Trump says tougher ICE enforcement is forcing violent criminal illegal immigrants out of the US, citing reverse migration, foreign prison releases and expanded metro raids. (Photo by Celal Gunes/Anadolu via Getty Images)
TRUMP ADMITS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT MAY HAVE BEEN TOO 'TOUGH' IN FIRST INTERVIEW SINCE MIDTERMS
They said, "There has never been a President stronger on immigration enforcement than President Trump."

"Thanks to his efforts more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the U.S. and we have the most secure border in American history. Like the President has said, he’s willing to work with anyone to improve the lives of Americans and Make America Safe Again."
In a "60 Minutes" interview that aired on Sunday, host Ross Douthat asked Trump how he is open to working with Democrats on immigration as he enters a lame-duck final stretch of his presidency.

"I'd love to do something on immigration," the president replied. "I think [immigration] both helped and hurt. I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out, but I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation or breaking of the law — that was that they came into the country illegally."
Trump, however, maintained that there are people in the United States who want to see all illegal aliens deported.
FOX NEWS POLL: MAJORITY SAYS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT HAS CROSSED THE LINE

But, Trump said, "if they're good people working in a landscaping company or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases paying taxes, and there's a large group of people that think they should be allowed to stay."

"When you go into a hotel and you have a woman that's working there as a maid, as a cleaner as a this as a that, as a waitress, a lot of good things, great jobs, and all of a sudden they're being taken out of the country, it's tough. It's a tough thing," he said, adding that people who he called "far-right" want deportations regardless of whether the illegal alien is working.
A man was killed Wednesday after fleeing through a U.S. Border Patrol checkpoint in Texas. (Herika Martinez/AFP via Getty Images)
FIRST ON FOX: DEMS' AFFORDABILITY CRUSADE COLLIDES WITH EYE-POPPING PRICE TAG FOR SOCIALIST IMMIGRATION PLANS

While Trump didn't say "amnesty," as the White House noted, he signaled in the interview his willingness to "work a deal" for people who have been in the United States illegally for "10 and 15 years" who haven't committed other crimes.
Rep. Maria Salazar, R-Fla., a longtime proponent of giving legal status to illegal aliens, celebrated Trump's comments on X.
"Well done, Mr. President! What you described on 60 Minutes is what the Dignity Act is all about," she said in the post.

Salazar's Dignity Act would offer legal status to people who have been in the United States continuously since 2020, provided they haven't committed other crimes and pay a restitution fee and back taxes.
Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., arrives for the House Republican Conference caucus meeting in the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
The White House wouldn't clarify what such a deal could entail when asked Monday.
Notably, the interview was taped before Stephen Miller, a notorious immigration hawk, was selected to be Trump's new chief of staff.

Immigration restrictionism has been Trump's calling card since he first ran for president beginning in 2015. His comments in the interview that aired Sunday drew a sharp reaction from those favor immigration restriction.
TED CRUZ SAYS 'BLUE TSUNAMI' TOOK OVER TEXAS AFTER DEMOCRATS SWEPT STATEWIDE RACES

"To be clear, if President Trump struck an amnesty deal with the Democrat-controlled Congress, it would be a bigger betrayal than starting the foolish war in Iran," commentator Steve Cortes said on X, adding a clip of Trump promising "the largest deportation operation in the history of our country" during a campaign rally in 2024.
Incoming House Oversight Committee leader Rep. Robert Garcia warned that Democrats could investigate President Donald Trump's pardons as well as allies of the president. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

"This plan absolutely guarantees that Texas never again votes Republican," said radio show host Anthony Cumia. "More states will turn permanently blue if illegals are given amnesty. Regan did the same this and California became a forever democrat state. Trump can do the same to Texas. Disgusting."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Someone needs to tell Trump: Any amnesty deal with Democrats will destroy the Republican Party," said X personality Kelly McCarty. "We voted for NO amnesty and mass deportations of ALL illegals. No compromises. No exceptions."
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Hegseth impeachment vote looms as House Republicans privately warn it could pass
summary: Several House Republicans believe Pete Hegseth's impeachment could pass as Rep. Thomas Massie forces a privileged resolution vote this week.
story: Rep. Thomas Massie is accusing Secretary of War Pete Hegseth of attempting to stifle Sen. Mark Kelly's freedom of speech over a video in which the Democrat senator urged troops to not obey unlawful orders.
The House of Representatives is barreling toward a vote on impeaching Secretary of War Pete Hegseth this week, and several GOP lawmakers think it could very well pass.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., is triggering a vote on impeaching Hegseth by introducing a privileged resolution on Monday, a mechanism for forcing consideration of bills that House majority leaders otherwise would have ignored. A privileged resolution must be considered within two legislative days, putting the vote on Wednesday at the latest.
Massie read his resolution on the House floor on Monday, as is custom, which took over an hour.
It comes as fallout from the war in Iran, including high gas prices, is blamed as a key factor in Republicans' significant losses in Tuesday's midterm elections.
HEGSETH FACES BIPARTISAN IMPEACHMENT THREAT AFTER IRAN WAR GETS BLAME FOR GOP MIDTERM SLAUGHTER
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth testifies before the House Armed Services Committee in the Rayburn House Office Building on April 29, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
Massie told Fox News Digital last week that he would trigger the vote when Congress returned after the midterms if Hegseth did not first resign.
Hegseth, for his part, called the impeachment effort against him a "shame" that "won't work" in a video posted to X on Friday.
HEGSETH DEMANDS $350B FOR MILITARY, FIRES BACK AT DEM IMPEACHMENT PUSH

But several House Republicans told Fox News Digital on Thursday that they believed Hegseth could very well be impeached. Sources said a combination of absences of Republican members who lost their elections and negative sentiment toward Hegseth's conduct could be enough to tip it over the edge.
The majority of Republicans are still expected to oppose the move, however.
Rep. Warren Davidson, R-Ohio, a critic of the war, said he was not in favor of impeaching Hegseth.

"I think it's an effort to scapegoat Pete Hegseth for Congress shirking their own duty and, frankly, the president taking action that, in my view, is unconstitutional — but it's also not unprecedented," Davidson told Fox News Digital.

"What would be unprecedented is to hold the Secretary of Defense accountable for a decision the president makes. Or frankly, it would have been unprecedented for the Secretary of Defense to kind of break ranks on something that is clearly not unprecedented in terms of what has become the standard operating procedure for administrations going back to the Korean War."
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., leaves the U.S. Capitol after the last votes of the week on June 25, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

Massie's impeachment resolution includes eight articles having to do with the war in Iran, striking suspected drug boats in the Caribbean, U.S. strikes against Yemen, and the extradition of now-former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.
GOP REP THOMAS MASSIE INTRODUCES 8 ARTICLES OF IMPEACHMENT AGAINST WAR SECRETARY PETE HEGSETH
Notably, another impeachment article accuses Hegseth of suppressing free speech by retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., over a video in which Kelly urged troops to resist "unlawful orders."

A privileged resolution notably carries two steps. Before a vote on the measure itself, leaders can call up a vote to "table" the bill or refer it to the relevant committee, which in both instances effectively kills it.
President Donald Trump and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth listen to questions from the press during a Cabinet meeting at Camp David in Maryland on July 31, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/AFP via Getty Images)

The last Cabinet secretary to be impeached was Biden administration Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, whom Republicans accused of a dereliction of duty at the U.S.-Mexico border. It was quickly scuttled without a trial in the last Democrat-controlled Senate.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
It's not immediately clear how House GOP leaders plan to deal with Massie's resolution.
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

title: Alaska Senate fight heats up as Sullivan moves to block Peltola lawsuit over rejected absentee ballot records
summary: Dan Sullivan's campaign accuses Mary Peltola of trying to "rig the system" by suing Alaska's Division of Elections amid a razor-thin Senate race.
story: The Alaska Senate race remains undecided as Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola are separated by fewer than 700 votes. Finn and Dunleavy discuss the impact of same-name candidate Dan J. Sullivan, who received thousands of votes, as the closely watched race remains unresolved.

Sen. Dan Sullivan's re-election campaign filed a motion to intervene in a lawsuit from Democrat Mary Peltola's Senate campaign on Monday, arguing the lawsuit was seeking to force Alaska elections officials to ignore state law.

Sullivan and Peltola remain locked in a razor-thin race for U.S. Senate after last week's election. Peltola's campaign filed a lawsuit against the Alaska Division of Elections on Friday seeking access to records for absentee ballots that were preliminarily rejected in the midterm election.

The Division responded to the lawsuit by stating that individual voters have yet to be notified that their ballots were rejected, and it would be improper to grant Peltola's campaign access to that data before voters themselves.
DUNLEAVY CALLS ALASKA VOTING SYSTEM ‘VERY CONFUSING’ AS RAZOR-THIN SENATE RACE FROZEN IN TIME

Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and former Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images) (Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images) (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images; Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Sullivan's campaign argued on Monday that the lawsuit is an attempt to "rig the system" in Peltola's favor.

"It should surprise no one that the same D.C. lawyers who spent more than a year conspiring with Mary Peltola’s campaign to deceive Alaskan voters are now asking a court to let her campaign ignore Alaska law and change the rules while votes are still being counted," said Nate Adams, campaign spokesman. "Peltola’s lawsuit is only further evidence that she is not confident she can win on the merits alone, which is why her campaign is once again attempting to rig the system in her favor."
ALASKA VOTERS APPEAR POISED TO PRESERVE RANKED-CHOICE VOTING AMID 'DECOY DAN' SENATE DRAMA

"Our campaign is following Alaska precedent to make sure every legally cast ballot is counted, and we remain confident that when every one of those ballots is counted, Senator Sullivan will win," Adams continued.

Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and former Rep. Mary Peltola, a Democratic from Alaska and U.S. Senate candidate, right, raise paddles during the 2026 Alaska Fisheries Debate in Kodiak, Alaska, on Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026. (Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
As of Monday, Peltola leads Sullivan by just over 600 votes, with over 25% of votes remaining to be counted.
PELTOLA INSISTS 'I KNEW NOTHING' ABOUT ALLEGED 'DECOY DAN' SCHEME AS SULLIVAN ALLEGES SHE IS 'STILL LYING'
Sullivan and the GOP have condemned Democrats for a "Decoy Dan" scheme that saw an independent, Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot in an alleged plot to siphon votes from the Republican incumbent.
Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy said the other Sullivan tried to get on the general election ballot as Daniel S. Sullivan, using the middle initial of the incumbent instead of his own.
SEN DAN SULLIVAN BRANDS PELTOLA’S ALLEGED BALLOT SCHEME A ‘SCANDAL AT THE HIGHEST ORDER’
Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy speaks during a proclamation signing ceremony in the Oval Office of the White House on June 11, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

"That kind of opened our eyes and we began an investigation back there, the Division of Elections did, to determine if this was a legitimate candidacy, and the Division of Elections at that time found that was not and did not put him on the ballot," Dunleavy said. "Then there was a court case and the Supreme Court in the end ruled against the Division of Elections in Alaska, and they must go on the ballot."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
After a New York Times report tied potential knowledge of the "Decoy Dan" scheme to Peltola's campaign, Dunleavy reopened the investigation of possible wrongdoing.
Fox News' Eric Mack contributed to this report.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: Schumer's grip on power slips as Dems begin to revolt against him, eye new leadership
summary: Chuck Schumer says he expects no challenge for Senate Democratic leader, but newcomers and Chris Van Hollen are reportedly mulling alternatives.
story: Several newlyelected Democratic senators suggest they are not committed to supporting Sen. Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., is riding high after flipping the Senate, but a growing rebellion among longtime and fresh-faced Senate Democrats may throw a wrench in his plan to seek another term as the top dog in the upper chamber.
The top Democrat, who has led the Senate Democratic caucus for nearly a decade, has made clear he intends to run for another term as leader and take on the role of majority leader once more.
Schumer only needs a majority of Senate Democrats to vote for him to keep the job, but some want to take stock before jumping in to back him.
CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER'
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speaks during a press conference on Capitol Hill on July 22, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Getty Images)
"We need a conversation about leadership going forward, because we need new energy and ideas," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told reporters on Tuesday when asked whether he supported Schumer.

But he quickly followed up by noting that he expected that Schumer would be "re-elected as leader, because no one has come forth willing to take the position. But we need a conversation about leadership."
Schumer, during an appearance on the New York Times’ "The Daily" podcast, was asked if he expected a challenge in running for another term as leader.
"No," he said.
THE HITCHHIKER’S GUIDE TO WHAT HAPPENS NEXT ON CAPITOL HILL
When pressed, Schumer argued that the Senate Democratic caucus is "focused on moving forward."

"Everyone’s very happy with what we all did. But this is just the beginning," Schumer said. "As I said before, and I’ll say it again and again to my caucus, to the country, to everybody: If we don’t deliver, all this will go away. This is just the first step. But I think we’re united together to do that."
Fox News Digital reached out to Schumer’s office for comment on unrest among Democrats over his plan to seek another term.

Many of the newcomers to the Senate, which spans the ideological gamut from moderate to progressive, have made clear they won’t support Schumer, including the likes of Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton and Troy Jackson.
JOE MANCHIN WARNS DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS ARE GAINING GROUND AS DEMOCRATS REMAIN SILENT
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., speaks during a rally at the National Mall in Washington D.C., on Sept. 19, 2025. (Celal Gunes/Anadolu via Getty Images)

And the sentiment that the immediate future of Democratic leadership needs to be litigated is percolating among some Senate Democrats, including Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who is favored by progressives in the upper chamber to run for the job.
"I’ve said very clearly that we need to have a discussion in the Democratic caucus," Van Hollen said during an appearance at Crooked Con over the weekend.

"We need to understand what the Democrats are going to do with this new responsibility and these new powers," he continued. "And that nobody should get a blank check without a full understanding from the caucus as to where we’re going to go."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
And Van Hollen, who has previously said his focus was more on "kicking the tires" on a run for higher office in 2028, is reportedly mulling a bid for Schumer’s job, according to Politico.
Fox News Digital reached out for comment from Van Hollen’s office to confirm if he was considering a leadership bid.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Gaza-born Democratic Socialist launches primary bid against Sen John Fetterman
summary: Democratic Socialists of America member Ahmed Moor launched a Pennsylvania primary challenge against Sen. John Fetterman over Israel support.
story: Fox News' Alexandria Hoff reports on Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer calling for Democratic unity as a feud between Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., and Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich. threatens their push.

A Gaza-born member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) has launched a primary challenge against Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., setting up a race against one of the Senate's most vocal supporters of Israel.
In a post on X, Palestinian-American writer and businessman Ahmed Moor, 42, announced his campaign to unseat Fetterman in Pennsylvania's Democratic primary.

"I’m running to end the war in Iran and to promote the dignity agenda: free healthcare, free childcare, and affordable housing," Moor wrote. "I’m calling for accountability for genocide, for ICE and for corruption. And finally, for the protection of our civil liberties in America."
DSA-BACKED CANDIDATES ARE WINNING PRIMARIES AND THEIR VISION FOR AMERICA IS VERY DIFFERENT
Ahmed Moor, 42, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, announced that he will run for a U.S. Senate seat occupied by Sen. John Fetterman. (Ahmed moor; Getty Images)
Moor is part of a broader wave of DSA members seeking public office amid growing progressive dissatisfaction with moderate Democrats.
Fetterman has drawn ire from his party's left wing for his staunch support of Israel in its war against Hamas, as well as his willingness to align with President Donald Trump on select policy issues.
FETTERMAN TROLLS THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS OF AMERICA AS ISRAEL KILLS HAMAS TERRORISTS: 'CRY HARDER'

According to The Philadelphia Inquirer, Moor moved to Pennsylvania as a child, earned degrees from the University of Pennsylvania and Harvard University, and worked in finance before embarking on a career in journalism.
President Donald Trump said he would welcome Democratic Sen. John Fetterman into the Republican Party, praising the Pennsylvania lawmaker's judgment and common sense. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)
Prior to launching his campaign, he lived in Jordan before returning to Philadelphia with his wife to raise their children.
On his campaign website, Moor sharply criticized U.S. foreign aid to Israel.

"A few years ago my birthplace was turned to rubble in a genocide funded by our tax dollars, with the support of politicians on both sides of the aisle who can't find money for transit or removing asbestos from our schools," the website states. "It’s clear the United States funds wars based on corruption and lies and has turned its back on its own people. We must make sure this never happens again."
FETTERMAN WINS PRAISE FOR 'GUTS' AFTER GOING TOE-TO-TOE WITH JON STEWART OVER ISRAEL SUPPORT
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fetterman has not yet announced whether he will seek re-election. Fox News Digital reached out to his office for comment.
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Newly elected Dem's blistering GOP attacks emerge after she courted Republican voters: 'Lit on fire'
summary: South Carolina Democratic Senator-elect Annie Andrews' old posts trashing Republicans and championing transgender rights resurfaced after Election Night.
story: Democratic nominee Dr. Annie Andrews gathers with supporters in Charleston as South Carolina Senate votes roll in.

South Carolina’s Democratic senator-elect has a history of trashing Republicans and advocating passionately for transgender rights on social media, with many of those posts reemerging after her victory earlier this month.

"The T in LGBTQ+ stands for TRANSGENDER," Annie Andrews, who is set to represent a state President Donald Trump won by roughly 18%, posted in 2023. "If you don’t support trans people, keep your cute pride post in your draft tweets, be better, and try again next year."
"Periodic reminder that I support trans kids because I am not an a--hole," she posted around the same time.

The posts stand in stark contrast to the more moderate image Andrews presented during her successful campaign against Republican Sen. Darline Graham, when she courted Republicans and independents in the deep-red state and distanced herself from some of her earlier positions on transgender issues.
MASSIVE UPSET: ANDREWS DOWNS TRUMP-BACKED GRAHAM IN RUBY-RED SOUTH CAROLINA
Annie Andrews, candidate for U.S. Senate, speaks with people Monday, March 30, 2026, during the campaign event in Greenville, South Carolina. (REUTERS)

Beyond transgender issues, where she later distanced herself from certain positions in a campaign ad, Andrews also made her disdain clear for the Republican Party before running for Senate — statements that clashed with the emphasis she placed on bipartisanship while on the campaign trail.

In August 2024, Andrews stated that the Republican Party "needs to be lit on fire & thrown in the dumpster & plunged into the deepest depths of the ocean never to be seen again," after some individuals on social media mocked Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz’s son.
SC DEM SENATE CANDIDATE CLAIMS SHE WILL STAND UP TO HER PARTY AS GRAHAM TIES HER TO 'SOCIALIST DEMOCRATS'

South Carolina Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Annie Andrews greets supporters during a midterm campaign rally on November 1, 2026, in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina. Andrews is running against Sen. Darline Graham (R-SC). (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images)
"Herpes is forever," she said in another post. "JD Vance doesn’t have to be."

"Wow they let you out of the kitchen. Congrats," Andrews wrote in a post reacting to GOP Sen. Katie Britt talking about a White House visit, making a jab at Britt with a reference to women being confined to traditional homemaking roles.
While Andrews had strong words for Republicans before launching her Senate bid, she worked to appease them in the lead-up to Election Day.

At an October town hall billed as "Republicans and Independents for Annie," for instance, she said the campaign was for people more concerned about bills, rural hospitals and government integrity than party labels. She repeatedly stated that she intended to work across the aisle if elected and that her campaign was "not just for Democrats."
DEMOCRATS ARE CHANGING THEIR TRANSGENDER MESSAGE. REPUBLICANS SAY THEY’RE JUST FLIP-FLOPPING

Democrat Dr. Annie Andrews participates in a debate with Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., for South Carolina's 1st Congressional District, Oct. 19, 2022, in Charleston, S.C. (Brad Nettles/The Post and Courier via AP, File)

Andrews made scores of other posts expressing support for abortion access, drag queen story hours and increased restrictions on firearm ownership, among other issues. She reposted one post calling semi-automatic rifles "weapons of war," for instance.

"Republicans spent all their money trying to defeat Abdul and hired zero opposition researchers on Annie," independent journalist Zaid Jilani wrote on X, responding to one of Andrews’ pro-transgender resurfaced posts.
WHERE TOP DEMOCRAT SENATE CANDIDATES AND THEIR GOP OPPONENTS STAND ON TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS

South Carolina Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Annie Andrews speaks during a campaign stop at the Columbia Bethlehem Community Center on October 6, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
While some have criticized Republicans for not capitalizing on Andrews’ posts while on the campaign trail, the GOP did dredge old statements in an attempt to dissuade voters from backing her.

"Annie Andrews launched her political career fighting for her trans agenda … dozens of comments and tweets advocating for dudes in girls' sports, procedures on minors, and more," National Republican Senatorial Committee advisor Nathan Brand posted in October, responding to an ad released by Andrews disavowing biological men in women’s sports. "Now she is walking it ALL back."

Republicans leaned heavily into transgender issues, particularly banning sex change procedures for children and biological men from competing in women’s sports, during the 2026 electoral cycle. While the focus on such issues did not prevent the GOP from losing what are usually safe seats, a number of ballot measures rolling back transgender rights passed in liberal states.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The Andrews campaign did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Monday.

title: Former GOP governor heads to Capitol Hill before election count is complete: 'Already at work'
summary: Former Republican Gov. Paul LePage heads to Washington as Maine's ranked choice voting process plays out after he topped his rival by 5,000 votes.
story: Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, the Republican nominee who declared victory in his congressional race, says in an exclusive Fox News Digital interview he’ll ‘fight against’ Democrats if ‘the hurt the country.'
Former Republican Gov. Paul LePage of Maine is in Washington this week after declaring victory in his congressional race, even as the state’s ranked-choice count continues.
LePage narrowly edged out Democratic rival Matt Dunlap, and last week declared victory in the race for Maine's 2nd Congressional District. Dunlap conceded on Thursday, Nov. 5.
The mostly rural seat is the largest congressional district east of the Mississippi River by area and was won by President Donald Trump in all three of his presidential elections.

The apparent victory by LePage would be the only flip from blue to red by House Republicans in a non-redistricted seat in the midterm elections. And it would be rare good news for the GOP after getting trampled by a blue wave that saw Democrats storm back to grab a large House majority as well as recapture the Senate.
HEAD HERE FOR THE LATEST RESULTS FROM THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS

Former Gov. Paul LePage, the Republican nominee in the state's 2nd Congressional District, declares victory in the midterm elections, at an event in Bangor, Maine on Nov. 4, 2026. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

Even though Dunlap conceded to LePage last week, a ranked-choice count kicked off Monday morning. That's because while LePage topped Dunlap by more than 5,000 votes, he fell short of grabbing a majority, which would have prevented ranked-choice voting. According to the Maine Secretary of State, LePage received 49.894% of the total votes cast in the 2nd District race.
LePage was in the nation's capital as ranked choice voting got underway.

"Paul is already at work in Washington D.C. while the perfunctory process plays out back home. Just like our opponent, who conceded, we are confident in the outcome," longtime LePage campaign strategist Brent Littlefield told Fox News Digital.
MAGA VOTERS WEIGH IN ON WHO THEY'D LIKE IN 2028

State auditor Matt Dunlap, the Democratic congressional nominee in the 2nd District, is interviewed by Fox News Digital, on July 25, 2026, in Bangor, Maine. Dunlap conceded to his Republican rival, former Gov. Paul LePage, two days after the midterm elections. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

The former governor is expected to take part Tuesday in a scheduled vote by returning GOP congressional lawmakers and newly elected House Republicans to choose the next minority leader in the race between current House Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Judiciary Chair Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio. Outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson decided against a bid to lead the House Republicans following the GOP's crushing ballot-box setback.
Asked how he succeeded when so many Republicans went down to defeat last week, LePage pointed to "my brand."

"I've been governor twice. I've won this district now for the fourth time... My brand. People know me and people trust me and know what I'll say, I'll do," LePage said in a Fox News Digital interview last Wednesday in Bangor, Maine, after declaring victory.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Looking ahead, LePage said, "Hopefully there's still some commonsense in the Democratic Party down there and I hope that I can work with them."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
But pointing to far-left Democrats aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), LePage argued, "I think we have to rid ourselves of DSA Democrats."
And he said Republicans and non-DSA Democrats "have to work together because DSA is a poison for this country."
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Senate GOP rebels move to delay leadership vote, demand reckoning after midterm disaster
summary: Senate Republicans face a push from Ron Johnson and four allies to delay Tuesday's leadership elections after last week's stunning Election Night losses.
story: Sen. Ron Johnson discusses his efforts to preserve records related to Alaska's 'decoy Dan' ballot controversy and allegations of coordination involving Democratic operatives.
Last week’s pummeling on Election Night has a cohort of Senate Republicans wanting to take stock as lawmakers return to Washington, D.C.
The Senate GOP is slated to hold its leadership elections Tuesday morning, where Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., is expected to seek another term as top Republican.

But a small group led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., wants to delay the leadership elections to debrief after last week’s stunning losses and chart a path forward heading into the minority. Senate Democrats flipped the chamber by clinching 54 seats, and that number could grow depending on the outcomes in Mississippi and Alaska.
THE HITCHHIKER’S GUIDE TO WHAT HAPPENS NEXT ON CAPITOL HILL

Ranking Member Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., speaks as U.S. Coast Guard Commandant Adm. Linda Fagan testifies at a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Subcommittee on Investigations hearing on Capitol Hill on June 11, 2024, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Johnson, in a letter obtained by Fox News Digital to Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., the conference chair for the Senate GOP, argued the election should be delayed "until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats."

"Tuesday's result was a stunning defeat, and there are multiple reasons for it," Johnson wrote. "We need to have serious discussions within our conference as to what we can do to improve the outcome in 2028."

"Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice," he continued. "It is certainly not the way leadership elections should be conducted in the world's greatest deliberative body."
GOP EYES SENATE COMEBACK AFTER DEMOCRATIC BLOODBATH, BUT ANOTHER POLITICAL NIGHTMARE COULD AWAIT

The Senate GOP’s rules do allow for the consideration of such a delay, as long as Johnson can get five signatures on his letter, and he did, securing Sens. Rick Scott, R-Fla., John Kennedy, R-La., Ted Budd, R-N.C., and Mike Lee, R-Utah, as his base of support.
"We first need to digest what happened last week and make plans to move forward," Lee said on X. "Turning to leadership elections Tuesday morning would put the cart before the horse."
Others who didn’t sign onto the letter, like Sens. David McCormick, R-Pa., and Jim Banks, R-Ind., similarly want to take a beat before casting their votes for the leadership structure.

"Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank discussion about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here," Banks said in a statement.
TREY GOWDY: THE MIDTERMS WERE A PAINFUL LESSON THAT REPUBLICANS CAN'T SKIP LEARNING
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., talks with reporters as he walks to his office after arriving at the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 28, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Getty Images)

But Republican leadership had already planned for a meeting heading into the elections, and part of Thune’s popularity among Republicans is his willingness to take feedback from lawmakers rather than "rule with an iron fist," a GOP aide told Fox News Digital.

Whether trying to slow down leadership elections turns into a shake-up in the Senate GOP’s power structure remains in the air, even with conservative voices outside the Senate calling for Thune to step aside.
So far, Thune is expected to run unopposed for another term and still remains popular among the conference. Possible challengers, like Scott, have already said they wouldn’t mount a bid against him.

"I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice," Scott said on Fox News’ "Saturday in America."
When pressed if he would support Thune, however, Scott said, "We’ll see what happens."
"We’ll see who else is going to run," he said. "I don’t know if somebody else is going to run."

title: Secret Service arrests two after car crash and barricade breach outside White House
summary: Police arrested two individuals in separate incidents near the White House on Monday morning. The Secret Service has launched investigations into both.
story: Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos allegedly told Secret Service agents that voices directed him to travel to Washington and kill President Donald Trump.
Police arrested two people outside the White House in separate incidents on Monday near Lafayette Square Park.

Video from the park circulating on social media shows a vehicle that appeared to run into a barrier, with the engine emitting smoke. Authorities say the driver was "combative" with law enforcement and was arrested.

"Just before 10:00 a.m., Secret Service Police and National Guard responded to the north side of Lafayette Park at 16th Street and H Street, NW, where a vehicle crashed onto the sidewalk. The driver was combative with law enforcement, but was quickly placed under arrest," a Secret Service spokesperson said in a statement.
"MPD’s Explosive Ordinance Disposal team has been called to sweep the vehicle as a precaution. Subsequently, roads around Lafayette Park have been closed," the statement continued.
CAR RAMS INTO WHITE HOUSE BARRICADE, SUSPECT ARRESTED: OFFICIALS
Police block off a road near the White House after a vehicle crashed into Lafayette Square Park on Monday, November 9, 2026. (Nicole McManus/Fox News)
"Around the same time, a second individual jumped a barricade near the northwest corner of Lafayette Park. That individual was also quickly placed under arrest," it added.
The Secret Service briefly moved reporters and the press inside the White House briefing room after the incident, but they have since been released.
Authorities say both incidents are currently under investigation.
The arrests come just days after authorities arrested an illegal immigrant from Venezuela outside the White House on Thursday.
The Department of Homeland Security says officers found the man inside a stolen vehicle carrying multiple guns and threatening to kill President Donald Trump.

U.S. Secret Service officers approached the suspect Thursday evening after spotting him "acting suspicious in his car while it was parked on Constitution Avenue in Washington, D.C.," DHS told Fox News.
The suspect, Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos, is an illegal alien from Venezuela. (DHS)
The suspect told officers he had heard voices in his head telling him to travel to the nation's capital and kill Trump, DHS said.
Officers subsequently learned that the vehicle had been reported stolen, and the suspect admitted to having weapons inside, according to DHS.
A search of the vehicle reportedly turned up three guns, including an AR-15-style rifle and two handguns, along with dozens of rounds of ammunition.
SECRET SERVICE DETAINS, QUESTIONS INDIVIDUAL WHO DROVE VEHICLE INTO BARRICADE NEAR WHITE HOUSE
The suspect was identified as Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos, who illegally entered the country through Texas in March 2024 and was subsequently arrested by U.S. Border Patrol, according to officials.
The weapons and ammunition retrieved from the suspect’s car, including an AR-15 style weapon, a Mac 10, and a Glock 43X.  (DHS)
He was later released into the country under the Biden administration, authorities said.
After his arrest, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) lodged a detainer for Chrinos with the U.S. Marshals Service, which currently has custody of Chrinos.

The U.S. Secret Service said the incident reflects a growing threat posed by armed individuals "drawn to the White House complex."
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: New AI malware ranks victims by how much they're worth
summary: VOLTA-AUTODOXER malware uses AI to analyze stolen data and rank victims by potential value, helping criminals target the most profitable accounts.
story: Kurt Knutsson, the 'CyberGuy', weighs in on warnings of rising AI cyber threats after Bill Gates sounds the alarm. Gates warns of negative surprises within a year and cautions that the world is not prepared for AI upheavals.

You probably know that hackers want your passwords, credit card information and other personal details. But what if they could also figure out how much you're worth to them? That's exactly what researchers say a newly discovered malware strain is designed to do. It steals information from your computer, studies your digital life and then uses artificial intelligence to build a detailed profile of you. The goal? Help criminals decide which victims deserve more attention and which stolen accounts could bring in the most money.

The malware is called VOLTA-AUTODOXER, and researchers at Cisco Talos uncovered it through a cybersecurity research project focused on AI-powered threats. What caught my attention is how it can take everyday details about your life and turn them into something criminals could use against you. Even a food delivery receipt could help reveal where you live. Here's how this malware works, what it could reveal about you and the steps you can take to protect yourself.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
WINDOWS MALWARE USES GROK AI TO HELP STAY HIDDEN, RESEARCHERS SAY
VOLTA-AUTODOXER steals sensitive information from Windows computers, then uses artificial intelligence to assess which victims could be most valuable to criminals. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How this new AI malware works

Most information-stealing malware follows a familiar pattern. It gets onto your computer, collects whatever sensitive information it can find and sends that data back to criminals. VOLTA-AUTODOXER takes that process further by using AI to evaluate the information after collecting it. According to Cisco Talos, the Windows malware can steal saved browser passwords, payment card information and login sessions. It also targets cryptocurrency wallets and certain work-related credentials. Once it collects that information, it builds a detailed report about the person using the computer.

That report can include your location, employer and clues about your age. The malware can also collect saved Wi-Fi passwords, screenshots and information from applications such as Microsoft Outlook and Slack. Researchers even found that it attempts to crack cryptocurrency wallet vaults. Then comes the AI component. The malware sends the information to an AI model through a platform called OpenRouter. The model receives instructions to act like an intelligence analyst and determine which stolen information could be the most valuable.

Think about that for a moment. Instead of a criminal manually reviewing hundreds of stolen accounts, AI can help sort through the information and identify potentially profitable targets. And the AI analysis is optional. Even if that part fails or cannot run, the malware can still collect information and send it to the attacker.
Your food delivery history could reveal more than you think

Here's where this gets especially personal. VOLTA-AUTODOXER can search for clues about your home address, employer and financial information. Researchers found that it can also use stolen account access to examine Gmail receipts and food delivery orders. For example, the malware looks for purchase information from services such as Uber Eats and DoorDash. It can also examine receipts from Amazon and other retailers. Those records may help confirm where you live.

And it goes further. Using stolen login sessions, the malware can retrieve order histories directly from Uber Eats and DoorDash. It can also search Gmail for receipts from Grubhub, Walmart and PayPal. That gives criminals another way to connect your online activity to your actual identity.

The information goes well beyond your address. The malware can collect clues about your age, workplace and online accounts. It can even look at Roblox accounts to estimate the value of virtual items. Individually, some of these details might seem harmless. But when AI combines them, criminals could develop a much clearer understanding of your personal and financial life.
AI decides which stolen information could be worth money

The most concerning part of VOLTA-AUTODOXER comes after the information has been collected. The malware asks AI to create a report that ranks the victim's assets according to their potential value. Researchers found that the instructions include a section called "WHAT THEY'RE WORTH." The AI is asked to identify valuable information and assign low, medium or high rankings.

Another section called "THEIR OPSEC" examines the victim's security habits, including password practices. In other words, the malware is designed to help criminals understand what they might gain and how well someone has protected their accounts. Cisco Talos found that the malware uses Anthropic's Claude as its default AI model. If the model refuses the request, the malware can try Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 and Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash.

That fallback system is especially revealing. Whoever developed the malware anticipated that an AI model might refuse to help and built a way to try another model. The malware can also send the resulting assessment to criminals through Telegram. That means an attacker could potentially receive an organized report without having to study all the stolen information personally. There's an important point here. Researchers identified these capabilities by analyzing the malware's code. They have not established that criminals have successfully used these AI-generated rankings to select real-world victims for additional attacks.
AI-POWERED CYBERATTACKS FUEL 'BLACK OCTOBER' FEARS
New AI-powered malware can steal saved passwords and other sensitive information from a computer, then assess how valuable that data could be to hackers. (Felix Zahn/Photothek via Getty Images)
The malware can delete itself after stealing your data

Another concerning capability is VOLTA-AUTODOXER's ability to remove its main executable after completing its work. That could make an infection harder to investigate. However, Cisco Talos found that the malware may leave behind a diagnostic file called volta_debug.txt. That file can contain a record of what the malware collected and whether the AI analysis succeeded. For security investigators, it could provide valuable clues about what happened.

There's another detail worth knowing. The malware uses the infected computer's own internet connection to contact the AI service. Researchers also found that its observed network destinations belong to third-party services rather than infrastructure owned by the attacker. That could make suspicious activity less obvious, although it does not guarantee the malware will escape detection.

Researchers also found evidence suggesting the malware was designed as a customizable product. Its developer appears to have created a system where different criminals could supply their own settings and receive a customized version. Cisco Talos believes this could make AI-powered victim profiling available to criminals who lack advanced technical skills. However, researchers have not confirmed that the malware is being sold.
What researchers still don't know

There are some important unanswered questions. Cisco Talos first observed the analyzed sample on October 11, 2026, but researchers have not established how many computers VOLTA-AUTODOXER has infected or how widely it has spread. They also have not confirmed a specific campaign distributing this malware.

That means there's no evidence in the published findings that this malware is currently infecting large numbers of everyday computer users. Still, its capabilities show how criminals could use AI to get more value from information they already know how to steal. And for now, there's no confirmed method of distribution for VOLTA-AUTODOXER. That's why it's important to focus on protecting your computer against information-stealing malware in general rather than assuming this particular threat arrives through a specific type of message or download.
How to protect yourself from AI-powered malware

You don't need to understand how AI works to reduce your risk. VOLTA-AUTODOXER still needs access to your computer before it can collect sensitive information. That means many of the same precautions that protect against traditional malware can help here, too. Here are some practical steps worth taking.

One of the best ways to protect yourself is to have strong antivirus software running on your devices. Good security software can help detect malicious downloads, suspicious programs and other threats before they steal your information. Keep your protection updated and run regular scans. Look for software that monitors suspicious behavior in addition to scanning for known threats. That's especially helpful when dealing with malware designed to hide its activity or delete itself after an attack. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

VOLTA-AUTODOXER specifically targets credentials stored in web browsers. Consider using a reputable password manager that protects your passwords in an encrypted vault instead. Create a strong, unique password for every important account. That way, one stolen password won't automatically give criminals access to other services. However, a password manager alone cannot guarantee protection if your computer has already been compromised. Some malware can steal active login sessions or capture sensitive information while you're using it.

Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) for your email, financial accounts and other important services. Whenever possible, use passkeys or a hardware security key. However, remember that some information-stealing malware can steal active login sessions. That means 2FA alone may not stop every account takeover. If you suspect an infection, sign out of existing sessions after securing your device.

Install Windows security updates and keep your browser current. Updates can close vulnerabilities that attackers exploit to install malware. Also, avoid downloading software from unfamiliar websites. Be especially cautious about unexpected attachments or messages urging you to install something immediately. And never copy commands into Windows PowerShell, Command Prompt or the Run dialog because a random website tells you to fix a problem. Criminals have used these tactics to trick people into installing other information-stealing malware.
HACKERS HIDE DANGEROUS FAKE AI DOWNLOADS BEHIND GOOGLE ADS
Cisco Talos researchers uncovered malware that can steal passwords, payment information and login sessions before using AI to build a profile of its victim. (Pornyot Palilai via Getty Images)

VOLTA-AUTODOXER shows how seemingly unrelated personal details can help criminals build a profile of you. Consider using a personal data removal service to reduce the information that data brokers publish about you. These services cannot erase information already stolen from your computer. However, they can help reduce the amount of personal information available through public data broker listings. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Because this malware collects financial and identifying information, consider using an identity theft protection service. Such services can monitor for certain signs of misuse and alert you to suspicious activity. You should also review your financial statements and credit reports regularly. If criminals gain access to your information, early detection could help limit the damage. You can also place a free credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. That can help prevent criminals from opening new credit accounts in your name, even if they've stolen personal information. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

VOLTA-AUTODOXER can also target information connected to your workplace. That includes certain Microsoft account tokens, cloud credentials and Slack workspace details. If you use your computer for work, avoid storing sensitive access keys in unprotected files. Follow your company's security policies and report suspicious activity to your IT department immediately. Cisco Talos also identified a technique that attempts to bypass Chrome's App-Bound Encryption protection. Organizations can reduce that risk by controlling which programs can launch Chrome in headless mode. That is a more technical safeguard your IT or security team can evaluate.
What to do if you think your computer has been infected
If you suspect malware has stolen your information, act quickly.

Disconnect the affected computer from the internet to help stop additional unauthorized activity. Avoid signing into sensitive accounts from that computer until it has been checked.Use a trusted antivirus or security tool to investigate. If you cannot confirm the infection has been removed, consider getting professional help. In some cases, reinstalling Windows from trusted installation media may be the safest recovery option.Change your important passwords from a separate, trusted device, starting with your email and financial accounts. Revoke suspicious login sessions and replace any compromised security tokens or API keys.Contact your employer's IT or security team if your work accounts may have been exposed. Let your bank or credit card company know if you see suspicious transactions or believe your payment information has been stolen.Protect your cryptocurrency holdings. If you store cryptocurrency wallet recovery phrases on your computer, treat them as compromised. Move funds to a new wallet with a freshly generated recovery phrase using a trusted, secure device. For particularly sensitive holdings, Cisco Talos recommends generating the new recovery phrase on an offline device.Preserve potential evidence. Cisco Talos recommends preserving the volta_debug.txt file if investigators find it. That file could help establish what information the malware collected. Avoid deleting potential evidence before a security professional has examined it.
Disconnect the affected computer from the internet to help stop additional unauthorized activity. Avoid signing into sensitive accounts from that computer until it has been checked.

Use a trusted antivirus or security tool to investigate. If you cannot confirm the infection has been removed, consider getting professional help. In some cases, reinstalling Windows from trusted installation media may be the safest recovery option.

Change your important passwords from a separate, trusted device, starting with your email and financial accounts. Revoke suspicious login sessions and replace any compromised security tokens or API keys.

Contact your employer's IT or security team if your work accounts may have been exposed. Let your bank or credit card company know if you see suspicious transactions or believe your payment information has been stolen.

Protect your cryptocurrency holdings. If you store cryptocurrency wallet recovery phrases on your computer, treat them as compromised. Move funds to a new wallet with a freshly generated recovery phrase using a trusted, secure device. For particularly sensitive holdings, Cisco Talos recommends generating the new recovery phrase on an offline device.

Preserve potential evidence. Cisco Talos recommends preserving the volta_debug.txt file if investigators find it. That file could help establish what information the malware collected. Avoid deleting potential evidence before a security professional has examined it.

Most importantly, don't assume you're safe because the suspicious program has disappeared. This malware can delete itself after stealing your information, and the stolen credentials may still be usable by criminals.
Kurt's key takeaways

What concerns me most about VOLTA-AUTODOXER is how much someone could learn about you just by getting into your computer. Think about what's sitting on your device right now. Maybe you've saved a few passwords in your browser. Your email probably contains years of receipts, including orders delivered right to your front door. Now, consider what happens when a criminal feeds all that information into AI and asks one simple question: How much is this person worth? That's what caught my attention about this research. The malware is designed to do the homework for the criminal and help identify which stolen information deserves the most attention. We still don't know how widely VOLTA-AUTODOXER has spread, so there's no reason to assume your computer has been targeted. But I do think this gives us a pretty good idea of where cybercrime could be heading. The less work criminals have to do themselves, the easier it could become for them to target more people. And that's one more reason to take your personal information seriously before someone gets hold of it.

How would you feel knowing that hackers could use AI to put a dollar value on your personal information? And do you think AI companies should do more to prevent criminals from using their technology this way? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: New big rig safety tech could save your life
summary: Daimler Truck's Oregon demos show how a Freightliner Cascadia's automatic emergency braking responds when dummy cars suddenly cross a moving truck's path.
story: Daimler Truck's advanced safety systems use radar and cameras to monitor surrounding vehicles and help prevent dangerous collisions. (Joe Raedle/Newsmakers via Getty Images)

Ever find yourself driving next to a massive 18-wheeler and wondering if the driver can actually see your car? It's a reasonable concern. Big rigs have enormous blind spots, and stopping one takes a lot more time and distance than stopping your car. Now, new big rig safety tech from Daimler Truck could help prevent some of the most dangerous crashes on our roads.

The company behind Freightliner is upgrading its trucks with technology that can recognize potential collisions and automatically hit the brakes. We're talking about situations where another driver suddenly cuts across a truck's path or a pedestrian gets dangerously close during a turn. And demonstrations at Daimler's Oregon proving grounds offer a revealing look at what happens when this technology faces situations that could turn deadly on public roads.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
100 KODIAK DRIVERLESS TRUCKS ARE HEADED FOR PUBLIC ROADS
What happens when a car suddenly cuts in front of a big rig?

At Daimler Truck's testing facility in Oregon, engineers recreated situations that could easily turn deadly on a public road. They used dummy cars mounted on remote-controlled platforms to simulate vehicles suddenly crossing in front of a moving Freightliner Cascadia. In one demonstration, the truck successfully avoided a collision. In another, it clipped the dummy car after braking. That second test may sound like a failure, but consider what could have happened if the truck had continued at full speed. Slowing down before impact can make an enormous difference when a passenger car comes face-to-face with a fully loaded truck.

The demonstrations generally took place at speeds between 40 and 55 mph. Daimler said the truck's trailer carried approximately 30,000 pounds during the tests. That's a lot of weight pushing forward when the brakes suddenly engage. And here's what caught my attention. The technology was designed to recognize these developing dangers and respond even when the driver had little time to react. That's especially important because a few seconds can determine how serious a collision becomes.
How big rig safety tech spots trouble before a crash

The technology comes from Detroit Assurance, Daimler Truck North America's collection of advanced driver assistance systems. At the center is Active Brake Assist 6, also known as ABA6. It uses five radar sensors and a camera to monitor what's happening around the truck. Together, they provide approximately 270 degrees of coverage, including areas alongside a standard 53-foot trailer.

Think of it as another set of electronic eyes helping the driver keep track of nearby traffic. The system can identify certain vehicles that have stopped unexpectedly, including cars sitting at unusual angles after an accident. For example, a truck approaching a crash scene might encounter a disabled vehicle partly blocking the roadway. Active Brake Assist 6 is designed to recognize these situations and warn the driver. If necessary, it can also apply the brakes.

The technology can recognize pedestrians and cyclists in certain scenarios, too. That's particularly useful when a large truck travels through busy areas where people may be difficult to see from the cab. And Daimler is now expanding those capabilities to address another dangerous situation.
WHAT HAPPENS IF THE WAYMO COMPUTER FAILS?
Freightliner’s latest safety systems use radar and cameras to monitor traffic around big rigs and respond when a collision threat develops. (Stock Photos)
New Freightliner safety systems can brake at intersections

Intersections can be especially challenging for truck drivers. They have to maneuver a massive vehicle while watching traffic that may approach from several directions. All it takes is one person making an unexpected move. That's where a new feature called Cross Traffic Assist comes in. The system uses radar to detect vehicles crossing the truck's path at intersections. If it recognizes a potential collision, it can alert the driver with audible and visual warnings. When the danger becomes more serious, it can also apply partial or full braking. Now, think about what that could mean if someone accidentally pulls out in front of an approaching truck. The system may give the driver extra time to respond or help reduce the force of a collision.

Another improvement involves Active Side Guard Assist 2. The enhanced system adds protection when the truck makes a left turn across oncoming traffic. With the left turn signal activated, it can recognize certain approaching vehicles and warn the driver. If necessary, it can also apply the brakes. The new left-turn protection builds on existing safety technology that monitors the passenger-side blind spot during right turns. That system can detect pedestrians and cyclists and apply braking when necessary.

These improvements are scheduled to become standard on Freightliner Cascadias built beginning in 2027, with production planned for January. Active Brake Assist 6 itself is already standard on the fifth-generation Cascadia. According to Daimler Truck North America, the goal is to give professional drivers additional support when visibility or reaction time becomes limited.
What if a truck driver suddenly stops responding?

There's another feature that deserves attention because it addresses a frightening possibility. What happens if someone behind the wheel of a big rig suddenly becomes unresponsive? Freightliner's optional Active Lane Assist 2 can help keep the truck centered in its lane and correct unintended drifting. It can also provide steering assistance during certain challenging driving conditions, such as strong crosswinds.

But the feature I find particularly interesting is called Attentive Driver Protection. When the lane-keeping system is active, Attentive Driver Protection monitors whether the driver continues responding. If the driver fails to respond to escalating warnings, the technology can slow the truck to a stop while helping keep it centered in its lane. It can also activate the hazard lights to warn surrounding traffic.

Consider the potential consequences of a driver becoming unresponsive while operating a massive truck on a busy highway. Having an additional safety system that can help bring the vehicle to a controlled stop could make a significant difference. However, the feature doesn't diagnose medical emergencies or determine why a driver has stopped responding. It reacts to a lack of driver response under specific conditions. And like the other safety systems, it still depends on factors such as road conditions and sensor performance.
HUMANLESS BIG RIG COMPLETES FIRST US FREIGHT RUN
Freightliner’s Attentive Driver Protection can slow a truck to a stop if the driver stops responding to escalating warnings. (Noah Berger, File/AP Photo)
What this means to you

You may never drive a Freightliner, but chances are you share the road with big rigs regularly. And that's why these improvements should interest you. If a truck can recognize a dangerous situation and begin braking before the driver has time to react, the people in nearby vehicles could have a better chance of avoiding serious injuries. Even reducing the speed of an unavoidable collision could make a significant difference.

But don't assume every truck you encounter has these features. Many older trucks won't have the newest technology, and even equipped vehicles have limitations. Sensors can struggle in poor weather or when visibility becomes limited. Automatic braking also cannot guarantee that every collision will be avoided.

So, continue giving big rigs plenty of room. Avoid lingering beside a truck where the driver might have trouble seeing you. And when passing, make sure there's sufficient space before moving back into its lane. Remember that even the smartest technology cannot change the physics of a massive truck traveling at highway speed. The safest approach is to stay alert and avoid putting yourself in a situation where a truck driver has to make a sudden move.
Kurt's key takeaways

Here's what I find encouraging about Daimler's latest safety technology. It recognizes something we all know about driving. People make mistakes. Someone misjudges an intersection or pulls out without realizing how quickly a truck is approaching. Those split-second decisions can have terrible consequences, especially when a massive vehicle has little room to stop. The demonstrations in Oregon showed why this technology has potential. In one scenario, the truck avoided a collision. In another, contact still occurred, but the braking reduced the impact. That second result is an important reminder that a safety system can still provide protection even when it cannot prevent every accident. I also think we're seeing an interesting shift in how truck manufacturers approach safety. There's been plenty of attention on trucks that can drive themselves. Yet here we have technology designed to help professional drivers do their jobs more safely. And when you consider how many trucks share our highways, even modest improvements in collision prevention could have an enormous impact. Of course, controlled demonstrations are one thing. Everyday traffic brings unexpected challenges that are much harder to predict. I'll be interested to see how these systems perform as more equipped trucks reach the road. If the technology can prevent serious crashes, that's something we can all appreciate.

Would you feel safer knowing an 18-wheeler could automatically brake to avoid hitting your car, or would you still be nervous driving alongside a massive truck that relies on software to react? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Facebook recovery scams use fake FBI profiles
summary: Facebook ads promising to recover stolen funds are targeting scam victims again, and Meta confirmed removing flagged accounts after investigation.
story: From voice cloning to fake arrests, cyber expert Morgan Wright breaks down how scammers use high-tech tools to exploit basic human fears.

You've already lost money to a scam. You're frustrated and probably wondering whether you'll ever see that money again. Then, while scrolling through Facebook, an advertisement appears promising to recover your stolen funds. Suddenly, there's a little hope. Maybe someone out there can actually help. Unfortunately, that moment of hope is exactly what scammers are trying to exploit.

One of our loyal CyberGuy followers, Patrick K, recently tipped us off to suspicious fraud recovery advertisements and profiles appearing on Facebook. He shared screenshots of what he was seeing and urged us to warn others.

His tip caught our attention, so we decided to dig deeper and contacted Meta about the suspicious accounts and advertisements. After reviewing the examples we provided, Meta confirmed to CyberGuy that it removed the flagged accounts and ads for violating its impersonation policies. The screenshots Patrick shared are especially concerning. One promotes stolen-asset recovery services. Another uses FBI-related imagery and claims to help people navigate the Internet Crime Complaint Center, better known as IC3. Together, they show how convincing these offers can appear.

WHY IDENTITY THEFT COMES BACK FOR THE SAME PEOPLE
Scammers are using Facebook pages and advertisements as fronts to exploit previous scam victims. (Gabby Jones/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Facebook recovery ads promise to get your money back

The first screenshot Patrick shared shows a Facebook advertisement displayed under the name Adam Molina. The promotional image features a smiling man in a business suit against a purple background. The graphic bears the name "DARKTRACER" and asks whether you've lost assets or funds to scammers. Below that message, the ad promotes services like recovering stolen assets and retrieving hacked cryptocurrency wallets. At the bottom, there's a Facebook Messenger button inviting people to send a message.

That's what concerns me. Someone who just lost thousands of dollars could see this advertisement and believe they've finally found a solution. After all, it looks like a company offering specialized assistance. And because it appears as a paid Facebook advertisement, some people may assume the advertiser has been thoroughly vetted.
Fake FBI investigator profiles create another trap

The second screenshot Patrick sent us is even more troubling. It shows a Facebook page displaying the title "Director of Fraud Investigations" and the name Grace K. The cover image features the White House, the FBI's J. Edgar Hoover Building and cryptocurrency graphics. It also displays references to IC3 and the U.S. Department of Justice. The page description claims to help fraud victims navigate the IC3 reporting process. It even suggests that people who lost more than $4,000 may qualify for federal review. That claim appears on the page, but we found no support for such a dollar threshold in the FBI's published guidance.

It's a convincing presentation for someone desperately searching for help. The American flags and official-looking graphics create the impression that a federal agency may be involved. But here's what you need to know. The FBI says IC3 has no official social media presence. It never investigates crimes or recovers stolen money through Facebook Messenger or Telegram. That means any Facebook page claiming to represent IC3 should immediately raise suspicion, regardless of how official it looks. Meta's subsequent removal of the flagged accounts and advertisements reinforces those concerns.
Meta removes Facebook recovery scam accounts after CyberGuy inquiry

After CyberGuy shared Patrick's screenshots with Meta, the company investigated and confirmed that it removed the flagged accounts and advertisements for violating its impersonation policies. Meta also provided broader details about its efforts to combat these schemes. According to the company, it removed more than 179 million accounts, Pages and Groups for misrepresenting identity during the first half of 2026. Most were removed before anyone reported them. Since 2025, Meta says it has also removed more than 17.3 million Facebook and Instagram accounts linked to criminal scam centers.

This problem isn't new to Meta. The company previously worked with cybersecurity researchers at Graphika to identify fraudulent websites impersonating the FBI's IC3 complaint center. The scammers promised to help victims recover stolen money, including cryptocurrency. Meta says it blocked the fraudulent websites and removed accounts connected to those operations. However, the examples Patrick discovered show how these impersonation schemes continue to reach Facebook users.
FBI warns about fake IC3 recovery investigators

On July 20, 2026, the FBI issued an updated public warning about scammers impersonating IC3 investigators. According to the agency, criminals create fraudulent social media profiles that appear connected to the FBI. They then approach people who have already reported losing money to online scams. In one documented scheme, a victim realizes they've been defrauded and threatens to report the crime to the FBI. Later, someone pretending to be an FBI agent contacts the victim through Facebook Messenger. The conversation may move to Telegram, where the impersonator provides a link supposedly connected to the victim's IC3 complaint. That link may contain malicious code or collect additional financial information. Either way, the victim faces another potential loss.

The FBI also warns about AI-generated videos impersonating federal officials. Some of these videos direct victims to fraudulent websites designed to resemble the real IC3 complaint center. Once there, visitors may be asked to submit personal information under the impression they're dealing with federal investigators. And this type of impersonation extends well beyond Facebook. In a separate September 17, 2026, warning, the FBI reported nearly 61,000 complaints involving law enforcement or government impersonation scams between January 2025 and July 2026. Reported losses exceeded $1.6 billion. Those figures cover a broad range of government impersonation schemes, not Facebook recovery scams specifically. However, they show how costly impersonating official authorities has become.
SCAMMERS ARE COMING FOR YOUR MONEY. HERE’S THE ONE THING YOU MUST NEVER DO
Scammers increasingly target previous fraud victims with online offers promising to recover stolen money. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why scammers target people who already lost money

There's a particularly cruel element to recovery fraud. The criminals approach people who may already be dealing with serious financial hardship. Some have lost retirement savings, while others have been tricked into sending cryptocurrency to someone they trusted. When an offer arrives promising to recover those funds, it's understandable why someone might want to believe it.

In August 2026, the Federal Trade Commission warned that recovery scammers sometimes purchase lists of people who previously lost money to fraud. They use those details to make their offers appear credible. For example, someone may contact you claiming they've located your stolen funds. They might even know approximately how much you lost. That information can make the person sound legitimate, especially when they claim to represent a government agency or law firm.

Eventually, the supposed recovery agent introduces a fee. They might call it a processing charge or claim the payment will release your recovered funds. But after you pay, the promised refund never arrives. In some cases, the scammer also collects enough personal information to attempt identity theft. We've previously covered the scripts criminals use in cryptocurrency scams, including fake recovery services that demand additional cryptocurrency payments.
How to spot Facebook recovery scams before losing more money

A convincing advertisement or official-looking Facebook profile can fool someone who's searching for answers. Fortunately, there are warning signs you can look for before responding. Here's how to protect yourself.

Anyone claiming they can definitely retrieve stolen cryptocurrency or recover all your lost money deserves close scrutiny. Recovery depends on the circumstances, and no legitimate service can guarantee success. Be especially cautious when someone promises fast results.

The FTC warns that scammers often demand processing fees before supposedly releasing recovered funds. These payments may be described as taxes or administrative charges. However, the FBI says IC3 never charges victims to recover stolen money.

If someone on Facebook claims to work for IC3, don't engage. The FBI says IC3 has no official social media presence. Instead, type IC3.gov directly into your browser to verify information or submit a complaint.

Scammers may begin contacting you through Facebook Messenger before asking to continue on Telegram. The FBI specifically identified this behavior in IC3 impersonation cases. Be cautious when an unexpected contact pressures you to switch platforms.

Never share banking passwords or cryptocurrency wallet recovery phrases with someone advertising recovery services. Also, don't install remote-access software at the request of an unexpected contact. Doing so could give scammers access to your accounts or device.

Search for the company's name alongside terms such as "scam" or "complaint." Look for independently verifiable business information and a legitimate track record. Keep in mind that scammers can create fake testimonials and misleading websites to appear trustworthy.

Scammer Facebook pages used FBI branding to promote fraud assistance before Meta removed the flagged accounts and advertisements. (Photo by Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious websites, phishing links and harmful downloads associated with recovery scams. Choose protection with real-time threat detection and web security features. Keep it updated to help defend against emerging threats. However, antivirus software cannot prevent every scam, especially if you're tricked into sending money yourself. Take screenshots of the advertisement or suspicious profile before blocking it. Also, preserve the page URL and any messages you received. These details may help Facebook and law enforcement investigate the activity.
What to do if you already contacted a recovery scammer

If you've exchanged messages with someone offering to recover stolen money, stop communicating until you've independently verified who you're dealing with. And if you've already sent money, act quickly. Here's what to do next.

Stop communicating with the suspected scammer. Don't send additional payments or share more personal information.
