title: Fake Amazon invoice scam uses $988 iPad order as bait
summary: A fake Amazon invoice charging $988.18 for an iPad lists the same customer support phone number three times to steer panicked victims into calling.
story: A fake Amazon invoice scam uses a realistic $988 iPad receipt to trick victims into calling a fraudulent customer support number. (Getty Images)

You open your email and see an invoice from Amazon. It says you bought a new iPad for nearly $1,000. The order has supposedly shipped, and your payment has already gone through. There's even a customer support number to call if something looks wrong. Your first reaction might be to grab your phone and stop the charge. That's exactly what makes this fake Amazon invoice scam so dangerous. It uses a realistic-looking receipt and an expensive purchase to make you worry about your money. Then it offers what appears to be an easy solution. Matt, who lives in California, recently sent us one of these suspicious emails. He wanted to help others recognize the warning signs before someone falls for the same trick. After examining the message, we found several clues worth sharing.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
DO NOT CLICK FAKE 'ACCOUNT RECOVERY' AMAZON EMAIL
A fake Amazon invoice sent to a California man claims he purchased an iPad for $988.18 and repeatedly urges him to call a suspicious customer support number. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
A fake Amazon invoice that looks surprisingly convincing

Matt received the email on Oct. 28. Its subject line addressed him by name and claimed his order had already left the facility. Inside was a professionally formatted invoice featuring Amazon's familiar logo. The invoice listed an Apple iPad Air 11-inch (M4) with 256GB of storage and cellular connectivity. It showed a price of $973.19. Below that was an additional $14.99 charge labeled "Amazon Protect+ (Auto-Renew)." The grand total came to $988.18.

The document also included an invoice number, shipping details and a delivery date. It even displayed Amazon's corporate address in Seattle. All those details helped create the appearance of a legitimate transaction. However, the email also included a phone number for canceling or modifying the order. That number appeared prominently near the top, again in the payment instructions and once more at the bottom. That's where the real concern begins. The message appears designed to make someone call before checking whether the purchase actually happened.
Red flags in this fake Amazon invoice scam
Let's look at the warning signs hiding in Matt's email. Some are obvious once you notice them. Others are more subtle and help explain why these scams can fool people.

This is the biggest giveaway. The email claimed to come from someone named Jack Campos. However, the actual sender address used Outlook.com with a different personal name embedded in the address. It had no apparent connection to Amazon. Amazon says its legitimate customer emails come from Amazon domains, including amazon.com. A personal Outlook account claiming to send an official Amazon invoice deserves immediate suspicion. Scammers can write almost anything in the sender's display name. That's why I always recommend checking the actual email address before trusting a message.

The invoice displayed the same customer support number in three separate locations. It appeared inside a shaded banner, within the payment instructions and again near the bottom. That's a significant warning sign because the email steers the recipient toward making a phone call. Rather than directing Matt to verify the purchase through his Amazon account, it emphasizes contacting the number printed on the invoice. That number should be treated as unverified and potentially controlled by scammers. We have not independently established who operates it. Amazon warns that fraudulent order confirmations often encourage customers to contact supposed support representatives. Those calls can turn into attempts to obtain payment information or gain access to an account.

Look at the amount: $988.18. That's enough money to get almost anyone's attention. If you saw that charge for a product you didn't buy, you'd probably want to fix it immediately. Scammers understand that reaction. They often choose expensive electronics because the potential financial loss feels serious. The detailed iPad description makes the transaction appear more believable. However, the amount on an email invoice proves nothing about your actual bank account. Until you verify the charge independently, treat it as an unsupported claim.

Here's a detail I find especially revealing. The subject line claims the order has already left the facility. Yet the invoice says cancellations are accepted only before dispatch. So which is it? Has the package already shipped, or can the customer still cancel it? The conflicting language creates confusion while encouraging the recipient to seek help quickly. A concerned shopper may decide to call the listed number rather than spend time figuring out the inconsistency.

The email addresses Matt by name in the subject line. However, the billing section identifies the customer as "Amazon Account Holder." The invoice also lacks a clear, personalized billing and shipping address. Instead, it provides broad fulfillment details and an estimated delivery date. Generic customer information alone doesn't prove fraud. Still, it raises questions when an email claims to document a completed purchase worth nearly $1,000. If the order were genuine, Matt should be able to locate its actual details inside his Amazon account.

The invoice uses terms such as "Standard Account Allocation" and "active ledger." It also claims the authorization has been verified and automated order fulfillment is underway. Those phrases may sound official, but they provide little useful information about how the payment occurred. The email never gives Matt a reliable way to verify the transaction through his account. Scammers sometimes use corporate-sounding language to make a document seem authoritative. Don't assume unfamiliar financial terminology means the message came from a legitimate company.

Alongside the iPad, the invoice lists "Amazon Protect+ (Auto-Renew)" for $14.99. An unexpected recurring charge can create another reason for someone to contact support. Even if they aren't immediately concerned about the iPad, they might worry about paying for a subscription they never requested. The label alone doesn't establish whether the service exists or whether Matt was actually charged. However, any unfamiliar subscription on an unexpected invoice deserves verification through the company's official website.

The document features an invoice identifier beginning with "AMZ" followed by additional letters and numbers. It looks technical enough to seem convincing. However, scammers can generate invoice numbers as easily as they can copy a company logo. An unfamiliar invoice identifier should never replace independent verification. Check Amazon's Your Orders section for a matching purchase instead.

The invoice shows October 28, 2026, as both the order date and estimated delivery date. It also claims that fulfillment has already moved forward. Same-day delivery can happen with legitimate Amazon orders, so that detail alone doesn't establish fraud. Still, the message offers no independently verifiable tracking information. It relies on its own claims about shipment and delivery. The document also lists zero estimated sales tax on the nearly $1,000 transaction. That may have a legitimate explanation depending on the circumstances. However, it adds another detail worth comparing with a real order record.

Here's one of the more interesting details. The invoice includes the Amazon logo and lists Amazon.com Services LLC at 410 Terry Avenue North in Seattle, Washington. That address corresponds to an actual Amazon corporate location. This helps explain why the invoice can look credible. Scammers don't have to invent every detail. They can copy real company information and place it inside a fraudulent document. A legitimate address on a receipt doesn't authenticate the sender. The same goes for company logos and polished formatting.
IDENTITY THIEVES DON’T NEED YOUR PASSWORD ANYMORE; HERE ARE 6 NEW ACCOUNT TAKEOVER THREATS
Scammers use fake purchase invoices to create panic over unexpected charges, hoping recipients will reveal sensitive financial information. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What happens if you call the number on a fake Amazon invoice?

The likely goal of this type of scam is to move you from an email conversation to a phone call. Once someone calls, a person posing as customer support may offer to cancel the purchase or reverse the charge. To complete that supposed refund, they might request payment details or account verification information. Some scammers also ask victims to install remote-access software. They may claim the installation is necessary to resolve a billing problem. In reality, that software could give a stranger access to the person's computer.

Amazon specifically warns that its representatives will never ask you to share a one-time password over the phone. The company also cautions customers against providing financial details or granting unexpected remote access. These are documented tactics in Amazon impersonation scams. We haven't established what would happen if someone called the particular number in Matt's email. The most important point is that receiving a fake invoice does not mean you've actually been charged.

"Scammers that attempt to impersonate Amazon put consumers at risk," an Amazon spokesperson told CyberGuy. "We will continue to invest in protecting consumers and educating the public on scam avoidance. We encourage consumers to report suspected scams to us so that we can protect their accounts and refer bad actors to law enforcement to help keep consumers safe. Please visit our help pages to find additional information on how to identify scams and report them at amazon.com/ReportAScam."
What to do when a fake Amazon invoice arrives

If an unexpected Amazon invoice lands in your inbox, don't rush to cancel the order or call the number provided. A few simple checks can help you determine whether the purchase is real. And if you've already contacted the supposed support team, there are steps you can take to protect your information.

Open the official Amazon app or type Amazon.com into your browser. Select Your Orders and look for the alleged purchase. Avoid using links or phone numbers in the suspicious email. Going directly to your account helps you determine whether the order actually exists.

Sign in to your Amazon account and look for Your Messages or Message Center under your account options. Amazon says authentic customer emails appear there. When a suspicious message doesn't appear, that's another reason to question its legitimacy.

Expand the sender details instead of trusting the name displayed in your inbox. Scammers can make an email appear to come from Amazon while sending it through a personal account. Be especially suspicious of unfamiliar domains or addresses that have no connection to the company.

A fake customer support number can connect you directly to a scammer. Instead, find customer service through Amazon's official app or website. Remember, the person who sent the questionable invoice also supplied that phone number.

Amazon now lets U.S. customers use Alexa for Shopping on Amazon.com or in the Amazon Shopping app to check suspicious emails, texts and phone calls. Simply ask, "Is this email from Amazon?" and provide details about the message. The tool checks the information against Amazon's records to determine whether the communication came from the company. If it can't verify the message, it will let you know. You can also forward suspicious emails to verify@amazon.com for verification.

Never share your Amazon password or one-time security codes with someone who contacts you unexpectedly. Consider setting up a passkey or enabling two-step verification for additional protection. These safeguards can make unauthorized account access more difficult, even when someone obtains your password.

Strong antivirus protection can help detect malicious links, unsafe websites and harmful downloads that scammers may use to steal information. Choose reputable security software with real-time protection and keep it updated. While antivirus software cannot prevent someone from being tricked over the phone, it adds protection against other threats that often accompany scams. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Review your bank and credit card transactions through their official apps or websites. Look for unfamiliar purchases or charges that don't match your records. Contact your financial institution immediately if you discover unauthorized activity. You can also enable transaction alerts to help catch suspicious charges sooner.

Scammers may use personal information found on data broker websites to make fraudulent emails more convincing. A personal data removal service can help remove your name, address, phone number and other details from covered people-search sites. Although these services cannot prevent every scam email, reducing your online exposure can make it harder for criminals to research and target you. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com

Identity theft protection services can help monitor certain types of suspicious activity involving your personal information. Depending on the plan, you may receive alerts about unfamiliar credit activity or signs of identity misuse. Some services also offer professional restoration assistance if your identity becomes compromised. These protections can provide valuable support when criminals obtain sensitive information, although no service can detect every type of fraud. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

Visit Amazon's official scam reporting page to report the message. You can also report attempted fraud to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov/. Amazon recommends that people without an Amazon account forward suspicious communications as an attachment to reportascam@amazon.com. Reporting these attempts helps companies and authorities identify fraudulent activity.
For additional protection, we've also covered how Amazon alerts customers about impersonation scams and the precautions the company recommends.
Calling the customer support number on a fake Amazon invoice could connect you directly to a scammer posing as a legitimate representative. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What to do if you already called the fake support number
Already called the number on a suspicious Amazon invoice? Your next steps depend on what information you shared and whether you gave anyone access to your device. Here's how to protect yourself.

End the call and stop communicating. Hang up immediately and avoid responding to follow-up calls or messages. Even without sharing sensitive information, check your Amazon account directly to verify any claimed purchases or charges.Change your Amazon password . Shared your password with the caller? Sign in through Amazon's official website or app and change it immediately. Review your account for unfamiliar activity. Also, update any other accounts that use the same password.Contact your bank or credit card company. Anyone who provided payment information should contact their financial institution immediately. Explain what happened and ask about replacing the card or disputing unauthorized transactions.Remove any suspicious remote-access software. Scammers may convince victims to install software that gives them control of a computer. Disconnect the affected device from the internet and get professional help checking for unauthorized access. Use a separate, trusted device to change important passwords.Take steps to protect your identity. Shared personal information such as your Social Security number? Visit IdentityTheft.gov for guidance on protecting your identity and recovering from potential fraud.Monitor your accounts for suspicious activity. Watch for unfamiliar purchases, password reset requests or unexpected account changes. Enable transaction alerts through your bank and turn on two-step verification wherever available.

End the call and stop communicating. Hang up immediately and avoid responding to follow-up calls or messages. Even without sharing sensitive information, check your Amazon account directly to verify any claimed purchases or charges.

Change your Amazon password . Shared your password with the caller? Sign in through Amazon's official website or app and change it immediately. Review your account for unfamiliar activity. Also, update any other accounts that use the same password.

Contact your bank or credit card company. Anyone who provided payment information should contact their financial institution immediately. Explain what happened and ask about replacing the card or disputing unauthorized transactions.

Remove any suspicious remote-access software. Scammers may convince victims to install software that gives them control of a computer. Disconnect the affected device from the internet and get professional help checking for unauthorized access. Use a separate, trusted device to change important passwords.

Take steps to protect your identity. Shared personal information such as your Social Security number? Visit IdentityTheft.gov for guidance on protecting your identity and recovering from potential fraud.

Monitor your accounts for suspicious activity. Watch for unfamiliar purchases, password reset requests or unexpected account changes. Enable transaction alerts through your bank and turn on two-step verification wherever available.

The sooner you act, the better your chances of preventing additional damage. Even a short conversation with a scammer deserves attention if you shared personal information or allowed access to your device.
Kurt's key takeaways

I appreciate Matt taking the time to share this email with us. It's a good reminder of how much effort scammers put into making fraudulent communications look credible. What caught my attention was the combination of a detailed invoice and that repeatedly displayed phone number. The message creates concern about a large purchase, then conveniently offers a way to fix it. That's where people can get pulled into a scam before they realize what's happening. And here's something worth remembering: You don't have to spot every strange detail on an invoice to protect yourself. You only need to recognize that an unexpected charge deserves independent verification. The lesson I take from Matt's experience is simple. Don't let a scary email decide whom you call or how quickly you act. Check your account through an official channel before you give anyone access to your money or personal information. I'm glad Matt reached out because sharing these examples gives more people a chance to recognize the warning signs.

title: Why are people attacking food delivery robots?
summary: A handful of food delivery robots from Uber Eats and other platforms have gotten kicked and knocked over in Philadelphia and Los Angeles.
story: An Avride delivery robot covered in graffiti travels along a Philadelphia sidewalk as frustration with AI-powered delivery machines grows. (Aluminum-001/Wikimedia Commons/CC BY 4.0)

There's something pretty strange happening on American sidewalks. People are picking fights with food delivery robots. Yes, those little four-wheeled machines that roll around carrying somebody's meal are getting kicked and knocked over. Some people are even filming themselves doing it.

Now, I can understand being curious about a robot delivering your dinner. After all, watching a small machine navigate city streets with a bag of burgers inside is pretty impressive. But apparently, some people have had enough of these rolling delivery machines. And when you look at what's happening, you start to see just how frustrated some Americans have become with artificial intelligence showing up in their neighborhoods.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
DOORDASH GETS FAA APPROVAL FOR ITS OWN DELIVERY DRONES
Food delivery robots are getting beaten up

In Philadelphia, an Uber Eats delivery robot found itself on the receiving end of two kicks in late March 2026. The second kick reportedly knocked it over near a parking garage. The people involved eventually put it back on its wheels, but the encounter became another example of people taking out their frustrations on delivery technology. And Philadelphia is hardly alone. Similar attacks have surfaced in Los Angeles and other cities. Videos circulating online show robots being tipped over or deliberately kicked. Some encounters have attracted enormous attention, turning attacks on delivery robots into viral entertainment.

Think about that for a second. These machines generally move at walking speed. Some even have friendly-looking digital eyes that make them look like little cartoon characters. Yet somehow, they've become targets for people who seem determined to teach them a lesson. Here's what I find particularly strange. A robot can't argue with someone who attacks it. It certainly can't defend itself the way a person might. So what is it about these little machines that makes some people so angry?
Why are some people angry at delivery robots?

I suspect some of this anger has very little to do with the robots themselves. For many people, artificial intelligence represents a pretty unsettling change, especially when it comes to their jobs. We've already seen AI take on tasks that people once handled. Now we're watching robots roll down sidewalks doing work that someone used to get paid for. And unlike software running quietly in the background, these machines are right there in front of us.

Consider someone who earns money delivering meals for Uber Eats. Every order completed by a robot could potentially mean one less opportunity for a human delivery worker. Companies say automation can make deliveries more efficient. But what happens to the people who rely on that income as these fleets get bigger?

That concern recently led to a confrontation in Philadelphia. On Oct. 14, police arrested 78-year-old retired University of Pennsylvania professor Carolyn Marvin after she deliberately blocked an Uber Eats delivery robot. Marvin said she was protesting companies replacing human delivery workers with machines. We covered her arrest, and one detail really caught my attention. Pennsylvania law requires delivery robots to yield to pedestrians in pedestrian areas. Marvin's arrest followed her refusal to comply with police instructions, and her case raises questions about how people can legally protest these machines.
An autonomous food delivery robot passes a man pushing a stroller in downtown Los Angeles on May 1, 2026. (Reuters)

I can understand why someone would be frustrated watching technology potentially replace jobs. That doesn't give anyone a free pass to damage property, of course. Still, companies should recognize that they're introducing these machines into neighborhoods where people may already feel anxious about automation.
MAJORITY OF YOUNG ADULTS SAY THEY ARE 'MORE CONCERNED THAN EXCITED' ABOUT AI: PEW RESEARCH
Sometimes the delivery robots create their own problems

Of course, not every complaint about delivery robots comes from someone worried about losing a job. Sometimes the robots themselves cause a headache. Remember the robot traffic jam in Chicago? In September 2026, video showed at least a dozen Coco delivery robots clustered together on a sidewalk near Lincoln Park. Instead of delivering food, they appeared to be stuck trying to get around one another. Coco told CyberGuy that a deployment error caused several robots to reroute at the same time. The company said it fixed the problem within minutes and added safeguards to prevent it from happening again. Now, I have to admit, watching a bunch of robots get tangled up in their own traffic jam is pretty funny. But consider someone using a wheelchair who needs to get through that sidewalk. Suddenly, the situation becomes a lot more serious.

And there have been other problems. In May 2026, a delivery robot reportedly entered a crosswalk against a traffic signal and was struck by a truck. Even more surprising, the damaged robot kept moving afterward. I give these companies credit for developing machines that can navigate busy streets. But if a robot can't reliably handle a crosswalk or stay out of someone's way, it's reasonable to question whether it's ready for crowded city sidewalks.
Are delivery robots becoming a target for people's anger at AI?

Here's another part of this story that I find fascinating. For most of us, artificial intelligence lives inside a computer or smartphone. You might use it to answer a question or help write an email. But there's usually nothing physical standing in front of you. A delivery robot changes that. Suddenly, AI is rolling past your apartment building. It's waiting at the same crosswalk you use every morning. And if you're already frustrated about artificial intelligence taking over more parts of daily life, that little machine becomes an easy target.

Social media can make things worse. Someone records an outrageous encounter with a robot, posts it online and suddenly thousands of people are watching. That attention may encourage others to do something similar. But here's an important reality check. These viral videos can make it seem like robots are getting attacked everywhere. The available numbers suggest otherwise.

In April 2026, Serve Robotics CEO Ali Kashani told Semafor that mistreatment occurred on fewer than 1% of approximately 100,000 trips. That's the company's experience, so it doesn't tell us what's happening across the entire industry. Still, it's worth keeping in perspective. Most of these little machines appear to be making their deliveries without anybody trying to knock them over.
Delivery robots are becoming big business

Whatever people think about these robots, the companies behind them are moving ahead. Serve Robotics reported that it had deployed 2,000 robots by the end of 2025. The company works with delivery platforms including Uber Eats and DoorDash. Other companies, including Coco and Avride, are also pursuing expansion.

If you haven't encountered one yet, here's how they generally work. The robots use cameras and sensors to navigate sidewalks while avoiding obstacles. Customers track their delivery through an app and unlock the robot's compartment when their food arrives. We've previously explained how Uber Eats delivery robots work, and I can certainly see the appeal. A small robot handling a short delivery could mean one less car making a trip through a crowded neighborhood. And if your lunch arrives quickly, you're probably not going to complain about who, or what, brought it.

Of course, there's a big difference between getting a robot to deliver lunch and making money doing it. Serve reported approximately $2.7 million in revenue for 2025 while recording substantial losses. That tells you companies are spending a lot to get these robots on the streets, with no guarantee they'll turn a profit anytime soon. The potential savings are certainly appealing. Robots can handle short deliveries without paying a human courier for each trip. However, the machines still need maintenance, and people have to step in when something goes wrong. So while the technology looks promising, the big question is whether delivering food by robot will eventually pay off.
A fleet of Serve Robotics delivery robots sits inside a truck in Miami as companies push to bring more autonomous deliveries to American cities. (Phillip Pessar/Wikimedia Commons/CC BY 4.0)
Cities are setting new rules for delivery robots

As more delivery robots roll into neighborhoods, city officials are starting to ask some tough questions. Where should these machines be allowed to operate, and who gets to decide? In September 2026, Glendale, California, approved a one-year pilot program allowing up to two delivery robot operators. The city also adopted an ordinance requiring companies to have operating agreements before deploying these machines on public streets and sidewalks. Los Angeles is taking a closer look, too. In November 2025, the City Council approved a motion calling for a review of existing delivery robot regulations. Officials want to better understand how these machines affect pedestrian access and whether current rules do enough to protect people using sidewalks.

Then there's the privacy question. Most delivery robots use cameras to see where they're going. But what happens to the information they collect as they travel through neighborhoods? And how much of that information do companies keep? Those are questions I'd want answered. On the positive side, some companies are finding ways to use this technology to help pedestrians. Coco Robotics partnered with BlindSquare, an accessibility app, to share information about sidewalk obstacles. The goal is to help people with visual impairments navigate their surroundings more safely. I like that idea. If these robots can help people get around more safely, that's a real benefit. But before companies start talking about making sidewalks better for everyone, they need to make sure their own robots aren't getting in the way.
What should you do if a delivery robot gets in your way?

As more delivery robots appear in cities, there's a good chance you'll eventually encounter one. Most of the time, you'll probably just walk past it and continue on your way. But what if one stops right in front of you or blocks a sidewalk? My advice is to give it a little space and avoid trying to move it yourself. If the robot creates a genuine accessibility or safety problem, look for the company's name on the machine. You can usually report the issue directly to the operator.

Some cities also let people report sidewalk obstructions through their local 311 services. If you can safely take a photo, document where the robot is and when the problem happened. That information may help the company identify the machine and investigate. And please, resist the temptation to give it a kick. Deliberately damaging someone else's property can lead to criminal charges, even when that property happens to have wheels and digital eyes. Reporting the problem is a much better way to get someone's attention.
Kurt's key takeaways

I have to give these delivery robots some credit. It's pretty impressive that a little machine can make its way through a busy city and show up with your dinner. I can absolutely see the appeal, especially if it means faster deliveries and fewer cars on crowded streets. But I also get why some people aren't thrilled about sharing their sidewalks with robots. Nobody wants to see jobs disappear, and I certainly wouldn't be happy if a robot blocked my way while I was walking down the street. These are legitimate concerns that companies need to take seriously.

What bothers me is that we're seeing more of these robots before we've really figured out how they should operate around people. Who's responsible when one causes an accident? What happens when it blocks a wheelchair ramp? I think companies should have clear answers before sending thousands more onto our sidewalks. And while I understand the frustration with AI taking over more jobs, kicking a robot that's trying to deliver somebody's pizza seems like a pretty ridiculous way to protest. I'm all for technology that makes life easier. But the people living in these neighborhoods should have a say in how it's used. After all, they're the ones who have to share the sidewalk.

title: Why removing your data online may still leave your family exposed
summary: Data broker opt-out forms may not protect your family. People search sites can still expose your info through a spouse's or parent's profile.
story: Data privacy expert Brittany Kaiser says restrictions on data center development could force American companies to process information abroad, raising concerns over where sensitive data ends up.

You removed your information from data broker sites. You submitted the opt-out forms, did the work and maybe even felt good about it. Here's what you may have missed: Your family members' personal information could still be exposed. And because their profiles may point directly back to you, some of your information could remain accessible, too.

That's the problem with approaching family data broker removal one person at a time. People-search sites often connect relatives through shared addresses, public records and family relationships. In fact, the Federal Trade Commission warns that even after you opt out, your information may still appear in reports about relatives, neighbors or associates. Here's how those connections can leave your household exposed and what you can do about them.

WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES
Data broker sites can connect family members through shared addresses and public records, potentially exposing personal information even after someone opts out. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Your family is already connected in these databases

Data broker profiles often contain more than one person's information. They can include family relationships that help connect individual records. Search for yourself on people-search sites such as Spokeo, Whitepages, BeenVerified or Intelius. Depending on the site and available records, you may find a section identifying possible relatives or associates.

That list could include your spouse, adult children, parents or people who once shared your address. Some connections may even be outdated or incorrect. For someone trying to learn about your household, those details can provide a starting point. Now consider what happens when you remove your own listing. Your name might disappear from the site's direct search results, but your spouse's profile could still identify you as a relative. Your parent's listing might include an address where you previously lived. As a result, removing one profile may leave behind information that points to the same person.
How one remaining profile can expose your household
Family connections can create privacy gaps in several ways. Here are three examples worth checking.

Married couples often share address histories, property records and other identifying information. When one spouse removes a people-search listing, but the other remains visible, the remaining profile may still reveal their shared address, possible relatives and other household details. Some people-search reports may also include property ownership or estimated financial information, although the details vary by service. For a scammer, a spouse's publicly available information could provide another way to identify or contact someone whose direct listing has been removed.

This is one of the scenarios that concerns me most. Many adults help their parents manage online accounts and avoid scams. Yet they may overlook the personal information already available through people-search sites. An older parent's profile could include previous addresses, relatives' names and other public-record details collected over many years. That information may help criminals make a scam sound more believable. Consider the grandparent scam. Someone calls an older adult, pretends to be a grandchild facing an emergency and demands money immediately. The FTC warns that scammers may already know personal details about their targets or the family members they impersonate. Reducing publicly available information can remove some of the details criminals might use to support their stories.

The reverse can happen, too. Parents may remove their own information without checking whether their adult children have searchable profiles. A young adult's address history, voter registration information or other public records may contribute to people-search listings. Those listings can also identify possible relatives. Someone searching for that adult child could potentially discover connections to their parents and other family members. For example, a scammer might use a child's name and location to make a fake emergency call to a parent sound more credible. That's why checking only one generation of your family may leave important privacy gaps.
A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO?
Older relatives may have searchable online profiles that reveal personal details and family connections scammers could exploit. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why removing one profile may not be enough

Data brokers collect information from multiple sources, including public records, publicly available online information and other data brokers. Even after a successful opt-out, some information can reappear when a site obtains updated records. Meanwhile, another people-search service may still have a copy of the same details. The FTC specifically warns that opting out of people-search sites does not remove the underlying information from government public records. It also recommends checking periodically for new listings. That's why I recommend taking a household approach to personal data removal rather than concentrating on one individual.
How a family data removal service can help protect your household

Manually removing personal information from data broker sites takes time. Doing it for multiple family members adds even more work, especially when you have to check whether profiles have returned. That's why I recommend considering a family data removal service that can manage the process for several household members at once.

These services can automatically submit removal requests to hundreds of covered data broker and people-search sites, depending on the provider. Some offer family plans that protect multiple people under one subscription. They can also send recurring removal requests when personal information reappears, helping maintain protection without requiring every family member to handle the process individually.

Look for a service that provides ongoing removal requests, covers multiple family members and lets you track progress. While no service can erase every public record or guarantee complete removal from the internet, ongoing data removal can significantly reduce the amount of personal information available about your household. By protecting several family members together, you can help close privacy gaps that individual removals might leave behind.
Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.
People-search databases can link relatives across multiple profiles, making it important to check and remove exposed information for the entire household. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What a family privacy audit looks like
Before you can reduce your household's exposure, you need to understand what information is already available.

With their knowledge and permission, search for each adult's name on several major people-search sites. Look at more than the primary profile. Check whether the listings identify relatives, current addresses or previous locations. Keep in mind that people-search databases can contain inaccurate information. A listed relationship does not automatically mean the connection is correct.

Check whether your parents or older family members have searchable profiles. If they need help, walk them through the available removal options or assist them with their permission. Pay particular attention to addresses, phone numbers and family relationships that could be useful in an impersonation scam. Also remind them to verify unexpected emergency calls by contacting family members through numbers they already know.

Adult children may have their own people-search listings, even when they have never knowingly signed up for one. Check whether those profiles reveal current addresses, previous residences or connections to other family members. Then help them understand how to request removal and why they should check again later.

After identifying exposed profiles, you can submit opt-out requests individually or use a service to manage the process. For households with several adults, I recommend considering a family data removal service that can protect multiple people under one subscription. These services can automatically submit removal requests to hundreds of covered data broker and people-search sites, saving you the time and effort of handling each family member's information separately.

Because listings can reappear, look for a service that offers recurring removal requests, ongoing monitoring and progress tracking. This helps reduce the amount of personal information that strangers and scammers can find about your family. The goal is to make it harder for someone to connect individual profiles and build a detailed picture of your household.
Kurt's key takeaways

I've talked a lot about removing personal information from data brokers, but there's another side to this that deserves more attention. You can spend hours cleaning up your own online profile and still have your name, address or family connections exposed through someone else's listing. That's what concerns me. Most people have no idea how much information about their families can be pieced together from publicly available records.

I think protecting your household should be part of any serious privacy plan. Start by checking what information appears about your spouse, parents and adult children. If you find exposed details, take steps to remove them. I recommend using an ongoing data removal service, especially when you're trying to protect multiple family members. It can handle requests across hundreds of covered sites and keep checking for information that returns. You may never be able to erase every public record, but you can make it harder for strangers and scammers to put together a detailed profile of your family.

title: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook comes at a price
summary: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899 with a PROLED XDR OLED display, but the non-touch M6 model costs $900 less at $1,999.
story: People try out the new MacBook Pro with a touchscreen following the launch by Apple CEO John Ternus in Los Angeles, on Oct. 28, 2026. (REUTERS)

Apple has finally given the MacBook Pro something many people have wanted for years: a touchscreen. The company unveiled its first touchscreen MacBook Pro on Oct. 28, introducing a new way to interact with its laptop. It also brings a stunning OLED display, a thinner design and some serious processing power. However, there's one detail that might make you think twice before reaching for your wallet. The new touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899.

That's a lot of money for a laptop, even by Apple's standards. So, what exactly are you getting for that price? More importantly, will touching your MacBook's screen make enough of a difference to justify an upgrade? Let's look at what Apple has introduced and who might benefit most.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
8 BIGGEST THINGS WE LEARNED FROM APPLE'S 2026 EVENT
Apple's first touchscreen MacBook Pro lets users interact directly with the display, bringing familiar iPhone and iPad gestures to the Mac. (Apple)
Apple finally brings touch to the MacBook Pro

For years, Apple maintained that the Mac worked best with a keyboard and trackpad. Meanwhile, Windows laptop owners have enjoyed touchscreen options for a long time. Apple even experimented with touch controls through its Touch Bar, but that feature never replaced the traditional laptop experience.

Now Apple has changed course. Its new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display lets you interact directly with the screen. You can scroll through websites with your finger or pinch to zoom into photos. Apple also lets you drag content between windows and interact with supported creative apps.

Think about how often you instinctively touch your laptop screen, especially after spending years using an iPhone or iPad. Now that gesture will actually do something on the new MacBook Pro. Apple also redesigned the hinge to keep the display steadier when you touch it. That's a thoughtful addition because nobody wants a screen wobbling every time they tap a button.

However, this remains a traditional laptop. It doesn't fold into a tablet, and it doesn't support Apple Pencil. You'll still use the keyboard and trackpad for much of your work. That may disappoint anyone hoping to replace both a MacBook and an iPad with one device.
The OLED display could be the bigger story

While everyone is talking about the touchscreen, Apple's new display technology might have an even greater impact on your everyday experience. The company calls it the PROLED XDR Display, and it uses tandem OLED technology. Unlike traditional laptop screens that rely on a backlight, OLED pixels produce their own light. That allows the display to show deep blacks alongside bright highlights without the same backlight glow.

Apple says the new screen reaches up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness for both HDR and SDR content. It also delivers a claimed 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and supports refresh rates up to 120Hz for smoother motion. Those numbers sound impressive, but what will you actually notice?
Apple CEO John Ternus mingles at the launch of a new MacBook Pro with a touch screen in Los Angeles on Oct. 28, 2026. (REUTERS)

Photos should look more vibrant, especially when you're viewing pictures taken on your iPhone. Movies can show more detail in dark scenes. If you edit videos or work with photography, the improved color accuracy could be especially useful.

Apple has also added an antireflective coating to help reduce glare. An optional nano-texture finish provides additional reflection control for people who work in bright environments. For someone who spends hours looking at a laptop screen, these improvements could be more valuable than touch alone.
A touchscreen MacBook Pro with serious processing power

Apple isn't holding back on performance. The new touchscreen MacBook Pro comes with either an M5 Pro or M5 Max processor. Both target people who need more processing power than a basic laptop typically provides. If you're editing high-resolution video or working with large photo libraries, these chips are designed to handle that workload. Apple also offers configurations with up to 128GB of unified memory and 16TB of storage. However, those upgrades can drive the price considerably higher.

The new MacBook Pro runs macOS 27 and includes Apple Intelligence alongside Apple's upgraded Siri AI. It also brings Dynamic Island to the Mac for the first time. That familiar feature from the iPhone sits near the top of the display and gives you access to live updates and useful controls. For video calls, Apple includes a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera. Meanwhile, an upgraded six-speaker system promises deeper bass. The laptop also includes Thunderbolt 5 connectivity and an HDMI port, which should appeal to people connecting external displays.
12 BIGGEST APPLE WWDC 2026 TAKEAWAYS YOU NEED TO KNOW
Apple's new touchscreen MacBook Pro comes in 14-inch and 16-inch models, with prices starting at $2,899. (Apple)
Apple's new MacBook Pro is thinner and lighter

One concern with touchscreen laptops is whether all that additional technology makes them heavier. Apple says it has managed to move in the opposite direction. The new 14-inch touchscreen MacBook Pro weighs about three pounds, roughly half a pound less than its predecessor. The 16-inch model comes in at four pounds, approximately 0.7 pounds lighter. Both models also feature slimmer designs. That should make carrying a MacBook Pro between meetings or packing one for a trip a little easier.

Apple promises up to 24 hours of battery life, depending on the configuration and usage. That's an impressive claim for a machine with this much performance and such a bright display. However, we'll need independent testing to see how battery life holds up during real-world work.
How much does Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro cost?

Apple has positioned its touchscreen MacBook Pro firmly in premium territory. The 14-inch model with the M5 Pro chip starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch version starts at $3,399. If you want the more powerful M5 Max processor, prices jump to $4,499 for the 14-inch model and $4,799 for the 16-inch version. And remember, those are starting prices for each configuration. Adding more memory or storage can increase the total substantially.

There is another important detail. Apple introduced a separate 14-inch MacBook Pro with its newer M6 chip on Oct. 27. That model starts at $1,999, but it uses a Liquid Retina XDR Display without touch support. That means you're looking at a $900 difference between Apple's entry-level M6 MacBook Pro and its least expensive touchscreen model. Of course, the more expensive version also includes an M5 Pro processor and the upgraded OLED display. These are different performance configurations, so the additional $900 doesn't represent the cost of touch alone.

For another perspective, the previous 14-inch MacBook Pro with the M5 Pro chip started at $2,499. That makes the new touchscreen version $400 more expensive than its comparable predecessor. Still, this gives you a meaningful choice. You can buy a powerful new MacBook Pro for considerably less if you don't need to interact directly with the screen. We've previously reported on how rising AI chip costs have pushed Apple prices higher. This latest introduction adds another premium option to an already expensive lineup.
Will your favorite Mac apps work with touch?

Apple says many existing Mac apps will respond to touch immediately because macOS can translate finger taps into mouse clicks. That should make basic interaction straightforward, even before developers fully optimize their software. However, Apple's bigger ambition involves creative applications. The company demonstrated touch controls in Final Cut Pro that let editors manipulate clips directly on the screen. Musicians can use Logic Pro to play virtual instruments with their fingers.

Apple also expects third-party apps, including Adobe Lightroom and Microsoft Office applications, to take advantage of the new touch capabilities. That sounds promising. Still, a touchscreen doesn't automatically make every app easier to use. Tiny buttons and crowded menus can be frustrating when you're trying to select something precisely with a finger.

Early hands-on reports suggest that touch works smoothly for common gestures. However, some smaller macOS controls can still be awkward to tap. Those are preliminary impressions rather than findings from extended testing. It will be interesting to see how quickly developers adapt their interfaces and whether people continue using touch regularly after the initial excitement wears off.
The new PROLED XDR Display combines OLED technology with touch controls. (Apple)
Should you upgrade to Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro?

This is the question I'd ask before spending nearly $3,000. If you already own a relatively recent MacBook Pro that handles everything you throw at it, I wouldn't rush to replace it solely for touchscreen capabilities. A mouse or trackpad still gives you excellent control, especially when you're working on detailed projects.

However, if you edit video professionally or spend your days working with photos, the OLED display could make a real difference. The improved portability also makes the new model appealing to people who regularly travel with demanding workloads. For everyday activities like email and web browsing, a less expensive MacBook Air or standard MacBook Pro will probably be more than enough.

Before making that decision, take a look at our guide explaining how to know when it's time to replace your Mac. A computer that still performs well may have several good years left. You can also explore our best laptops for 2026 at CyberGuy.com to compare other options before committing to Apple's premium model.

One more suggestion: If you're considering the touchscreen MacBook Pro, visit an Apple Store when it becomes available on Nov. 6. Spend some time using the touchscreen alongside the keyboard and trackpad. That hands-on experience could tell you more than any specification sheet.
Pro tip: Don't forget to protect your new MacBook

If you're spending nearly $3,000 on a new MacBook Pro, protecting that investment should be a priority. While macOS includes built-in security features, Macs can still face malicious downloads and online scams. I recommend keeping your software updated and using strong antivirus software for an additional layer of protection. Strong antivirus software can help detect malware and warn you about dangerous websites before they cause trouble. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

I have to give Apple credit for finally bringing a touchscreen to the MacBook Pro. It feels like a feature that should have arrived years ago, especially when we're all so accustomed to touching the screens on our phones and tablets. I'm also impressed by what Apple is promising with its new OLED display. For people who work with visual content, that could be the most compelling reason to upgrade.

But here's where I hesitate. At $2,899, Apple is asking a lot for a feature that many competing laptops have offered for years. And with the standard M6 MacBook Pro starting at $1,999, there's a pretty compelling argument for saving that extra $900. I want to see how useful touch becomes in everyday work before calling this a must-have upgrade. My advice is to try it in person before spending the money. A touchscreen sounds great, but the real test is whether you still reach for it after the excitement wears off.
Would you pay nearly $3,000 for a touchscreen MacBook Pro? Let us know why or why not by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: 'SNL' writer’s sister vanished — now her boyfriend and rival face charges in deadly love triangle
summary: "Saturday Night Live" writer Jimmy Fowlie's sister Christina Downer faced alleged stalking and blackmail before her disappearance and presumed death.
story: Christina Downer's boyfriend Delorean Bijon Brandon faces murder charges months after court records revealed alleged stalking, threats, and domestic violence involving both suspects.

Months before a "Saturday Night Live" writer's sister disappeared, court records showed a pattern of alleged stalking, threats, and domestic violence involving two suspects now charged with her death and disappearance.

Last month, Los Angeles County prosecutors charged Christina Downer’s boyfriend, Delorean Bijon Brandon, 41, with first-degree murder. Brandon’s former girlfriend, Kaylee Nicole Markowski, 34, is facing two felony counts of being an accessory after the fact.
Investigators believe Brandon killed Downer, 38, on or around Sept. 19, 2025. Her remains have not been located.
Christina Lynn Downer, the missing sister of "Saturday Night Live" writer Jimmy Fowlie, was last seen in Los Angeles' Koreatown neighborhood in September 2025. (LAPD)

Before Downer disappeared, she and Brandon sought separate restraining orders against Markowski, accusing her, in part, of stalking and blackmail, court records showed. Both cases were dismissed after Downer and Brandon failed to appear in court, according to court documents obtained by Los Angeles Magazine.
'SNL' WRITER'S MISSING SISTER CASE LEADS HOMICIDE DETECTIVES TO JOSHUA TREE MONTHS AFTER FAMILY'S MURDER CLAIM
Downer’s disappearance and presumed death
Authorities learned of Downer’s disappearance in December 2025, when her ex-husband reported her missing, saying he had not heard from her in months.
Downer’s brother, "Saturday Night Live" writer Jimmy Fowlie, began posting public pleas on Instagram that same month, asking for information about his sister’s whereabouts.
Brandon, who shared an apartment with Downer in Koreatown, told police that she had moved out months prior, leaving her belongings behind, including her car and beloved miniature pinscher named Rex.
TEACHER FOUND DEAD WITH THROAT SLIT; DETECTIVES SCRUTINIZE HUSBAND’S SHIFTING STORY
The LAPD’s Robbery-Homicide Division took over the investigation after Downer’s cellphone washed ashore at Santa Monica Beach.
Investigators believe Brandon and Markowski used Downer’s phone to send messages, fabricating a story that she voluntarily disappeared, according to court documents.
HORSE FARM OWNER GETS LIFE IN PRISON FOR BOYFRIEND'S MURDER AFTER CLAIMING SELF-DEFENSE

"The individual(s) in possession of her phone used it to hide the fact she was gone, to ask for money, and to create a false narrative that she was going ‘off the grid,’" Fowlie wrote on Instagram in April.

"I am sharing this because I believe that whoever is responsible is hoping to erase her in every way possible. I want to amplify her story in the only way I know how. And express that she was a beautiful person who matters in this world, especially to me."
Jimmy Fowlie attends the premiere of Netflix's "Roommates" at The Egyptian Theatre Hollywood on April 13, 2026, in Los Angeles, California. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images)
Fowlie did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Restraining orders, prior domestic violence allegations
In a September 2024 restraining order petition obtained by the Los Angeles Times, Downer accused Markowski of terrorizing her since December 2023.

Markowski harassed Downer by threatening to break into her home, beat her up and by calling her racial slurs, court documents stated. She also allegedly stole Downer’s cat and a storage device containing intimate videos, which she allegedly used to blackmail Downer.
"She calls us n-----, threatens to beat me up, stole my spare key and copied it, threatens to break into my home," Downer claimed in her request.
'HOW I MET YOUR MOTHER' ACTOR NICK PASQUAL CONVICTED OF ATTEMPTED MURDER FOR STABBING EX-GIRLFRIEND

In July 2025, Brandon filed a domestic violence restraining order request against Markowski, alleging she harassed him, targeted his vehicle and attempted to interfere with Downer’s job, according to ABC7’s court records review.
Judges dismissed both cases after Downer and Brandon failed to appear in court.

In September 2025, Brandon sought another protective order against Markowski, accusing her of hitting and kicking him when he tried to leave. He said she also threatened to shoot him in the head for having a relationship with Downer.
A Los Angeles County Superior Court judge rejected the request and set a Sept. 23, 2025, hearing.

Alyce LaViolette, a licensed marriage and family therapist and domestic violence specialist not affiliated with the case, explained that courts usually examine specific details of each allegation rather than the number of complaints filed before deciding if a case proceeds. Court backlogs and limited domestic violence training can make it more difficult to assess a full abuse history, she said.
On Sept. 18, 2025, however, Brandon withdrew the request. Investigators believe Downer died within a day of Brandon withdrawing the request.
Christina Downer disappeared and is believed to have been killed. (Instagram/jimmyfowlie)
Previous accusations

The latest criminal complaint detailed allegations of domestic violence carried out by Brandon against a different woman. Brandon allegedly used scissors during one of the assaults, according to documents obtained by Los Angeles Magazine.
He is now charged with two felony counts of injuring a cohabitant in connection with the alleged 2022 assaults.

In a separate April 2022 court case, a woman filed a civil harassment restraining order petition against Markowski in Los Angeles County Superior Court. The judge dismissed the case in June 2022 for "lack of prosecution."

Markowski’s attorney, Arvand Naderi, also declined to comment on a pending case.
Risling said Brandon is being represented by the Alternate Public Defender’s Office. The office was not immediately available for comment.

title: Quiet serial killers may hide in plain sight as DNA unmasks dead 1970s Pennsylvania strangler, expert says
summary: James Richard Clark Sr. left DNA at both 1970s crime scenes, but advanced cybergenetics testing has only recently linked him to the two killings.
story: Dr. Kris Mohandie, a former FBI behavioral analysis consultant and LAPD psychologist, discussed why serial killers often have more victims than they are linked to after DNA tied a dead Pennsylvania man to two 1970s killings.
Quiet serial killers may be hiding in plain sight, an expert warns, after new DNA technology helped unmask a Pennsylvania man authorities say killed at least two women in the 1970s.
At a Thursday news conference, Pennsylvania State Police identified James Richard Clark Sr. as the man who sexually assaulted and strangled Brenda Ritter, 18, and Susan Rush, 21, in the 1970s.

Rush vanished on Nov. 24, 1976, after leaving a shopping mall, according to the City of Washington Police Department. She was supposed to meet her family at church but never arrived. Her brother spotted her car along a street the next morning, Thanksgiving Day, and her body was discovered in the trunk.
TED BUNDY LINKED TO ANOTHER DECADES-OLD HOMICIDE NEARLY 40 YEARS AFTER HIS EXECUTION
Pennsylvania State Police identified James Richard Clark Sr., who died in 2023, as the man who killed Brenda Ritter and Susan Rush in the 1970s. (Pennsylvania State Police)
Ritter disappeared from her boyfriend's house in 1977, police said. Her body was later found on a hillside, and authorities determined she had been sexually assaulted and strangled.
The suspect, Clark Sr., died at 66 on July 17, 2023, of natural causes.
DNA BREAKTHROUGH LEADS TO ARREST IN GRISLY 33-YEAR-OLD COLD CASE INVESTIGATORS NEVER GAVE UP ON

In late 2008, evidence from Ritter's killing was sent to the state police crime lab, which produced an unknown male DNA profile. The DNA was put into an FBI database, CODIS, which was searched weekly with no match. In May 2025, testing at Cybergenetics' laboratory showed the same man was responsible for the deaths of both women.

Clark left DNA at both crime scenes, according to police, and advances in testing at several labs, including Identifinders International, helped investigators zero in on him before more testing sealed the match.

Brenda Ritter, 18, disappeared from her boyfriend's house in 1977 and was later found sexually assaulted and strangled on a hillside, police said. (Pennsylvania State Police)
Police said Clark would have been 20 at the time of Ritter's homicide and 19 when Rush was killed.

Pennsylvania State Police Cpl. James Petrosky said he thinks there may be more victims.

"I believe that once you're a serial killer, you're always a serial killer. I believe there could potentially be more victims out there," Petrosky said.

Dr. Kris Mohandie, a former LAPD psychologist and FBI behavioral analysis consultant, told Fox News Digital it's "normal" for the number of known victims to fall short of a serial killer's true toll, and that new technology is often what closes the gap.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"I think it's normal and normative that the number of known cases is always less than what has been detected," Mohandie said. "These kind of guys often have more victims out there than they've been known to be connected to. The reality is that there are usually more crimes attributable to serial offenders than they're ever held to account for."

Mohandie said it's not unusual for a serial killer to go quiet for years, either because they sense investigators closing in or because their lives get busy with things like raising a family.

"There are a lot of cases where they do go dormant, what we call a cooling-off period, and that can be because they realize it's too hot for them to continue to offend, that they'll get caught, so it's a strategy to avoid being captured. It may mean that they've had a close call with being captured, and it spooked them, so they'll go quiet for a while because of that," he said.

title: NTSB recovers cockpit voice recorder from Learjet crash site in Florida
summary: The NTSB recovered the cockpit voice recorder from the Learjet 60 crash site near Greenacres, Florida, as investigators probe the cause of the incident.
story: Retired Navy fighter pilot Matthew 'Whiz' Buckley discusses the aircraft's damaged tail components, rapid descent and encounter with severe weather, as investigators work to determine what caused the deadly Florida Learjet crash.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) announced on Monday that it has recovered the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) of the Learjet 60 that crashed last week near Greenacres, Florida, killing all nine people on board.
"NTSB investigators have recovered the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) of the Learjet 60 that crashed on Nov. 1 near Greenacres, Florida," the NTSB said on X.
The CVR was found at the location of the initial impact​, according to the NTSB.
The NTSB said the CVR is being evaluated in the board's Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, D.C.
TIMELINE OF LEARJET CRASH THAT KILLED AUSTIN FAMILY TRACES FINAL MINUTES FROM TAKEOFF TO FLORIDA PLUNGE
NTSB investigators recovered the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) of the Learjet 60 that crashed in Florida. (NTSB)
The excavation work at the impact site has been completed.
This comes after investigators said on Friday that they recovered part of an engine from the Learjet.
Crews started excavating the site on Wednesday after utility workers had drained water and cleared other hazards, the NTSB said.
Once investigators began digging, they found a part of one engine, the board said.
Earlier last week, investigators recovered the left tail elevator, which controls the jet's pitch, in three separate pieces. One of them was found nearly four miles from where the Learjet 60 crashed.
FLORIDA PLANE CRASH VICTIMS IDENTIFIED AFTER 9 PEOPLE KILLED IN FIERY WRECK
The cockpit voice recorder was found at the location of initial impact and is being evaluated in the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, D.C. (NTSB)
"Even small pieces of the wreckage may contain important evidence that could help investigators determine what happened," the agency wrote last week on X.

The Learjet 60 left Austin-Bergstrom International Airport around 10:37 a.m. on Sunday, bound for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas. The aircraft plunged into the ground in Palm Beach County shortly before 1 p.m., killing everyone aboard.

Austin tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, 45, was killed in the crash alongside his wife, Helen Sharp, 40, their children, Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, the children's nanny, Anita Maria Cetina, and couple Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr.
Heavy rain and thunderstorms were reported across South Florida when the Learjet crashed. Investigators said the weather will be a major focus of their probe.
Investigators work at the scene of a plane crash in Greenacres, Florida, on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

At about 41,000 feet, an air traffic controller told the flight crew that moderate precipitation was roughly five miles away and said they could move either left or right, stressing that the turn toward Freeport in the Bahamas "looks pretty bad."

The crew was then instructed to fly to a waypoint near Naples, Florida. The crew made a deviation toward Palm Beach County and reported that weather conditions were deteriorating. The crew told air traffic control that there was icing and turbulence, asking the controller if there was a "better ride" ahead.
Fox News' Adam Sabes contributed to this report.

The massive Japanese media franchise, centered on fictional creatures, remains exceptionally popular among both children and adult collectors. While standard booster packs retail for around $5, rare cards can command thousands on the secondary market.

title: Next Generation OPIR GEO: Building America’s gateway to the future of space-based missile warning and tracking
summary: As missile threats grow faster and more maneuverable, detecting and tracking them presents new challenges. Explore how Lockheed Martin’s Next Gen OPIR GEO is designed to improve infrared sensing and support timely military decision-making.
story: Next Gen OPIR GEO (Lockheed Martin)

America is advancing next-generation overhead persistent infrared capabilities to strengthen space-based missile warning and tracking for the Joint Force. Next Gen OPIR GEO is designed to provide timely warning and tracking information against evolving missile threats, supporting force protection, informed decision-making, and efforts to save lives. Building on the Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS) heritage, the program is designed to improve sensing, tracking, resiliency, and data processing in support of unified combat.

Missile threats have evolved in speed, complexity, and maneuverability over the last decade. As these threats proliferate, our military requires resilient capabilities to support timely missile warning and tracking. Next Gen OPIR GEO builds on existing space-based missile warning capabilities to address those evolving requirements.

Lockheed Martin is developing the system in partnership with the U.S. Space Force, subcontractors, and supply-chain partners. The effort combines scientific, engineering, systems-integration, and program-management expertise to support current and future missile warning and tracking needs.
A Bridge from Today to Tomorrow

The defense technology company is developing Next Gen OPIR GEO, building on the SBIRS foundation to advance space-based missile warning and tracking capabilities.  The system is designed to improve the detection, tracking and characterization of increasingly complex missile threats, including threats with challenging signatures, high speeds, and maneuvering flight profiles.

"For more than a decade, SBIRS has provided reliable space-based early missile warning capability," said Jim Sprunck, OPIR portfolio director at Lockheed Martin. "Next Gen OPIR GEO builds on that strong foundation and brings enhanced capabilities intended to support advanced missile warning and tracking for our nation."

Hypersonic glide vehicles can travel at high speeds and maneuver in flight, making them more challenging to detect and track.  Next Gen OPIR GEO is designed to operate in geosynchronous orbit and provide persistent missile warning and tracking coverage supporting timely awareness and decision-making.

Improved tracking requires advanced sensors with enhanced sensitivity and persistent coverage to support detection and tracking of challenging targets. Mission testing has demonstrated significant improvements over SBIRS in approved performance areas.
A Resilient Next-Generation Architecture

Next Gen OPIR GEO is being developed with modern infrared payloads designed to improve detection of launches and tracking of dim or maneuvering targets. The system also incorporates resiliency features intended to support mission continuity in contested space environments.
The space element is integrated with a next-generation ground architecture designed to process larger amounts of sensor data and provide timely decision-making for warfighters.

"Our engineers have built advanced analysis and modeling tools that simulate every phase of the mission from launch through on-orbit detection," Sprunk said. "We are leveraging decades of SBIRS experience and representative mission scenarios to inform development and integration. This work provides confidence that Next Gen OPIR GEO is positioned to meet and exceed established performance requirements, supporting enhanced missile warning and tracking operations."

Built on Lockheed Martin’s LM 2100 Combat Bus™, Next Gen OPIR GEO is designed to incorporate cyber-resilient systems, improved communications, resiliency features, enhanced spacecraft power, and improved propulsion and electronic subsystems. The system is designed to use onboard data processing to support mission continuity during communication disruptions.
The Unique Engineering Mindset
Lockheed Martin engineers and technical personnel support development of the Next Gen OPIR GEO program from early design through manufacturing and testing of the mission-ready satellite.

The team uses next generation digital-engineering methods to develop and integrate the U.S. Space Force’s next-generation missile warning and tracking capability. Engineering teams developed payload, ground systems, and spacecraft capability improvements, then validated these designs through early development demonstrations, and space-to-ground integration tests using digital simulations under representative mission conditions.

"We’ve built a collaborative environment that extends far beyond Lockheed Martin’s walls," said Theresa Ito, Next Generation OPIR GEO Principal Systems Engineer. "We are bringing together technical expertise across the program, the U.S. Space Force, subcontractors, and supply-chain partners to address complex development and integration challenges."
Developing the Workforce Behind Next Gen OPIR GEO

Next Gen OPIR GEO is more than a hardware upgrade; it brings together experienced SBIRS personnel and a new generation of engineers to develop next-generation missile warning and tracking capability for combined forces.

"Many members of the team bring years of SBIRS experience, but since Next Gen OPIR GEO began, we’ve welcomed new engineers with fresh perspectives," Ito said. "Their technical expertise and commitment complement the experience of the broader team and support the program’s mission."

SBIRS will continue to provide established early missile warning capability for traditional ballistic-missile threats. Next Gen OPIR GEO will build on the SBIRS foundation, building the gateway to the future of space-based missile warning and tracking.

title: Blue state repeat offender accused of murdering wife at family’s home months after domestic violence charge

story: Host of 'The Adam Carolla Show' Adam Carolla discusses California Gov. Gavin Newsom sparing more than 500 death row inmates on 'Hannity.'
