"The international force is not here to replace the state," Haitian Prime Minister Didier Fils-Aimé said Tuesday in his first remarks about the deployment. "They're here to support us."
Fils-Aimé added that Bukele "understands our fight. … He came to stand on the side of the Haitian people."
‘DONROE’ DOCTRINE AND CONSERVATIVE VICTORIES SQUEEZE CARTELS IN LATIN AMERICA

An armored personnel carrier of Haiti's U.N.-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) patrols an area after El Salvador announced a rescue mission for four air force members in the GSF who went missing after a gang ambush in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, Oct. 23, 2026.  (Patrice Noel/Reuters)

The operation has drawn criticism from human-rights advocates and gang leaders who warn that a military escalation could worsen civilian suffering. The U.N. says at least 5,700 people have been killed or injured due to the gang violence in Haiti since Jan. 1 as security forces struggle to contain the violence.
The U.N. has also indicated that El Salvador’s deployment is separate from the GSF and has warned El Salvador must follow applicable international law.

One of those gang leaders is Wilson Joseph, known as "Lanmò Sanjou," leader of the powerful 400 Mawozo gang. He accused rival gang Chen Mechan of carrying out the ambush and claimed the Salvadorans are dead, he told The Associated Press.

Joseph also sent a letter to United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres asking the U.N. for mediation and warning Bukele's "vengeful remarks, expectations, and threats … will lead to an escalation of violence and a logic of reprisals, of which the Haitian people would be the first victims."
EXCLUSIVE: HAITIAN ILLEGAL ALIEN GANG MEMBER WHO WENT VIRAL YELLING ‘BIDEN FOREVER’ DURING ICE ARREST DEPORTED
An armed member of the G9 and Family gang patrols a roadblock in the Delmas 6 neighborhood of Port-au-Prince, Haiti, March 11.  (AP Photo/Odelyn Joseph)

Joseph was indicted by the U.S. in 2022 on hostage-taking charges related to the 2021 kidnapping of 17 missionaries, including 16 Americans, and remains the subject of a reward of up to $1 million for his arrest.

Bukele dismissed such appeals, accusing gang leaders of attempting to use civilians and international concerns about human rights as a shield to preserve their power and avoid accountability. Bukele has said that negotiations have only prolonged the crisis that has devastated Haiti for years.

After years as one of the world's most violent countries, dominated by powerful gangs including MS-13, El Salvador launched an unprecedented crackdown in 2022 under a state of emergency. Authorities carried out tens of thousands of arrests, ultimately detaining more than 90,000 suspected gang members.

Supporters credit the strategy with driving homicide rates to historic lows and restoring public safety. Critics accuse Bukele's government of human-rights abuses, arbitrary detentions and erosion of due-process protections.

Salvadoran soldiers return to a base after El Salvador deployed thousands of troops to Haiti in response to four Salvadoran members of a UN-backed force that went missing in a gang ambush, in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, Oct. 30, 2026.  (Patrice Noel/Reuters)

The question now is whether that model can be exported to Haiti, where gangs control large portions of Port-au-Prince and wield influence over key transportation routes and neighborhoods. Despite years of international intervention, security conditions have continued to deteriorate.

The GSF has struggled with manpower shortages and operational limitations, operating below its Security Council-approved intended strength, leaving Haiti's government unable to reassert full control over much of the capital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"We can help you defeat them, but we are not your enemies," Bukele wrote on Tuesday. "We must stand up, take back control of our communities, and put under our control those who are making us endure all this pain, all this suffering. We are right there beside you… Haiti will be free."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Tyler Speicher is an American journalist living in Slovenia after spending 25 years covering stories ranging from the Little League World Series to hurricanes, 9/11 and its aftermath for New York City news outlets, including 20 years on the Fox News Channel assignment desk.

title: Netanyahu faces coalition showdown as rivals maneuver to form Israel's next government
summary: Benjamin Netanyahu faces a critical test as President Isaac Herzog decides who will receive the mandate to form Israel's next government.
story: Fox News senior White House correspondent Jacqui Heinrich joins ‘America Reports’ to report on President Donald Trump’s announcement that the U.S. will halt aid to Israel at the end of the year and his closing push as midterm voting gets underway.

TEL AVIV, Israel: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hold on power in Israel will be tested Wednesday as President Isaac Herzog begins consultations with leaders of all parties elected to the 26th Knesset before deciding which lawmaker to task with forming the next government.

The final vote count, published last Friday by Israel's Central Elections Committee, gave Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for the opposition alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot — 61 seats are needed to form a government.

On Monday, Netanyahu posted to X that "the public in Israel does not want a government that depends on Ra'am and the Joint List—parties that support terrorism and reject the existence of the Jewish state."
NETANYAHU DEFIES EXIT POLLS AS VOTE SHIFTS IN HIS FAVOR, BUT MAJORITY REMAINS ELUSIVE
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks to the audience at a conference in Jerusalem, Sunday, July 27, 2025. (AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg)

"A clear majority in the Jewish public chose the Likud as the largest party and me, as prime minister, to lead the next government. We aspire to form a broad government with our partners and with any party that wishes to do so and does not support terrorism. I am open to holding discussions on the matter," he added.

The two predominantly Arab parties he pointed his criticism at are the Joint List and Ra'am who secured a historic combined total of 19 seats, potentially positioning them as kingmakers in the government formation process.

A Joint List source told Fox News Digital that the alliance is likely to endorse Eisenkot to be the first lawmaker tasked with forming a government. If both predominantly Arab parties were to back him, he would receive recommendations from parties representing more than the 61 seats needed.
The lawmaker tasked with forming a government will have 28 days to do so, with the president authorized to grant an extension of up to 14 additional days.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog during an interview with Fox News Digital in Jerusalem, Israel. (Yoav Dudkevitch/TPS-IL for Fox News Digital)
Consultations will be held in ascending order of seat count, beginning with Religious Zionism-Zehut and Shas, which each won six seats, followed by Yisrael Beiteinu, which secured seven.

On Thursday, Herzog will meet with the leaders of United Torah Judaism and Otzma Yehudit, which each won seven seats, followed by The Democrats and Ra'am, which each won eight, the Joint List (11), BeYachad (12), Yashar (21) and Likud (27).

Defense and government affairs commentator Amir Oren told Fox News Digital that while Herzog is formally free to choose whom to task with forming a government, he would be inclined to select the candidate whose nomination is backed by parties representing a majority of Knesset seats.
FORMER ISRAELI PM EMERGES AS WILD CARD IN HIGH-STAKES ELECTION WITH MIDDLE EAST'S FUTURE AT STAKE
"He must then task Eisenkot with forming the next government. That does not mean Eisenkot will succeed. If he fails, he will have to return the mandate to the president," Oren said.

Eisenkot may, in fact, struggle to assemble a 61-seat governing coalition, given competing interests within the opposition bloc. BeYachad leader Naftali Bennett and Yisrael Beiteinu chief Avigdor Liberman are unlikely to agree to serve in a government reliant on the Joint List, given the latter’s pro-Palestinian positions and opposition to Zionism.
It is theoretically possible, however, that the opposition bloc could agree to form a minority government with the Arab parties providing support from outside the coalition.

While Israel has no precedent for forming a minority government immediately following an election, such arrangements have occurred during a Knesset term. Most recently, during Netanyahu’s current term, one of the ultra-Orthodox parties withdrew from the coalition over a dispute related to military conscription but continued to support the government from outside.

Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot attends the Jerusalem Residents Conference on Aug. 12, 2026, in Jerusalem. Gadi Eisenkot, a retired chief of the Israel Defense Forces and current leader of the Yashar Party, has emerged as the foremost challenger to Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of October's general election. (Erik Marmor/Getty Images)
Religious Zionism-Zehut, Otzma Yehudit and Shas each confirmed to Fox News Digital on Tuesday night that they would recommend Netanyahu to Herzog during consultations on forming a government.

Dan Diker, president of the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs, told Fox News Digital that Bennett and Liberman’s recent endorsement of Eisenkot suggests they are moving away from the prospect of a national unity government.

"I think it would behoove Netanyahu, Eisenkot, former Prime Minister Bennett and former Defense Minister Liberman to find a way to work together now, given the imminent clash between the apocalyptic death cult known as the Iranian regime, Israel and, by extension, the rest of the Western world," he said.

Complicating matters for Netanyahu, the 26th Knesset is scheduled to be sworn in on Nov. 10. Its newly elected members are expected to begin forming committees and advancing legislation, while the current prime minister and ministers remain in office and continue carrying out their duties under the oversight of the new parliament, ensuring continuity of government.
WHO IS ITAMAR BEN-GVIR, THE ISRAELI FIREBRAND RISING WITH THE POPULIST RIGHT ACROSS THE GLOBE?

A supporter of former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar Party, reacts to the exit poll at his party headquarters, on the evening of Israel's national election, in Tel Aviv, Israel, October 27, 2026. (Shir Torem/Reuters)

"They are doing everything they can to push Netanyahu out of office, and we are seeing that now with discussions about replacing the Knesset speaker. They can then begin trying to advance legislation in a Knesset with 19 seats held by Arab parties that would be very uncomfortable for Netanyahu," Diker said.

Oren highlighted another potential challenge, suggesting that the caretaker government's ability to launch military operations could face political constraints, potentially complicating any resumption of hostilities with Iran, even if U.S. President Donald Trump were to initiate such action.

Former Knesset member Dov Lipman told Fox News Digital that Eisenkot appears likely to be the first lawmaker tasked with forming a government, but suggested that most Israelis favor a national unity government built around Likud, Yashar and BeYachad, with one or more smaller parties also joining.

"As a first step, Eisenkot may approach Likud and ask it to join a government under his leadership, which Likud will reject. Eisenkot will then have to make a decision, as Liberman is unlikely to agree to serve in a government alongside Arab parties," Lipman said.
Mansour Abbas, leader of the Ra'am Party, speaks at the plenum at the Knesset, Israel's parliament, in Jerusalem, July 13, 2026. (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)
"Eisenkot will likely fail to form a government, after which the mandate will pass to Netanyahu, who will also likely fail."

That would trigger a 21-day period during which any Knesset member could attempt to form a government with the backing of at least 61 lawmakers. If the process reaches that stage, Eisenkot might agree to serve under Netanyahu for two years to avoid sending the country to another election, Lipman said.

Prof. Gideon Rahat, a senior fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute, told Fox News Digital that Netanyahu would need to make concessions to persuade opposition leaders that he would honor his commitments, given their experience with the 2020 power-sharing agreement with then-Blue and White party leader Benny Gantz.
NETANYAHU REVEALS HE WANTS AMERICAN FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL TO 'DRAW DOWN TO ZERO'

Under the agreement, Netanyahu was to serve as prime minister for the first 18 months, with Gantz serving as alternate prime minister and defense minister before taking over as premier on Nov. 17, 2021. However, the arrangement unraveled after the government failed to pass a state budget by the December 2020 deadline, triggering the Knesset's automatic dissolution and new elections. Gantz never assumed the premiership.
Rahat pointed to Israel’s 1984-1988 national unity government as a precedent, saying a similar arrangement could work.

"At the time, Israel was still embroiled in the Lebanon War, with IDF forces deployed in the country, while the economy was facing a severe crisis, with annual inflation exceeding 400%. Against that backdrop, Likud and Labor formed a national unity government under a rotation agreement, with Shimon Peres serving as prime minister for the first two years, followed by Yitzhak Shamir for the next two," he said.
While large parts of the public would likely support it, Rahat said, there are still issues that may create tension.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"They will have to freeze the judicial overhaul launched by Netanyahu’s government, find a way to investigate Oct. 7, as demanded by opposition parties and agree on a mechanism for Netanyahu to leave office when the time comes. But when it comes to major issues of security and the economy, unity governments can be quite effective," Rahat said.
"Once they resolve the major challenges, however, they start fighting among themselves and the magic is over."
Amelie Botbol is a freelance field reporter based in Tel Aviv, Israel, who reports on Israel-related news.

title: Gas prices fall below $4 per gallon for the first time since July
summary: The average nationwide price for regular gasoline on Tuesday fell below $4 per gallon for the first time since July 20, according to data from AAA.
story: The average nationwide price for regular gasoline on Tuesday fell below $4 per gallon for the first time since July 20, according to data from AAA.

The drop comes as oil prices have plunged, with President Donald Trump repeatedly playing down the prospect of a renewed war with Iran, and pushing for progress between Russia and Ukraine in new trilateral talks.
Still, gas prices remain elevated by more than 30% since the war with Iran started on February 28, and around 40% since the beginning of the year.

The drop in pump prices came after oil futures plunged 13% last week. For the global crude oil benchmark Brent, it was its biggest one-week percentage drop since April 2020, when the Covid pandemic began shutting down the global economy and demand for oil rapidly declined. Oil prices slid by another 5% on Monday, to their lowest point since August 31. And on Tuesday they briefly fell below $90 a barrel.

The slide in oil prices started after Trump told NBC News last week that he did not plan to attack Iran. The fall continued after Democratic candidates put up commanding vote totals in Tuesday’s midterm elections, which some called a “blue tsunami.”
Markets quickly began betting that Democratic control of the House and Senate would put a cap on some of Trump’s most economically-disruptive policies, such as the Iran war.

“Given the Democrats’ control of Congress, there will likely be more scrutiny over the war, while funding it could become more difficult,” said ING commodities strategists in a note. “The outcome of the elections means there could be more pushback from the Republican Party, too.”

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vice President JD Vance wrote in a post on social media in the wake of the results on Wednesday morning. Vance added that “any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

For traders, Vance’s acknowledgment of the unpopularity of the war bolstered the case for lower oil prices. But on Friday, Trump was briefed on a narrow window for a potential new military campaign against Iran, sources told NBC News. No decision has been taken, the officials also said.

Trump on Monday again reinforced that he was leaning against a major escalation.  “Iran militarily is effectively over,” the president told reporters at the White House. “We’re just keeping it the status quo.” He said there was there was “positive momentum” in talks and that he saw a “good chance” that the war “could get ended.”
He added that  “The military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing, but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason that changes.”

title: Inflation likely took a breather last month as fuel prices fell
summary: Tuesday’s CPI report will be the first snapshot of U.S. price growth since inflation-weary Americans voted for a Democratic sweep in the midterms.
story: Americans are tired of inflation, as last week’s election results showed, but there may have been some relief last month as gasoline, diesel and jet fuel prices eased.

The consumer price index, which is scheduled for release at 8:30 a.m. ET on Tuesday, is expected to show an increase of 0.3% month-over-month, according to a survey of economists conducted by Bloomberg. Economists also project that so-called core inflation, which does not include food or energy prices, rose 0.2%.

In September, the CPI report showed prices grew 0.6% from August along with a 3.7% increase from a year earlier. (The October data will not include a year-ago number after the U.S. government shutdown disrupted the agency’s data collection, forcing it to skip the October 2025 CPI report entirely.)

Even with some relief, the October data is set to illustrate the price pressures on consumers — a big factor in the Democrats’ sweeping victories in the congressional midterm elections last week. Eighty-four percent of voters told NBC News’ Exit Poll that they believed higher prices were a result of President Donald Trump’s policies, and 39% said the economy was their No. 1 issue at the ballot box, according to the exit poll.

Those policies include global tariffs that add to the cost of products imported into the United States, as well as the war in Iran. Launched in February, that conflict has driven regular gas prices up 40%. Diesel fuel prices are 70% higher than at the start of the year.

That, in turn, pushed inflation higher across the U.S.. Economists have warned that the rise in this commercial fuel can quickly ripple across the economy. Diesel is a major input cost for the transportation industry that delivers goods, such as groceries, to store shelves around the world.

Gas prices declined last month, as Americans either voted early or geared up to cast their ballots on Election Day. On Oct. 1, the AAA national gas price average was $4.41 per gallon. At the end of the month, it was $4.18, a more than 5% drop.

As a result, Citigroup economists predicted that Tuesday’s data will show “stabilizing and falling airfares, and limited pass through of higher energy costs into goods prices.” They also said shelter inflation and services prices could also show some slowing.
Gas prices have continued trending downward in November, falling to $4 on Monday — although it’s still significantly higher than before the Iran war.

Even as the oil price surge takes a breather, it may not last long. Throughout the Iran war, countries that are members of the International Energy Agency have released 400 million barrels of crude and related products, such as diesel, into the global market. “Restocking those inventories will create a floor under prices once the current conflict in the Middle East has faded,” said Diane Swonk, chief economist at KPMG.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Given inflation’s overall stubbornness, economists believe the Federal Reserve will remain on track to hike rates for the second time this year. The Fed’s next two-day interest rate meeting will take place Dec. 8-9, right before the next inflation reading on Dec. 10.
Market odds for a December hike sat at 85% Monday afternoon.
“Still, details of Q4 data will be important for shifting inflation risks into 2027,” Citi economists wrote.
Bank of America economists agreed, predicting that the report would be “a cooler start to fall,” after multiple months of rising inflation.

Meanwhile, AI is also stoking inflation in other parts of the economy. In August, JPMorgan estimated that memory costs were on track to rise more than 400% from the end of 2024 through the end of 2026.

Tech companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on data centers and the equipment that fills those facilities, pushing memory prices higher. Those costs are being passed down to consumers. Consumer tech companies, including Apple, have raised their prices as a result.

title: California voters reject new tax on billionaires in a blow to the left
summary: NBC News projects that Proposition 40, which split Democrats in the state and nationally, failed after facing a barrage of attack ads.
story: California voters have rejected a ballot measure that sought to impose a one-time tax on the state’s billionaires, NBC News projected Monday, dealing a blow to progressives who championed the proposal.

Proposition 40 sharply divided Democrats in the state and nationally as the party figures out what direction it wants to take heading into an open presidential contest. It also faced a barrage of ad spending funded by the billionaires it would have affected, particularly in Silicon Valley.

The ballot initiative proposed a 5% tax on the assets of state residents who have net worths of more than $1.1 billion, with the option for a smaller, phased-in tax for those worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion. It would require California to spend 90% of the created revenue on healthcare. The taxes would apply retroactively to anyone living in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026.

Proposition 40 would have been the first enactment of a billionaire tax in the U.S. But many progressives who support increasing taxes on the wealthy in general came out against it because it was a one-time tax, rather than a permanent one, and it primarily benefited one policy area, healthcare.
Critics in both parties argued that the tax would prompt wealthy Californians to flee the state in droves, which would dry up broader tax revenue streams and create more budget problems.

Democratic opponents included outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom, a possible 2028 presidential contender, and Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra. Many of California’s largest unions and Democratic-aligned advocacy groups also opposed the measure.
Meanwhile, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., another potential White House hopeful, were among its notable backers, holding several rallies in the state ahead of Election Day.
Opponents of Proposition 40 held a staggering upper hand on the airwaves. In late October, they were outspending supporters 250 to 1 on ads, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.

The biggest spender, “No on Prop. 40,” was a coalition that included the California Teachers Association, the California Medical Association and Planned Parenthood and received contributions from several billionaires. Other groups got millions from Google co-founder Sergey Brin and the California Business Roundtable.
The “Billionaire Tax Now” campaign, championed by the Service Employees International Union, said the matter is not over.

“The billionaires may have bought themselves a temporary victory at the ballot box, but they have not bought themselves an end to this debate, and this is only round one,” Suzanne Jimenez, a sponsor of Prop 40 and chief of staff at the union, said in a statement Monday.
Opponents of the billionaire tax also placed two dueling initiatives on California’s ballot — Proposition 41 and Proposition 42 — that would have effectively nullified Proposition 40.

Proposition 41 sought to require the state auditor to review new special tax measures and that any new tax be counted toward a voter-approved state spending limit. Proposition 42 proposed banning any new taxes on assets, including investment accounts and property and restricting increases in retroactive taxes. Both would have gone into effect by earning just one vote more than Proposition 40, even if it passed.

title: Republicans, reeling from an election drubbing, will choose their leadership in Congress
summary: Reps. Jim Jordan and Steve Scalise are vying for the top spot in the House, while John Thune is expected to remain Senate Republican leader, despite a conservative push to delay.
story: WASHINGTON — After a blue tidal wave swept them from power, House and Senate Republicans will try to pick up the pieces Tuesday and select their leadership teams for the new Congress.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., has already heeded his party’s call for new blood, announcing he will forgo a bid for minority leader and step down from leadership. But other GOP leaders in both chambers are fighting to hang on to power in the wake of last week’s historic midterm drubbing.
The House: Scalise vs. Jordan

In the House, Johnson’s decision has triggered a two-person race for minority leader. Johnson’s trusted top lieutenant and fellow Louisiana Republican, Majority Leader Steve Scalise, is fending off a challenge from Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio, the founding chairman of the hard-right House Freedom Caucus.

Both are allies of President Donald Trump and ran unsuccessfully for speaker in 2023 after Kevin McCarthy was ousted. The elections will be held behind closed doors and by secret ballot. Candidates will make their pitches to the conference beginning at 9 a.m. ET, with a vote in the afternoon.

Scalise made the pitch to colleagues that he can unify factions of House Republicans against the “socialists” coming to Washington, while Jordan, a former Oversight Committee chairman, argued that he’s best positioned to combat Democratic investigations of the Trump administration and its allies, telling colleagues he’s “battle-tested on the oversight front and I know the Democrats’ playbook.”
Either will need a majority of the conference to vote for him to secure the job.

Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., is seeking the whip job, the party’s top vote counter and the No. 2 post in the minority. But he faces an insurgent challenge from August Pfluger of Texas, the chairman of the Republican Study Committee, the largest caucus of conservatives on Capitol Hill.

And House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan is trying to beat back challenges from two colleagues: Erin Houchin of Indiana, who holds a lower-level leadership post, and Greg Steube of Florida, who berated the current leadership team for choosing “accommodation over conviction.”

“We’re ready to move on. We need a pivot,” a House GOP lawmaker who is backing Jordan over Scalise told NBC News on the condition of anonymity to speak frankly about the rival candidates. “Everything is on the table” after the Democratic landslide, the lawmaker said.
The Senate: Thune faces grumbling

Senate Republicans also are poised to hold a closed-door vote Tuesday to pick their leaders. Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota is running for minority leader, and so far nobody has announced plans to oppose him.
But a small group of Senate Republicans has sought to delay the elections, saying the party needs more time to process the election results.

“A week ago, we had the worst election result in decades. We need a discussion about what went wrong, how we fix it, what we stand for, and how our agenda must focus on the concerns of the American people,” Sen. David McCormick, R-Pa., said in a statement.

“As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward,” he said. “We need leadership in place fast, but Tuesday is too soon.”

Five other Senate Republicans, led by Budget Committee Chairman Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, sent a letter to Senate Republican Conference Chairman Tom Cotton of Arkansas asking for “a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead” before the elections are held Tuesday morning.
As in the House, senators’ votes are cast by secret ballot, and candidates require a simple majority of the conference to win.
Apart from Thune, Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso of Wyoming and Cotton are expected to win their races to stay on as the second-ranked and third-ranked Republicans in the next Congress.
Jeffries and Schumer favorites to lead Dems

After last week’s Democratic rout, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, both New York Democrats, are favorites to be the next House speaker and Senate majority leader.
But they, too, face grumbling from rank-and-file members.
For Subscribers

No one has emerged to challenge either for the top jobs, though Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., opened the door Monday to potentially running for majority leader amid a push from the grassroots to find an alternative to Schumer.
For Subscribers

A person familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking told NBC News on Monday: “The senator has received an outpouring of calls on running for majority leader and is now in active listening mode. The door is not shut.”
Democrats at the Senate’s new-member orientation Monday said the question of their leadership team hasn’t come up in private conversations.

“Most of us are just trying to figure out where our office is and how to find the bathroom,” said Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan, D-Minn. “It’s really exciting to be here and to meet a lot of my colleagues who’ve been campaigning. I know how hard we’ve been working. And to be here together — it’s really exciting.”
As for Van Hollen’s potentially running for majority leader, Flanagan said she is “certainly open to new leadership” but is “not ready to make any commitments at this point.”
Senate Democrats will elect their leadership team in a private meeting in early December, while House Democrats will pick their team next week.
Several progressives have said they are undecided about whether to back Jeffries for speaker as grassroots groups urge the party to more aggressively confront Trump and enact progressive policies.

“We’re not withholding votes. What we’re doing [is] saying we’re undecided,” said Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, D-N.J. “We want to sit and have a conversation about the issues and what’s the plan going forward.”

But Jeffries has such a large majority — NBC News projects Democrats will secure 259 seats — that he can afford roughly 40 defections and still win the 218 votes needed to become speaker on the House floor on Jan. 3.

“We’re going to work as hard as we can to get to the 218 number, and we’re confident that we will get to that number and beyond,” Jeffries told reporters when he was asked about disgruntled progressives.

Jeffries and his top lieutenants, Katherine Clark of Massachusetts, Pete Aguilar of California and Ted Lieu of California, are so far running unopposed for the top four leadership posts: speaker, majority leader, majority whip and Democratic Caucus chair.

title: U.S. moves military aircraft from British base amid Iran threats
summary: The United States has moved military aircraft from the RAF Mildenhall airbase in the United Kingdom amid threats from Iran.
story: LONDON — The United States has moved military aircraft from an airbase in the United Kingdom amid threats from Iran.
A U.S. official confirmed to NBC News that several military aircraft had left RAF Mildenhall as the security posture there had increased.
They were operating under “enhanced force protection measures,” the official said. They would not speculate on the exact nature of the threat that appears to have led to ramped up security.
At least eight air refueling tankers and three Ospreys left the base in Suffolk, eastern England, on Monday, flight tracking data showed.

Some of the tankers, Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers, were relocated to airbases in Germany and Spain, with one moved to the area of Glasgow Prestwick Airport in Scotland. The Ospreys were moved to nearby RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk.

It comes weeks after the U.S. withdrew bombers from another base in Britain, RAF Fairford, after police foiled a suspected terror plot linked to Iran. The U.S. has used bases in the U.K. to strike the Islamic Republic.

The Wall Street Journal was first to report on this week’s movements and said the evacuation came following a threat from Iran, citing people familiar with the matter. It said the exact nature of the threat was not yet known and remained under discussion by U.S. officials.
“We take proactive measures to ensure our aircraft, our people, and our installations remain safe and secure,” a U.S. official told NBC News.

“U.S. Air Force aircraft rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons including training and real world requirement,” a U.S. European Command official said. “U.S. military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our Allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets,” the European Command official added.
A spokesperson for the U.K.’s Ministry of Defense said it does “not routinely comment on the activity of other nations.”
“Aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements,” the spokesperson said.

It comes weeks after the U.S. pulled aircraft from RAF Fairford following reports of a possible Iranian drone attack, two U.S. officials previously told NBC News. That move came in the wake of an investigation into a possible planned terrorist attack at that base, located in Gloucestershire.
Five men were detained on Sept. 27 after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward RAF Fairford. Other arrests followed and two men were charged under the National Security Act.
The incident, which attracted huge international attention, remains largely unexplained although British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the activity was likely to have been coordinated in Iran.

Though Tehran has denied involvement in any plot against RAF Fairford, its powerful Revolutionary Guard warned in July that any base used to launch attacks against Iranian territory was a legitimate target.
Iran has vowed retaliation for any renewal of the American-Israeli war against it and has threatened to expand its response beyond the Middle East.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that Washington had addressed concerns around reported threats from Tehran against American diplomats overseas by “moving people away from the threat.”

“Obviously, we’re always worried about the safety and security of our personnel and their families overseas,” Rubio said. “And so, when we see anything that could pose a potential threat beyond a certain threshold, we’re going to address it.”
Citing new “momentum” in negotiations to end the war, President Donald Trump on Monday downplayed the prospect of new U.S. attacks.
“Iran militarily is effectively over,” Trump said following a meeting with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani.
Further U.S. attacks “won’t be necessary” at this point, but Washington remains “locked and loaded” should circumstances change, Trump told reporters at the White House.

title: The ‘slam dunk’ that wasn’t: Promising cholesterol drug fails to prevent heart attacks or stroke
summary: An experimental drug that held great promise in driving down a dangerous form of cholesterol didn’t show any measurable impact on heart attack or stroke in a clinical trial.
story: An experimental drug that held great promise in driving down a dangerous form of cholesterol didn’t show any measurable impact on heart attack or stroke in a clinical trial. The failure of the Novartis drug pelacarsen to help people who have high levels of lipoprotein(a) stunned researchers, who called it a massive blow to preventive cardiology.

Results of the clinical trial of pelacarsen, an injection, presented Saturday at a meeting of the American Heart Association, found there were zero decreases in stroke, heart attack, cardiovascular deaths or the number of procedures to open blocked arteries or restore blood flow to the heart.

“I really thought that this was going to be a slam dunk,” said Dr. Amanda Doran, an assistant professor of medicine in the division of cardiovascular medicine at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. Vanderbilt was one of nearly 800 sites involved in the clinical trial, called Horizon. “We were pretty invested, so it obviously hurts.”

Pelacarsen targets a stealthy and particularly lethal form of cholesterol called lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a). Much like low-density lipoprotein — LDL, or the “bad” cholesterol — Lp(a) causes plaque to build up in arteries. But it also helps form blood clots, and unlike LDL, it is entirely genetic.
About 1 in 5 Americans have high Lp(a), according to the American Heart Association. Most don’t realize they’re at risk.
Because people are born with those high levels, diet and exercise have no effect. That’s why heart experts have been so keen to find a drug that would handle the problem.
The Horizon trial included 8,322 people with high Lp(a) levels and who’d already had a heart attack, stroke or other heart problem within 10 years of starting the trial.
The drug did reduce Lp(a) significantly, by 78%, compared with a placebo drug that cut levels by 13%.
But that huge reduction ultimately meant nothing in terms of cardiovascular health.
Dr. Steven Nissen, the chief academic officer of the Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute at the Cleveland Clinic, led the trial. He said the dismal results took him by “extreme surprise.”

“Everybody, me included, believed that lowering levels of lipoprotein(a) substantially would reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events,” he said. “There is simply no evidence here that people that got more reduction did better.”

The findings, also published Saturday in the New England Journal of Medicine, confounded Nissen and other cardiologists who’ve long known that controlling other markers of heart health — LDL and blood pressure, for example — provides clear benefits.

“I have not seen a more shockingly neutral trial in a while,” said Dr. Karol Watson, co-director of the UCLA Program in Preventive Cardiology and a professor at UCLA’s David Geffen School of Medicine. Watson was not involved with the research.

There are several theories as to why the drug didn’t work as anticipated. It’s possible, Watson said, that the therapy was given too late in life to make a difference. The average age of Horizon’s study participants was 60, and they were followed for an average of five years.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
“Remember that Lp(a) is a genetic disorder, so from the time a baby’s conceived, their Lp(a) is high. If we just swooped in in the last five years, maybe that’s too late,” Watson said.

Study participants were also treated aggressively in other ways to drive down their LDL cholesterol and get blood pressure readings into a healthy range. Participants may have also been taking aspirin because of a history of heart attack or stroke, which could have lessened Lp(a)’s clotting risk.
“How much of the Lp(a)-associated risk was remaining? We just don’t know,” Watson said.
Does Lp(a) still matter as a marker of heart health?

Doctors have only recently begun screening for it. Earlier this year, the American College of Cardiology and the American Heart Association released guidelines that every adult should have their Lp(a) levels measured. It’s a blood test that’s done once because levels are fixed and don’t change over time.
Experts stress that Lp(a) remains an important and valuable indicator of heart disease risk, even though the Horizon study failed to show any health benefit to driving down Lp(a) levels.

“None of that invalidates Lp(a) as a robust marker of cardiovascular disease risk,” said Dr. John Wilkins, a cardiologist at Northwestern Medicine and a professor in the division of cardiology at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine. Wilkins was also one of the authors of the Lp(a) guidelines.

“It’s still worth testing for Lp(a) because it can help identify individuals with a higher probability of an event, and we do have other interventions that can help reduce their risk,” Wilkins said. “It’s just that at present, at least with this particular drug in this particular group of patients, we did not see benefit. That doesn’t mean that we might not find something or some way to lower Lp(a) that reduces risk. We just need more science to figure that out.”

UCLA’s Watson and Vanderbilt’s Doran agreed. “We have really good data to show that Lp(a) levels are predictive of disease,” Doran said. “People who have high Lp(a) need to be aware of that in order to pursue aggressive prevention strategies.”
What’s next in treating Lp(a)?
No further study of pelacarsen is planned, Nissen said, but similar drugs are in the pipeline: Eli Lilly’s lepodisiran, Amgen’s olpasiran and Silence Therapeutics’ zerlasiran.

All are injections that work by blocking the liver’s ability to produce Lp(a), but use different approaches. Pelacarsen is what’s known as an antisense oligonucleotide. The others use a technology called small interfering RNA, or siRNA, and may have fewer side effects, such as injection site reactions, Nissen said, than pelacarsen.
Like pelacarsen, all reduce Lp(a). Clinical trials to show whether they have any real-world heart health effects are ongoing.
Eli Lilly is also studying an oral drug called muvalaplin, and CRISPR gene-editing technology designed to permanently switch off the gene that produces Lp(a) is in early development.
“I’m still so hopeful,” Doran said. “We’re going to get it in the end.”

title: U.S. moves military aircraft from British base amid Iran threats
summary: The United States has moved military aircraft from the RAF Mildenhall airbase in the United Kingdom amid threats from Iran.
story: LONDON — The United States has moved military aircraft from an airbase in the United Kingdom amid threats from Iran.
A U.S. official confirmed to NBC News that several military aircraft had left RAF Mildenhall as the security posture there had increased.
They were operating under “enhanced force protection measures,” the official said. They would not speculate on the exact nature of the threat that appears to have led to ramped up security.
At least eight air refueling tankers and three Ospreys left the base in Suffolk, eastern England, on Monday, flight tracking data showed.

Some of the tankers, Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers, were relocated to airbases in Germany and Spain, with one moved to the area of Glasgow Prestwick Airport in Scotland. The Ospreys were moved to nearby RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk.

It comes weeks after the U.S. withdrew bombers from another base in Britain, RAF Fairford, after police foiled a suspected terror plot linked to Iran. The U.S. has used bases in the U.K. to strike the Islamic Republic.

The Wall Street Journal was first to report on this week’s movements and said the evacuation came following a threat from Iran, citing people familiar with the matter. It said the exact nature of the threat was not yet known and remained under discussion by U.S. officials.
“We take proactive measures to ensure our aircraft, our people, and our installations remain safe and secure,” a U.S. official told NBC News.

“U.S. Air Force aircraft rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons including training and real world requirement,” a U.S. European Command official said. “U.S. military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our Allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets,” the European Command official added.
A spokesperson for the U.K.’s Ministry of Defense said it does “not routinely comment on the activity of other nations.”
“Aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements,” the spokesperson said.

It comes weeks after the U.S. pulled aircraft from RAF Fairford following reports of a possible Iranian drone attack, two U.S. officials previously told NBC News. That move came in the wake of an investigation into a possible planned terrorist attack at that base, located in Gloucestershire.
Five men were detained on Sept. 27 after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward RAF Fairford. Other arrests followed and two men were charged under the National Security Act.
The incident, which attracted huge international attention, remains largely unexplained although British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the activity was likely to have been coordinated in Iran.

Though Tehran has denied involvement in any plot against RAF Fairford, its powerful Revolutionary Guard warned in July that any base used to launch attacks against Iranian territory was a legitimate target.
Iran has vowed retaliation for any renewal of the American-Israeli war against it and has threatened to expand its response beyond the Middle East.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that Washington had addressed concerns around reported threats from Tehran against American diplomats overseas by “moving people away from the threat.”

“Obviously, we’re always worried about the safety and security of our personnel and their families overseas,” Rubio said. “And so, when we see anything that could pose a potential threat beyond a certain threshold, we’re going to address it.”
Citing new “momentum” in negotiations to end the war, President Donald Trump on Monday downplayed the prospect of new U.S. attacks.
“Iran militarily is effectively over,” Trump said following a meeting with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani.
Further U.S. attacks “won’t be necessary” at this point, but Washington remains “locked and loaded” should circumstances change, Trump told reporters at the White House.

title: Republicans, reeling from an election drubbing, will choose their leadership in Congress
summary: Reps. Jim Jordan and Steve Scalise are vying for the top spot in the House, while John Thune is expected to remain Senate Republican leader, despite a conservative push to delay.
story: WASHINGTON — After a blue tidal wave swept them from power, House and Senate Republicans will try to pick up the pieces Tuesday and select their leadership teams for the new Congress.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., has already heeded his party’s call for new blood, announcing he will forgo a bid for minority leader and step down from leadership. But other GOP leaders in both chambers are fighting to hang on to power in the wake of last week’s historic midterm drubbing.
The House: Scalise vs. Jordan

In the House, Johnson’s decision has triggered a two-person race for minority leader. Johnson’s trusted top lieutenant and fellow Louisiana Republican, Majority Leader Steve Scalise, is fending off a challenge from Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio, the founding chairman of the hard-right House Freedom Caucus.

Both are allies of President Donald Trump and ran unsuccessfully for speaker in 2023 after Kevin McCarthy was ousted. The elections will be held behind closed doors and by secret ballot. Candidates will make their pitches to the conference beginning at 9 a.m. ET, with a vote in the afternoon.

Scalise made the pitch to colleagues that he can unify factions of House Republicans against the “socialists” coming to Washington, while Jordan, a former Oversight Committee chairman, argued that he’s best positioned to combat Democratic investigations of the Trump administration and its allies, telling colleagues he’s “battle-tested on the oversight front and I know the Democrats’ playbook.”
Either will need a majority of the conference to vote for him to secure the job.

Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., is seeking the whip job, the party’s top vote counter and the No. 2 post in the minority. But he faces an insurgent challenge from August Pfluger of Texas, the chairman of the Republican Study Committee, the largest caucus of conservatives on Capitol Hill.

And House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan is trying to beat back challenges from two colleagues: Erin Houchin of Indiana, who holds a lower-level leadership post, and Greg Steube of Florida, who berated the current leadership team for choosing “accommodation over conviction.”

“We’re ready to move on. We need a pivot,” a House GOP lawmaker who is backing Jordan over Scalise told NBC News on the condition of anonymity to speak frankly about the rival candidates. “Everything is on the table” after the Democratic landslide, the lawmaker said.
The Senate: Thune faces grumbling

Senate Republicans also are poised to hold a closed-door vote Tuesday to pick their leaders. Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota is running for minority leader, and so far nobody has announced plans to oppose him.
But a small group of Senate Republicans has sought to delay the elections, saying the party needs more time to process the election results.

“A week ago, we had the worst election result in decades. We need a discussion about what went wrong, how we fix it, what we stand for, and how our agenda must focus on the concerns of the American people,” Sen. David McCormick, R-Pa., said in a statement.

“As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward,” he said. “We need leadership in place fast, but Tuesday is too soon.”

Five other Senate Republicans, led by Budget Committee Chairman Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, sent a letter to Senate Republican Conference Chairman Tom Cotton of Arkansas asking for “a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead” before the elections are held Tuesday morning.
As in the House, senators’ votes are cast by secret ballot, and candidates require a simple majority of the conference to win.
Apart from Thune, Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso of Wyoming and Cotton are expected to win their races to stay on as the second-ranked and third-ranked Republicans in the next Congress.
Jeffries and Schumer favorites to lead Dems

After last week’s Democratic rout, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, both New York Democrats, are favorites to be the next House speaker and Senate majority leader.
But they, too, face grumbling from rank-and-file members.
For Subscribers

No one has emerged to challenge either for the top jobs, though Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., opened the door Monday to potentially running for majority leader amid a push from the grassroots to find an alternative to Schumer.
For Subscribers

A person familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking told NBC News on Monday: “The senator has received an outpouring of calls on running for majority leader and is now in active listening mode. The door is not shut.”
Democrats at the Senate’s new-member orientation Monday said the question of their leadership team hasn’t come up in private conversations.

“Most of us are just trying to figure out where our office is and how to find the bathroom,” said Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan, D-Minn. “It’s really exciting to be here and to meet a lot of my colleagues who’ve been campaigning. I know how hard we’ve been working. And to be here together — it’s really exciting.”
As for Van Hollen’s potentially running for majority leader, Flanagan said she is “certainly open to new leadership” but is “not ready to make any commitments at this point.”
Senate Democrats will elect their leadership team in a private meeting in early December, while House Democrats will pick their team next week.
Several progressives have said they are undecided about whether to back Jeffries for speaker as grassroots groups urge the party to more aggressively confront Trump and enact progressive policies.

“We’re not withholding votes. What we’re doing [is] saying we’re undecided,” said Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, D-N.J. “We want to sit and have a conversation about the issues and what’s the plan going forward.”

But Jeffries has such a large majority — NBC News projects Democrats will secure 259 seats — that he can afford roughly 40 defections and still win the 218 votes needed to become speaker on the House floor on Jan. 3.

“We’re going to work as hard as we can to get to the 218 number, and we’re confident that we will get to that number and beyond,” Jeffries told reporters when he was asked about disgruntled progressives.

Jeffries and his top lieutenants, Katherine Clark of Massachusetts, Pete Aguilar of California and Ted Lieu of California, are so far running unopposed for the top four leadership posts: speaker, majority leader, majority whip and Democratic Caucus chair.

title: Gas prices fall below $4 per gallon for the first time since July
summary: The average nationwide price for regular gasoline on Tuesday fell below $4 per gallon for the first time since July 20, according to data from AAA.
story: The average nationwide price for regular gasoline on Tuesday fell below $4 per gallon for the first time since July 20, according to data from AAA.

The drop comes as oil prices have plunged, with President Donald Trump repeatedly playing down the prospect of a renewed war with Iran, and pushing for progress between Russia and Ukraine in new trilateral talks.
Still, gas prices remain elevated by more than 30% since the war with Iran started on February 28, and around 40% since the beginning of the year.

The drop in pump prices came after oil futures plunged 13% last week. For the global crude oil benchmark Brent, it was its biggest one-week percentage drop since April 2020, when the Covid pandemic began shutting down the global economy and demand for oil rapidly declined. Oil prices slid by another 5% on Monday, to their lowest point since August 31. And on Tuesday they briefly fell below $90 a barrel.

The slide in oil prices started after Trump told NBC News last week that he did not plan to attack Iran. The fall continued after Democratic candidates put up commanding vote totals in Tuesday’s midterm elections, which some called a “blue tsunami.”
Markets quickly began betting that Democratic control of the House and Senate would put a cap on some of Trump’s most economically-disruptive policies, such as the Iran war.

“Given the Democrats’ control of Congress, there will likely be more scrutiny over the war, while funding it could become more difficult,” said ING commodities strategists in a note. “The outcome of the elections means there could be more pushback from the Republican Party, too.”

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vice President JD Vance wrote in a post on social media in the wake of the results on Wednesday morning. Vance added that “any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

For traders, Vance’s acknowledgment of the unpopularity of the war bolstered the case for lower oil prices. But on Friday, Trump was briefed on a narrow window for a potential new military campaign against Iran, sources told NBC News. No decision has been taken, the officials also said.

Trump on Monday again reinforced that he was leaning against a major escalation.  “Iran militarily is effectively over,” the president told reporters at the White House. “We’re just keeping it the status quo.” He said there was there was “positive momentum” in talks and that he saw a “good chance” that the war “could get ended.”
He added that  “The military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing, but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason that changes.”

title: California voters reject new tax on billionaires in a blow to the left
summary: NBC News projects that Proposition 40, which split Democrats in the state and nationally, failed after facing a barrage of attack ads.
story: California voters have rejected a ballot measure that sought to impose a one-time tax on the state’s billionaires, NBC News projected Monday, dealing a blow to progressives who championed the proposal.

Proposition 40 sharply divided Democrats in the state and nationally as the party figures out what direction it wants to take heading into an open presidential contest. It also faced a barrage of ad spending funded by the billionaires it would have affected, particularly in Silicon Valley.

The ballot initiative proposed a 5% tax on the assets of state residents who have net worths of more than $1.1 billion, with the option for a smaller, phased-in tax for those worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion. It would require California to spend 90% of the created revenue on healthcare. The taxes would apply retroactively to anyone living in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026.

Proposition 40 would have been the first enactment of a billionaire tax in the U.S. But many progressives who support increasing taxes on the wealthy in general came out against it because it was a one-time tax, rather than a permanent one, and it primarily benefited one policy area, healthcare.
Critics in both parties argued that the tax would prompt wealthy Californians to flee the state in droves, which would dry up broader tax revenue streams and create more budget problems.

Democratic opponents included outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom, a possible 2028 presidential contender, and Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra. Many of California’s largest unions and Democratic-aligned advocacy groups also opposed the measure.
Meanwhile, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., another potential White House hopeful, were among its notable backers, holding several rallies in the state ahead of Election Day.
Opponents of Proposition 40 held a staggering upper hand on the airwaves. In late October, they were outspending supporters 250 to 1 on ads, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.

The biggest spender, “No on Prop. 40,” was a coalition that included the California Teachers Association, the California Medical Association and Planned Parenthood and received contributions from several billionaires. Other groups got millions from Google co-founder Sergey Brin and the California Business Roundtable.
The “Billionaire Tax Now” campaign, championed by the Service Employees International Union, said the matter is not over.

“The billionaires may have bought themselves a temporary victory at the ballot box, but they have not bought themselves an end to this debate, and this is only round one,” Suzanne Jimenez, a sponsor of Prop 40 and chief of staff at the union, said in a statement Monday.
Opponents of the billionaire tax also placed two dueling initiatives on California’s ballot — Proposition 41 and Proposition 42 — that would have effectively nullified Proposition 40.

Proposition 41 sought to require the state auditor to review new special tax measures and that any new tax be counted toward a voter-approved state spending limit. Proposition 42 proposed banning any new taxes on assets, including investment accounts and property and restricting increases in retroactive taxes. Both would have gone into effect by earning just one vote more than Proposition 40, even if it passed.

title: A Haitian 8-year-old was taken by ICE at routine check-in, rattling a San Diego school district
summary: The school district and immigration advocates said the boy was separated from his cousins and uncle, who was taking care of him after his father was deported last year.
story: Wearing a pressed button-down white shirt and slacks, a Haitian boy showed up at a routine immigration appointment in downtown San Diego. Moments later, the neatly dressed 8-year-old was being led away by three immigration officers.
As of Monday, his loved ones do not know exactly where he is being held, a California lawmaker said.
The scene was captured on a video NBC San Diego obtained Friday. The video was recorded Wednesday by a volunteer observer of immigration proceedings at ICE’s field office.

The San Diego Unified School District and members of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, an immigrants rights advocacy group, said the boy was separated from his cousins and uncle, who has been taking care of him after his father was deported last year.

Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, said in a statement Monday that even though the uncle followed all the rules, “the child was taken into custody and subsequently transferred to the Office of Refugee Resettlement,” which takes custody of children deemed to be unaccompanied minors.

The boy, who has not been identified by name publicly, is a third grader at Fay Elementary School. He was stripped of his immigration protections this summer after a Supreme Court decision allowed President Donald Trump to end Temporary Protected Status for Haitians, according to a letter school district officials sent Friday to the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the Office of Refugee Resettlement.

Temporary Protected Status, better known as TPS, is a humanitarian designation that shielded hundreds of thousands of Haitians from deportation following Haiti’s 2010 devastating earthquake. The protections were renewed multiple times over the years as the Caribbean country sank deeper into crisis. Currently, a majority of the country’s capital is controlled by gangs after the president was assassinated in 2021.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

After TPS was terminated, the child in San Diego received a letter summoning him to meet with ICE officers last week, school district officials said in their letter. His uncle complied and took him to the appointment “because he did not want to break the law,” added the letter, which NBC News obtained Monday.

A DHS spokesperson told NBC San Diego that “a man claiming to be the child’s uncle took him to an ICE check-in.” ICE officers said that they could not confirm the man was related to the boy and that “the alleged uncle could not establish legal guardianship of the minor.”

As a result, they determined the boy to be an unaccompanied minor, the DHS spokesperson said. “Out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety, ICE determined it was best to remove the child from the household,” the spokesperson said.
The Office of Refugee Resettlement told NBC News on Monday that it “does not comment on specific cases” in accordance with its own privacy policies to protect the children in its custody.

The third grader is among the 1,640 children considered unaccompanied minors who are under HHS care, according to the agency’s data. Immigration authorities have taken more than 8,000 children into custody over the past year, according to data from the Deportation Data Project.
The office of Rep. Juan Vargas, D-Calif., said that the boy’s family does not know where he is being held and that he is helping them obtain the information they need to find him.

“Targeting a child, taking them away from their community and classmates, and forcing them into detention is despicable. It is inhumane,” Vargas told NBC San Diego in a statement Friday. “Additionally, TPS protections must be restored for all who’ve had them unfairly ripped away.”
DHS has deemed allegations claiming the boy was “placed in detention” as “false.”
DHS also said the child was “illegally brought into the United States” at an unspecified time by “a man who alleged to be his father,” who was removed to Mexico by Customs and Border Patrol, not ICE.
Jozef said, “His father has already been taken from him and deported, now this administration has stripped him of the stability, family, and community every child deserves.”

James Canning, a spokesperson for the school district, told NBC News in a statement on Monday that educators at the boy’s school have pointed to “a general sense of concern for the student’s safety and wellbeing.”

School district officials said they are sending additional crisis counselors to Fay Elementary School this week “because the child’s fellow third grade students have expressed concern and fear for their friend.”
Canning said no one at DHS or HHS has yet responded to the school district’s letter asking them to reconsider how immigration enforcement policies are affecting students.

title: Trump defends Pete Hegseth at surprise news briefing with Dana White
summary: The president said he would stand by the defense secretary if impeached and claimed, “We won the war in Iran,” despite ongoing conflict in the region.
story: In his first post-midterm news briefing, President Donald Trump on Monday talked about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, the effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the massive Republican losses at the ballot box last week.

Trump was joined at the impromptu briefing by Ultimate Fighting Championship CEO Dana White, to whom he jokingly offered the White House press secretary job last week. The president said he thought he would have “a little fun” by bringing White out to take questions from reporters.
The president, who ended up fielding most of the questions, downplayed Rep. Thomas Massie’s push to impeach Hegseth.
“He is a sick, sick guy,” Trump said of the Kentucky Republican who reintroduced articles of impeachment Monday that largely focus on the Iran war.

“I will say this: The soldiers, the actual soldiers, the great people that do the work, the great patriots, they love Pete Hegseth,” Trump said while saying the secretary “won the war in Venezuela” and “won the war in Iran,” where peace talks have stalled and sporadic U.S. strikes are ongoing.
“He’s done a very good job,” Trump said, adding that he would stand by Hegseth if he’s impeached by the House.

A simple majority is required in the still GOP-led House for the articles to be approved and sent to the Senate for a trial. Only two Cabinet members in history have successfully been impeached; neither was convicted.
Trump also defended Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Monday while revealing that he is under investigation by the FBI.

People familiar with the matter told NBC News on Sunday that U.S. intelligence agencies had determined that Alice Huang, the woman with whom Jensen Huang allegedly had the affair, was a Chinese spy. The two are not related.
Trump said that he had spoken to Huang on Monday “just to see if he’s feeling all right.”
“He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy,’ and I really believe him,” Trump said, adding that Huang is a “very honorable man.”
Huang said in a statement Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to my wife.”

Nvidia’s board of directors announced Sunday it was “initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” China denied involvement, calling it a “smear.”

The president also responded to comments he made about his immigration policy during a “60 Minutes” interview that aired Sunday, during which he said his deportations had been “too tough,” and signaled a willingness to work with Democrats on potentially creating legal status for some immigrants.
Trump said Monday that his policy “hasn’t changed” but that he’s “open” to an immigration deal with Democrats.

“We’re not going to have amnesty or anything,” Trump said, without saying what, exactly, a deal might look like. “People are going to do it the right way. I have to do it. It’s unfair to other people, but certainly I’m open to it.”
Trump also expanded on a Truth Social post from earlier in the day that questioned the midterm election results, despite his saying last week that he was willing to accept them.

“I think the numbers were terrible in terms of those early votes,” Trump said when asked by reporters if he thought the results had been rigged. He then repeated his claim of foul play in the tight Alaska Senate race, which hasn’t been called.
Trump concluded Monday’s briefing, where he spoke for a little more than 30 minutes, by jokingly offering Dana White the press secretary role one more time.
“Thank you for the offer, sir,” White said. “I do not want to be in politics.”
“I am devastated to hear this,” Trump responded before they both left the briefing room.
The White House has been without a press secretary since late August, save for the five days Katie Zacharia served in the role last month.

title: Trump Media cashes in on high-speed access to social media posts
summary: The firm’s revenue jumped more than 200% after it started selling a direct feed of posts from Truth Social, whose most prominent user is President Trump.
story: Trump Media and Technology Group reported Monday that revenue surged 205% in the third quarter, which it says was “primarily driven” by selling a high-speed feed of posts on Truth Social.

The “Truth API,” as the company calls it, allows news organizations, Wall Street trading firms and other services to pay $60,000 to $100,000 per month for a direct feed of posts on the social network. Critics have slammed the feed as an attempt to profit from President Donald Trump’s posts.
Trump, whose revocable trust is the largest single shareholder of Trump Media, is the most prominent user of Truth Social.

Trump’s trust owns more than 41% of Trump Media, according to S&P Capital IQ data. In a June filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the trust said Donald Trump Jr. was “the sole trustee and has sole voting and investment power” over its holdings.
Trump Media’s stock, which trades under the symbol DJT for Trump’s initials, closed at $4.06 on Monday, giving it a market valuation of $1.13 billion. It’s down 69% so far this year.
In July, Trump Media announced the high-speed feed offering, saying it would allow “real-time access to posts from the highest-ranking Truth Social accounts.”
The company acknowledged that the service could be market-moving and highly valuable to any trading firm.

“Markets already move on Truth Social posts,” Kevin McGurn, interim CEO of Trump Media, said at the time. He added that “high frequency and algorithmic trading firms that require a low-latency, machine-readable feed rather than manual tracking” could benefit from paying for the feed.
In August, the company said the service had gone live.

Last month, Reuters reported that Bloomberg and two Wall Street trading firms were some of the customers who had signed up for the service. Bloomberg declined to comment to NBC News in October, while the two other firms did not reply to requests for comment at the time.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Two top Democratic senators, Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Adam Schiff of California, said the Truth Social feed amounts to “an outrageous abuse of the President’s office for his personal benefit.” In July, they asked the SEC to “determine whether the proposed arrangement would violate applicable federal securities laws.”
Trump was asked Sunday whether he was using the presidency to enrich himself.

“I devote almost no time to my net worth,” Trump told CBS News’ “60 Minutes” in an interview. “I have a lot of money, and far more than I ever thought I’d have. And I guess it’s gone up. I don’t even know.”
Trump said his son “watches over” his money, adding: “I don’t even talk to him about it.”

Trump’s personal finances differ vastly from those of other recent presidents. In June, Trump’s most recent personal financial disclosure ran more than 900 pages. By comparison, President Barack Obama’s final disclosure form was eight pages, while President Joe Biden’s was 11. Vice President JD Vance’s form for last year is 17 pages.
Trump’s disclosure shows billions of dollars in earnings tied to cryptocurrencies, media settlements and vast personal investments in stocks and bonds.
The White House has repeatedly insisted that “neither the President nor his family has ever engaged — or will ever engage — in conflicts of interest.”

title: Inflation likely took a breather last month as fuel prices fell
summary: Tuesday’s CPI report will be the first snapshot of U.S. price growth since inflation-weary Americans voted for a Democratic sweep in the midterms.
story: Americans are tired of inflation, as last week’s election results showed, but there may have been some relief last month as gasoline, diesel and jet fuel prices eased.

The consumer price index, which is scheduled for release at 8:30 a.m. ET on Tuesday, is expected to show an increase of 0.3% month-over-month, according to a survey of economists conducted by Bloomberg. Economists also project that so-called core inflation, which does not include food or energy prices, rose 0.2%.

In September, the CPI report showed prices grew 0.6% from August along with a 3.7% increase from a year earlier. (The October data will not include a year-ago number after the U.S. government shutdown disrupted the agency’s data collection, forcing it to skip the October 2025 CPI report entirely.)

Even with some relief, the October data is set to illustrate the price pressures on consumers — a big factor in the Democrats’ sweeping victories in the congressional midterm elections last week. Eighty-four percent of voters told NBC News’ Exit Poll that they believed higher prices were a result of President Donald Trump’s policies, and 39% said the economy was their No. 1 issue at the ballot box, according to the exit poll.

Those policies include global tariffs that add to the cost of products imported into the United States, as well as the war in Iran. Launched in February, that conflict has driven regular gas prices up 40%. Diesel fuel prices are 70% higher than at the start of the year.

That, in turn, pushed inflation higher across the U.S.. Economists have warned that the rise in this commercial fuel can quickly ripple across the economy. Diesel is a major input cost for the transportation industry that delivers goods, such as groceries, to store shelves around the world.

Gas prices declined last month, as Americans either voted early or geared up to cast their ballots on Election Day. On Oct. 1, the AAA national gas price average was $4.41 per gallon. At the end of the month, it was $4.18, a more than 5% drop.

As a result, Citigroup economists predicted that Tuesday’s data will show “stabilizing and falling airfares, and limited pass through of higher energy costs into goods prices.” They also said shelter inflation and services prices could also show some slowing.
Gas prices have continued trending downward in November, falling to $4 on Monday — although it’s still significantly higher than before the Iran war.

Even as the oil price surge takes a breather, it may not last long. Throughout the Iran war, countries that are members of the International Energy Agency have released 400 million barrels of crude and related products, such as diesel, into the global market. “Restocking those inventories will create a floor under prices once the current conflict in the Middle East has faded,” said Diane Swonk, chief economist at KPMG.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Given inflation’s overall stubbornness, economists believe the Federal Reserve will remain on track to hike rates for the second time this year. The Fed’s next two-day interest rate meeting will take place Dec. 8-9, right before the next inflation reading on Dec. 10.
Market odds for a December hike sat at 85% Monday afternoon.
“Still, details of Q4 data will be important for shifting inflation risks into 2027,” Citi economists wrote.
Bank of America economists agreed, predicting that the report would be “a cooler start to fall,” after multiple months of rising inflation.

Meanwhile, AI is also stoking inflation in other parts of the economy. In August, JPMorgan estimated that memory costs were on track to rise more than 400% from the end of 2024 through the end of 2026.

Tech companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on data centers and the equipment that fills those facilities, pushing memory prices higher. Those costs are being passed down to consumers. Consumer tech companies, including Apple, have raised their prices as a result.

title: Glycerin vs. hyaluronic acid: Which ingredient is best for winter?
summary: Glycerin and hyaluronic acid are both common ingredients in your favorite hydrating skin care — I asked a dermatologist to find out which works better for dry skin.
story: When it comes to dry skin, hyaluronic acid and glycerin are two ingredients you’ve probably come across in your favorite moisturizers, serums, cleansers and more. But what does each ingredient really do, and more importantly — which is best for dry skin? I spoke to Dr. Michele Green, a board-certified cosmetic dermatologist in New York City, to find out the differences, along with which of the two you should be reaching for during the winter season.
